chapters.title: A Royal Wedding and Old Grudges
paragraphs: The son of Surendra Singh, King of Naugarh, Virendra Singh, was married to Chandrakanta, the daughter of Maharaj Jay Singh of Vijaygarh. On the day of the wedding procession, owing to Tej Singh's final prank, Maharaj Shivdutt of Chunar was forced to become a torchbearer. Many were of the opinion that Maharaj Shivdutt's heart had not yet been cleansed of old grudges, and thus it would be prudent to keep him imprisoned. However, Maharaj Surendra Singh disapproved of this, saying, "We have already released Maharaj Shivdutt. The recent quarrel with Tej Singh cannot be taken as proof that he still harbors enmity towards us. After all, Maharaj Shivdutt is a Kshatriya; when Tej Singh, disguised as him, set out to disgrace him, how could he possibly endure such an insult? I cannot claim that Maharaj Shivdutt's heart is entirely free of resentment towards us, for if it were, what need would there have been for him to come in secret to witness these events? Even so, considering that his fight with Tej Singh cannot be deemed a result of our enmity, I shall release him once more. And if he still chooses to oppose us, what harm is there? He is a man, and so are we. We shall see what comes."

Maharaj Shivdutt, once released, disappeared—no one knew where he went. After Virendra Singh's wedding, with the consent of Maharaj Surendra Singh and Jay Singh, Chapla was married to Tej Singh, and Champa was married to Devi Singh. Champa was a distant relative of Chapla, being her sister.

The rest of the ayyars were already married. Their households were established in Chunar itself, and there was no need for any change, for soon after the weddings, with great pomp and celebration, Prince Virendra Singh was enthroned on the seat of Chunar and began to be called Raja instead of Prince. Tej Singh was appointed his chief minister, and thus all the ayyars were also required to remain in Chunar.

Surendra Singh did not wish to have his son out of his sight, so, reluctantly, he entrusted the throne of Naugarh to Fateh Singh and himself took up residence in Chunar. However, the affairs of state were entirely in Virendra Singh's hands, though Surendra Singh would occasionally offer his counsel. Along with Tej Singh, Jeet Singh too began to live freely in Chunar. There was great affection between Maharaj Surendra Singh and Jeet Singh, and this affection only grew with each passing day. In truth, Jeet Singh was worthy of all the esteem he received, and even that seemed insufficient.

Two years after their marriage, Chandrakanta bore a son. That same year, both Chapla and Champa also gave birth to sons. Three years later, Chandrakanta was blessed with a second son. Chandrakanta's elder son was named Indrajeet Singh, the younger Anand Singh; Chapla's son was called Bhairon Singh, and Champa's son was named Tara Singh.

When these four boys grew a little older and were able to converse, arrangements were made for their education and instruction. Raja Surendra Singh placed all four under the tutelage and protection of Jeet Singh.

Bhairon Singh and Tara Singh proved to be exceptionally clever and adept in the art of ayyari. Their skills were constantly put to the test. Jeet Singh's command was that Bhairon Singh and Tara Singh should attempt to deceive all the other ayyars—even their own fathers—and, in turn, Pannalal and the other ayyars would try to mislead the two boys. Gradually, the boys became so sharp and cunning that even Pannalal and his peers' ayyari paled before them.

As for which of the two—Bhairon Singh or Tara Singh—was the more cunning, there is no need to say; the time will come when it will become clear. It is worth mentioning, however, that Bhairon Singh was especially close to Indrajeet Singh, while Tara Singh was more attached to Anand Singh.

The four boys grew into capable young men: Indrajeet Singh, Bhairon Singh, and Tara Singh reached the age of eighteen, and Anand Singh was fifteen. All this while, peace prevailed in the kingdom of Chunar; the past troubles and the villainy of Maharaj Shivdutt lingered in everyone's hearts only as a distant dream.

Indrajeet Singh was very fond of hunting. Whenever possible, he would go hunting every day. One day, a forest guard came and reported that the beauty of a certain forest had greatly increased of late, and so many game animals had gathered there that even if one were to hunt for a whole month, the supply would not diminish, nor would a single day go empty. Hearing this, both brothers were delighted. They sought their father Raja Virendra Singh's permission to go hunting, saying, "We intend to stay in the forest for eight days to hunt."
In response, Raja Virendra Singh said, "I cannot grant you permission to stay in the forest and hunt for so many days—ask your grandfather; if he permits it, I have no objection."

Hearing this, Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh went to their grandfather, Maharaj Surendra Singh, and presented their request. He gladly approved and ordered that a tent be set up for both of them in the hunting grounds, and that as long as they remained there, five hundred soldiers should always accompany them.
Receiving permission to go hunting, Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh were overjoyed. Taking their two ayyars, Bhairon Singh and Tara Singh, along with five hundred soldiers, they set out from Chunar.

After traveling five kos south from Chunar, they reached a dense and fearsome forest and set up camp. Since only a little daylight remained, it was decided that they would rest today and make arrangements for the hunt the next morning. However, the banrakhas¹ were instructed that very day to locate a tiger. There was no need to tie a buffalo², as the tiger would be hunted on foot.

The next morning, the banrakhas appeared before them and reported that although there were tigers in the forest, due to the nightfall, they had not been able to see any with their own eyes. If the hunt was postponed for another day, they would be able to spot and track them. Thus, hunting was suspended for that day as well. With a quarter of the day remaining, Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh, mounted on their horses and accompanied by their two ayyars, left the camp to wander and amuse themselves, strolling far into the forest.
These men were strolling along, talking quietly, when suddenly, from the left, came the roar of a lion. At the sound, all four halted and turned to look in the direction from which it had come.

About two hundred yards away, they saw a sadhu riding atop a lion. His long, thick matted locks hung down his back; in one hand he held a trident, in the other a conch shell. The lion he rode was enormous, its mane trailing all the way to the ground.
Some eight or ten paces behind, another lion followed, but instead of a man, it bore a load on its back. Perhaps this baggage belonged to the very mahātma riding ahead.
Because dusk had fallen, the sadhu's features were not clearly visible, yet the sight filled the four with wonder, and many thoughts crossed their minds.
Indrajit Singh: "To ride about on a lion like that seems almost impossible."
Anand Singh: "He appears to be a great mahātma."
Bhairon Singh: "Look at the lion behind, carrying baggage on its back, head bowed like a sheep as it walks along."
Tara Singh: "He has brought these lions under his control."
Indrajit Singh: "I feel compelled to approach and pay my respects."
Anand Singh: "A good idea. Let's go closer and see what kind of lion it is."
Tara Singh: "Without going near, we cannot tell whether he is a true mahātma or an impostor."
Bhairon Singh: "It's already evening, but let's go ahead and intercept him."
Anand Singh: "I hope he won't take offense if we step forward to stop him."
Bhairon Singh: "It is the way of us ayyārs never to trust someone's claim to sainthood at first glance!"
Indrajit Singh: "You fellows are always so suspicious, your mustaches forever curled in skepticism. Well, let's go, then."
Bhairon Singh: "Let's go."

The four men circled ahead and stood before the babaji riding the lion. Seeing them approach, the babaji halted. At first, Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh's horses balked at the sight of the lions, but with some urging, they advanced. After going a little further, the two brothers dismounted, and Bhairon Singh and Tara Singh tied the horses to a tree. Then, all four approached the mahātma on foot.
Babaji (from a distance): "Come, Prince Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh! Tell me, are you well?"
Indrajit Singh (bowing): "By your grace, all is well."
Babaji (Looking at Bhairon Singh and Tara Singh): "Tell me, Bhairon and Tara, are you well?"
Both (Folding their hands): "By your grace!"

Babaji: "Prince, I was about to come to you myself, since you have set up camp in this jungle to hunt lions. I am on my way to Girnar, and wandering about, I happened to come into this forest as well. This jungle seems quite pleasant, so I intend to stay here for two or three days. I will find a suitable spot and set up my dhuni. I have several lions with me, laden with my riding gear and baggage, so I warn you—do not, by mistake, kill any of my lions, or there will be trouble. Hundreds of lions will descend and cause a commotion in your camp, and many lives will be lost. You are the sons of the mighty King Surendra Singh¹, so I thought it best to warn you beforehand, so that no harm may come to anyone."
Indrajit Singh: "Maharaj, how will I know which lion is yours? If that is the case, I will not hunt."
Babaji: "No, you may hunt, but do not kill my lions!"
Indrajit Singh: "But how will I know which lion belongs to you?"
Babaji: "Look, I will call my lions—recognize them."

Babaji blew his conch shell. The deep sound of the conch echoed through the forest, and from all sides came the sound of lions roaring. In a short while, five lions came running from different directions. These were all fierce and valiant beasts—had it been anyone else, they would have died of fright. The horses of Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh began to rear and prance at the sight of the lions, but, bound with strong silk reins, they could not flee. The lions created quite a commotion—roaring, leaping, and bounding at the sight of Indrajit Singh and the others, but at Babaji's stern command, they immediately quieted, lowered their heads, and stood meekly like sheep and goats.

Babaji: "Look, recognize these lions. There are still two or four more; it seems they did not hear the sound of the conch. No matter, I am still in this forest, and I will show you the rest as well—just refrain from hunting for a day."
Bhairon Singh: "Then where shall we meet you? Where will you set up your dhuni?"
Babaji: "This very spot seems pleasant to me. Come here tomorrow, and we shall meet."
Babaji dismounted from the lion, and all the lions that had gathered there began to circle around him, licking and sniffing him affectionately.
The four men, after lingering there for a little while longer, took leave of the Babaji and returned to their tent.

When silence fell, Bhairon Singh said to Indrajit Singh, "Many thoughts are swirling in my mind at this moment. I think the four of us should sit together, form a committee, and come to a firm decision."
Indrajit Singh replied, "Very well, call Anand and Tara here as well."

Bhairon Singh went and brought Anand Singh and Tara Singh to the same spot. At that time, except for these four, there was no one else in the tent. Bhairon Singh spoke his mind, and everyone listened with great attention. Afterward, they held their council for about a quarter of the night and decided what must be done.

What kind of council this was, what Bhairon Singh intended, what decision they reached, and what they did throughout the night—there is no need to recount these things now; all will be revealed in due time.

At dawn, the four men emerged from the tent and, after summoning Kanchan Singh, the commander of their army, and giving him some instructions, set off toward the Babaji. When they had gone some distance from the camp, Anand Singh, Bhairon Singh, and Tara Singh hastened toward Chunar, while Indrajit Singh went alone to meet the Babaji.
Babaji sat amidst the lions, tending his sacred fire. Two lions circled around him, keeping watch. Indrajit Singh arrived, bowed in greeting, and Babaji, bestowing his blessing, invited him to sit.
Today, Indrajit Singh saw two more lions than he had the previous day. After a brief silence, conversation began.
Babaji said, "Tell me, Indrajit Singh, where have your brothers and the ayyaars gone? Why did they not come?"
Indrajit Singh replied, "Our younger brother Anand Singh has taken ill with a fever, so he could not come. I have left both ayyaars to care for him and have come alone to seek your audience."
Babaji said, "No matter, he will be well by this evening. Tell me, is all well in your kingdom these days?"
Indrajit Singh replied, "By your grace, all is well and joyful."

Babaji said, "Poor Virendra Singh has suffered greatly! Still, his name will be remembered in this world. In these thousand years, there has not been a king who has broken a tilism. There is yet another tilism—truly, that one is greater and more worthy of praise."
Indrajit Singh said, "Father says that tilism will be broken by your hand."
Bawaji: "Yes, so it shall be. Surely, victory will come by your hand; there is no doubt about it."
Indrajit Singh: "Let us see how long it takes. There is still no sign of the key to that tilism."

Bawaji: "If God wills, within a day or two you will begin to break that tilism. I am the key to that tilism. For many generations, our family has served as the wardens of that tilism. My great-grandfather, grandfather, and father were all wardens of that tilism. When my father was on his deathbed, he entrusted the key to me and appointed me as its warden. Now the time has come for me to hand over the key to you, for that tilism was bound in your name, and no one but you can become its master."
Indrajit Singh: "Then why delay any further?"
Bawaji: "Nothing remains. From tomorrow, you may begin to break it. But there is one thing I must say for your benefit."
Indrajit Singh: "What is that?"
Bawaji: "You should include your brother Anand in breaking the tilism. By doing so, you will gain double the wealth, and both your names will be remembered in the world forever."
Indrajit Singh: "But he is not well!"

Bawaji: "What harm is there in that? Go now, and bring him to me as best you can. I will cure him in no time. Come with me today itself, so that tomorrow you may begin breaking the tilism. Otherwise, you may not get another chance for a whole year."
Indrajit Singh: "Bawaji, the truth is, I do not wish for my brother's advancement. I do not want his name to be joined with mine."
Bawaji: "No, no, you should not think that way. In this world, there is no jewel greater than a brother."

Indrajit Singh: "Yes, in this world, there is no jewel greater than a brother, but there is no greater enemy than a brother either. This thought has so settled in my heart that even if Brahma himself were to come and try to persuade me, nothing would change."
Bawaji: "Without him by your side, you cannot break the tilism."
Indrajit Singh (Folding his hands): "Then let it be. Forgive me, I have no need to break the tilism!"
Bawaji: "Are you truly so obstinate?"
Indrajit Singh: "I have already said, even Brahma cannot change my mind."
Bawaji: "Very well, then you alone shall come, but you must come at once."
Indrajit Singh: "Yes, yes, I am ready. Let us go immediately."

At that very moment, Babaji stood up. He bundled up his belongings and loaded them onto one of the lions, then mounted another himself. After this, he looked at one of the lions and said, "Baccha Gangaram, come here!" That lion immediately came to him. Babaji said to Indrajit Singh, "You mount this one." Indrajit Singh leapt up and mounted the lion, and together with Babaji, they set off towards the south. The other lions, some ahead, some behind, some to the left, some to the right, began to accompany Babaji as well.

All the lions eventually fell behind, except for the two on which Babaji and Indrajit Singh were riding; these two surged ahead. They continued on until noon. As the day began to wane, Babaji said to Indrajit Singh, "We should stop here and have something to eat and drink." In response, the prince said, "Babaji, there is no need for food or drink. You are a holy man, and I myself feel no hunger. Then what is the need to delay? When one is engaged in a task, it is not right to be sluggish!"
Babaji said, "Well done, you are very brave. If your heart were not so strong, the elders would not have said that the tilism would be broken by your hand. Very well, let us go on."

After some time, they reached the foot of a mountain. Babaji blew a conch shell, and in a short while, hundreds of mountain bandits, armed with spears, could be seen approaching from all sides. At the same time, from the east, Raja Shivdutt appeared, accompanied by twenty or twenty-five men. As soon as Indrajit Singh saw him, he called out in a loud voice, "I recognize him! This is Maharaj Shivdutt. His portrait hangs in my room. Grandfather showed me his portrait and said, 'This Maharaj Shivdutt is our greatest enemy.' Ah, so Babaji has indeed turned out to be an ayyār, just as I suspected! Well, no matter. Arresting Indrajit Singh is no easy task!"
Shivdutt (coming closer): "Half my heart is cooled, but alas, both you brothers have not been captured."
Indrajit Singh: "Do not rely on the thought that you have ensnared Indrajit Singh. Even casting an evil glance at him is a very dangerous thing!"
Gandhakarta: "Is there any doubt about that?"
chapters.summary: Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh venture into the forest for a hunt, only to encounter a mysterious sadhu riding a lion, leading to unexpected danger.

chapters.title: Shivdutt’s Retreat to the Forest
paragraphs: At this point, it seems appropriate to give a brief account of Maharaj Shivdutt as well. In every way, Maharaj Shivdutt was forced to accept defeat at the hands of Kunwar Virendra Singh. Helpless, he left the city and, gathering several of his old loyalists...
headed south from Chunar.

Not far to the south of Chunar lies a vast, dense forest. This stretch of the Vindhya mountain forest extends through Robertsganj, Sarguja, and Singrauli, running for hundreds of kos, filled with towering mountains, valleys, passes, and caves. Here and there, at intervals of two or four kos, villages are settled. In some places, the ruins of grand old forts from ancient times can still be seen atop the hills. Eight or ten kos south of Chunar, near Ahraura, the remnants of an ancient ruined fort on a mountain still stir the heart upon viewing. Upon close inspection, it becomes clear that when this fort was intact, it must have covered more than three kos of land. In its final days, this fort belonged to the famous King Chet Singh of Kashi.

It was in these forests, wandering with his queen and several loyal followers along with their wives and children, that Maharaj Shivdutt, about fifty kos from Chunar, took shelter atop a lush, green, secluded hill in the ruins of a strong old fort. He named it Shivduttgarh. Even at that time, several rooms and halls in the fort were still fit for habitation. This small hill, nestled and concealed among the surrounding high mountains, was so hidden and pressed in that it was difficult for anyone to reach or discover it unexpectedly.

At this time, Maharaj Shivdutt had only twenty men with him, among whom were three Muslim ayyars, who were perhaps relatives of Nazim and Ahmad. They had joined Maharaj Shivdutt, thinking that by staying with him, they would someday get a chance to take revenge on Raja Virendra Singh. Besides Shivdutt, there was no one else who seemed fit to keep these rogues as ayyars in his service. The three ayyars were known by the following names: Bakar Ali, Khudabakhsh, and Yar Ali. All these ayyars and companions, to the best of their ability, also helped Maharaj Shivdutt with money and resources.

Shivdutt's heart remained bitter toward Raja Virendra Singh, but for lack of opportunity, he was forced to remain quiet for a long time. Through his cunning and intelligence, he became the king of the local hill tribes—Bhil, Kharwar, and others—and began collecting grain, ghee, honey, and many other wild products as tribute, sending them to the city for sale through these very people, and thus amassing wealth. By training these people, he also managed to raise a small army. Gradually, these hill tribesmen became shrewd themselves and began to go to the city to sell grain and other goods, gathering money on their own. Shivduttgarh too became well-inhabited and prosperous.

Meanwhile, Bakar Ali and the other ayyars trained some of their companions, who had come with them from Chunar, thoroughly in the art of ayyari. During this time, a son and later a daughter were born to Maharaj Shivdutt. Seizing the opportunity, he took many of his men and ayyars with him and ventured out of Shivduttgarh.

For several months, Maharaj Shivdutt wandered, consumed by thoughts of taking revenge on Raja Virendra Singh. Now, having written this brief account of Maharaj Shivdutt, we bring this narration to a close and turn once again to the tale of Indrajit Singh.

After Indrajit Singh was captured, those artificial lions too changed their appearance and revealed themselves as real ayyars, among whom Yar Ali, Bakar Ali, and Khudabakhsh were chief. Maharaj Shivdutt was overjoyed and thought, "Now my time has come again. If God wills, I shall once more ascend the throne of Chunar and take full revenge on my enemies."

He took Indrajit Singh prisoner and brought him to Shivduttgarh. Everyone was astonished that Prince Indrajit Singh, at the time of his capture, caused no disturbance, showed no anger, raised no weapon against anyone. Indeed, he did not even let sorrow, regret, or wrath show in his eyes. In truth, it was a matter of wonder that the lion-hearted son of the brave Virendra Singh should remain silent in such a situation and submit to chains without protest. But no, there must be some reason for this, which will become clear as the story unfolds.
chapters.summary: Fleeing defeat, Maharaj Shivdutt establishes a hidden fortress and plots revenge against Virendra Singh, training an army and biding his time for the perfect opportunity.

chapters.title: The Disguise and the Deception
paragraphs: Within a chamber of the Chunar Fort, Maharaj Surendra Singh, Virendra Singh, Jeet Singh, Tej Singh, Devi Singh, Indrajit Singh, and Anand Singh were seated, engaged in conversation.
Jeet Singh said, "Bhairon acted with great cleverness, disguising himself as Indrajit Singh and allowing himself to fall into the hands of Shivdutt's ayyars."
Surendra Singh replied, "Shivdutt's ayyars were cunning indeed, but…"
Virendra Singh added, "Babaji may have become a siddha riding a lion, but he could not accomplish his true purpose."
Indrajit Singh said, "Be that as it may, Bhairon Singh must be rescued very soon."

Jeet Singh reassured him, "Prince, do not worry. Your friend will not suffer any harm, but for now, it is best that he remains in Shivdutt's custody. He is no fool—he can escape on his own without assistance. Still, Pannalal, Ramnarayan, Chunnilal, Badrinath, and Jyotishiji have already been sent to aid him. Let us see what happens! After lying low for so many days, Shivdutt has once again girded himself to bring about his own ruin."
Devi Singh asked, "What orders are there now for the army that accompanied the princes to the hunting grounds?"
Jeet Singh replied, "For now, it is not advisable to break camp at the hunting grounds." (Tej Singh's…
Looking in that direction) Why so urgent?
Tej Singh (folding his hands): "Yes, sir. If we keep our camp in the hunting grounds, we'll be able to carry out our work with great ease and amusement."
Surendra Singh: "If any ayyār returns from Shivdattgarh, we might learn some news."
Tej Singh: "Not tomorrow, but by the day after, someone will surely come."

The conversation continued for more than a quarter of a watch. We do not find it appropriate to reveal the entire discussion, especially since even we could not ascertain the final matter that Jeet Singh explained to Tej Singh in private after the assembly dispersed. Well, let it be; whatever is to happen will be seen in due time—what's the hurry?

On the banks of the Ganga, in a lofty barahdari, the two brothers, Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh, sat observing the state of the waters. It was the rainy season; the Ganga was greatly swollen, the water had reached the base of the fort, and small waves were striking against the walls. The ruddy glow of the setting sun fell upon the water, doubling the beauty of the rippling waves. Silence reigned; in this barahdari, besides these two brothers, not a third soul was to be seen.
Indrajit Singh: "The water will rise a little more yet."
Anand Singh: "Yes, last year the Ganga was much higher than this, when Grandfather told us to swim across."
Indrajit Singh: "That day was quite an adventure. Bhairon Singh outpaced everyone; Badrinath tried his utmost to get ahead of him, but could not."
Anand Singh: "We both kept pace with the boat that accompanied us for our safety, for nearly a kos."
Indrajit Singh: "That was our last test. Since then, we've had no occasion to swim in the river."
Anand Singh: "Yesterday, I told Grandfather that the Ganga is very high these days, and I feel like swimming."
Indrajit Singh: "And what did he say?"

Anand Singh: "He said, "Enough, now it's not proper for you to swim; it would be laughable. Swimming is a skill in which you are already proficient. What need is there now? If you wish, take a boat and go for a ride."
Indrajit Singh: "He spoke very rightly. Come, let's take a boat and go for a little excursion."
As they were talking, the attendant arrived and announced, "An old jeweler is here and wishes to have an audience."
Anand Singh: "What sort of time is this?"

Attendant (folding his hands): "I had intended to send him away at this hour, but refrained, thinking that since his youth he has been a loyal servant of this court, and His Majesty also keeps a special eye on him. Moreover—"

He is an old man of eighty years, and thirdly, he says that he has just arrived in this city. He has already had an audience with the Maharaj, and now, after seeing Your Highness as well, he will settle comfortably at the inn—this has always been his custom.
Indrajit Singh: If that is so, then it is proper to let him come.
Anand Singh: Now, I do not feel in the mood for a boat ride today.
Indrajit Singh: What does it matter? Tomorrow will do.

The attendant saluted and left, and after a short while, returned with the merchant. In truth, the merchant was very old; dignity and nobility radiated from his face. Upon entering, he saluted and presented both brothers with two rings. After they accepted the rings, and at a gesture from them, he sat down on the floor.

The old jeweler was treated with honor; they inquired after his health and the circumstances of his journey. Then, he was ordered to go to his quarters and rest, and to present himself again the next day. The merchant saluted and departed.

Of the two rings the merchant had presented to the brothers, Anand Singh's ring was set with an exceedingly beautiful ruby, while Indrajit Singh's ring bore only a small portrait. The next day, Indrajit Singh glanced at it again and, lost in thought, remained silent.

When alone at night, by the light of the candelabrum, he examined the ring again—the one in which, instead of a gem, was set the portrait of a young woman. Though the portrait was very small, the artist had lavished astonishing skill upon it. As he gazed at it, Indrajit Singh became so absorbed that he forgot himself and the image; it seemed as if that delicate beauty sat before him in person, and he longed to speak to her, but, awed by her radiance, remained silent. Suddenly, he started and reproached himself for his foolishness, but what use was that? In a single instant, the portrait had swept away the innocence of his boyhood and set before him the fevered vision of youth. A little while ago, his mind had been occupied with the intricate rules of riding, hunting, and exercise; now he was entangled in a different dilemma, his thoughts plunging into the mystery of having found such a unique jewel. What new tricks would Maharaj Shivdutt's spies attempt? How and when would Bhairon Singh be released from captivity? What would Badrinath and the others do upon reaching Shivduttgarh? When would the chance to go hunting arise again? When would the opportunity come to bring down a tiger with a single arrow? When would he next ride a boat and sail upon the river? All these thoughts vanished.

Now, only one concern filled his mind: How had the merchant come by this ring? Was the portrait imaginary, or did it truly belong to someone who existed in this world? Could the merchant know her whereabouts? Was this the very limit of beauty, or was there more? Was this the treasury of delicacy, grace, and refinement?
Or someone else? In the river of his love, how will my boat ever reach the other shore?

Today, Prince Indrajit Singh learned the art of making excuses, and within an hour, he became a master at it. His stomach felt bloated—he would not eat; his head ached—he found everyone's words unpleasant; perhaps, if there were silence, he might be able to sleep—such were the excuses by which he saved himself. The whole night he tossed and turned on his cot, passing the hours in anxious thought, waiting for morning so he could summon the jeweler and question him.
At dawn, he ordered the jeweler to be brought before him, but after an hour, the chamberlain returned and reported that there was no trace of the merchant at the inn.
Indrajit Singh: "Where did he say he would be staying?"
Chamberlain: "Your servant only heard from his own lips that he would lodge at the inn, but upon inquiring there, it was found that no such merchant had arrived."
Indrajit Singh: "Perhaps he stayed somewhere else. Find out."

"Very well," said the chamberlain, and departed, leaving Indrajit Singh troubled. He lowered his head in thought, when the sound of approaching footsteps startled him. He looked up and saw Prince Anand Singh.
Anand Singh: "It's time for your bath."
Indrajit Singh: "Yes, I am a little late today."
Anand Singh: "You seem a bit out of sorts?"
Indrajit Singh: "I had a headache all night."
Anand Singh: "How is it now?"
Indrajit Singh: "It's better now."
Anand Singh: "Yesterday, I caught a glimpse—was there a picture set in that ring the jeweler examined?"
Indrajit Singh: "Yes, there was."
Anand Singh: "What kind of picture?"
Indrajit Singh: "I don't know where I put that ring—it's nowhere to be found. I meant to examine it closely in the daylight, but…"
Author: Truly, I can vouch for this myself!

If not for the fear of revealing the secret, Prince Indrajit Singh would have done nothing all day but sigh deeply and exclaim "Oh!" But what could he do? Out of helplessness, he had to perform all his usual duties and even sit with his grandfather for meals. Yet by evening, his restlessness had greatly increased when he learned that, despite searching the entire city, there was still no trace of the jeweler. It was also discovered that the jeweler had lied outright when he claimed to have met the Maharaj and said, "Once I have an audience with the prince, I will settle comfortably at the inn." In truth, he had not met Maharaj Surendra Singh or Virendra Singh at all.
On the third day, seeing Indrajit Singh so despondent, Anand Singh suggested they take a ride on the boat.
They insisted on taking a trip on the Ganga for amusement and to lighten their hearts, and at last, their wish had to be granted.

Indrajit Singh desired that, aboard a small, beautiful, and swift boat, no one else should accompany them—only the two brothers would ride and row along the river for their pleasure. Who would dare contradict their wishes? Yet, an old servant, who had once cradled Virendra Singh in his arms and now remained ever at their side, forbade them from doing so. When the brothers would not heed his warning, the old servant himself boarded the boat. Out of respect for his long service, the brothers said nothing, and were compelled to take him along.
Anand Singh: "Take the boat out into the current and let it drift. Later, we'll row it back."
Indrajit Singh: "Very well."
There were but two hours of daylight left when the brothers set out on their river excursion, for they wished also to enjoy the moonlit night on their return.

Two kos west of Chunar, on the banks of the Ganga, there was a small forest. As the boat neared it, the sound of a flute, accompanied by a fine, melodious singing, reached their ears. Music is such a thing that it draws every heart to itself, no matter how unfeeling or ignorant one may be; even animals, bewitched by it, forget themselves. For the past two or three days, Prince Indrajit Singh's heart had been restless; far from enjoying the beauty of the river, he had not even been aware of his own body. He sat, head bowed, lost in thoughts of his beloved's image, oblivious to all around him. But this sweet, melodious voice turned his head, compelling him to look toward its source.
Looking toward the shore, it was impossible to discern who played the flute or sang, but it was clear that those enchanting voices were not far off—their song cast a spell upon all who heard it.
Indrajit Singh: "Ah! What a melodious voice!"
Anand Singh: "There's another voice as well. Surely, several women are singing and playing together."
Indrajit Singh: (Turning the boat toward the shore) "Strange that they have chosen such a place for their music and merriment. We should see for ourselves."
Anand Singh: "Why not? Let us go."

The old servant tried to dissuade them from landing the boat and going ashore, pleading with them at length, but the brothers would not listen. They brought the boat to shore, disembarked, and set off in the direction from which the music came. After walking only a short distance into the forest, they saw ten or fifteen...

A group of young women came into view, who, adorned in colorful garments and precious jewelry, had doubled their beauty as they swung a swing hanging from a tall tree. Some played the flute, some the mridang, while others clapped their hands in rhythm and sang. Upon that swing, only one woman sat, facing towards the Ganga. It seemed as though fairies themselves were swinging a celestial maiden, singing and playing music to please her so that she might be granted the boon of ever-increasing beauty and everlasting youth. But no, even their hearts' desires remained unfulfilled, and upon seeing Kunwar Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh approaching, for some unknown reason, all the women—save the lovely one seated on the swing—fled at once.
Anand Singh said, "Brother, they have all run away!"
Indrajit Singh replied, "Yes. I shall go to the swing; you see where those women have gone."
Anand Singh answered, "Very well."

Whatever the case, Kunwar Indrajit Singh had recognized the one who remained alone upon the swing. And why would he not? He had already seen her portrait on the ring given by the jeweler, her image was engraved upon his heart, and now, at last, he had attained his heart's desire—she for whom he was willing to risk his very life, he had found her without effort. What more could he wish for?

Anand Singh went to search for the women, but they had fled so swiftly that not even a glimpse of them could be seen. Helpless, after half an hour of fruitless searching, he returned to the swing, but not only was the woman gone, even his brother was nowhere to be found. Distressed, he began to search here and there, calling out, until night fell. Thinking perhaps they had returned to the boat, he made his way there, but found no one except the old attendant. His heart grew restless. After telling the attendant everything, he said, "I shall not return home until I find my beloved brother. You go and inform everyone of what has happened here."

The attendant tried in every way to persuade Anand Singh to return home, but to no avail. Helpless, he left the boat at that very place and, weeping and lamenting, set out on foot towards the fort, for he deemed it necessary to inform Raja Virendra Singh of all that had transpired here.
chapters.summary: Indrajit Singh receives a mysterious ring with a woman's portrait, sparking an obsessive quest that leads him to her on the banks of the Ganga.

chapters.title: The Disappearance of Indrajit Singh
paragraphs: The attendant reached the fort and, upon learning that both were sitting together at that moment, went before Maharaj Surendra Singh and Virendra Singh to report the disappearance of Kunwar Indrajit Singh and the circumstances, just as Kunwar Anand Singh had recounted.

They submitted the report. Upon hearing this news, both of their hearts felt as if struck by a blow. For a while, due to anxiety, they could not think what ought to be done. The night had already passed beyond the first watch. At last, Surendrasingh summoned Jeetsingh, Tejsingh, and Devisingh, and recounted to them what the servant had reported, then asked what should be done now.
Tejsingh: "It is not without reason that so many women gathered in that jungle, singing and playing music, and then deceiving us in this manner."
Surendrasingh: "Ever since I heard of Shivdatt's resurgence, a constant unease has lingered in my heart. I believe this too is one of his devilish schemes."
Virendrasingh: "But both the boys are not so weak that anyone could capture them at will."
Surendrasingh: "That is true, but it is still unfortunate that Anand Singh remained there as well."

Tejsingh: "The poor servant was forced to accompany them; otherwise, we would not even have known where the two had gone. Well, whatever must be decided regarding them, think on it, but grant me leave quickly so that I may take a thousand soldiers and go there at once, surround that small jungle from all sides, and then let us see what comes of it."
Surendrasingh: (to Jeetsingh) "What do you think?"
Jeetsingh: "Tej speaks rightly; he should go at once."

Receiving the order, Tejsingh climbed the turret above the audience hall, where a large kettledrum and a heavy mallet were kept for such emergencies—so that, should the need arise to assemble the army at once, the mallet could be struck upon the drum. Its sound was unique, unlike any other kettledrum, and Tejsingh had also devised several signals for its use.

Tejsingh picked up the mallet and struck the drum forcefully once, its sound echoing throughout the city and even far beyond. Though the townsfolk might not have understood the reason, the commander-in-chief grasped at once that a thousand soldiers were needed immediately, and he arranged for them with great speed.
Tejsingh, fully equipped, left the fort, and, taking a thousand soldiers and many torchbearers, set out toward that small jungle, reaching it very quickly.

He stationed guards at intervals and surrounded the jungle from all sides. Indrajitsingh had already vanished, and many efforts were made to find Anand Singh, but he too could not be found. The night was spent in these endeavors. At dawn, Tejsingh ordered that the jungle be cut down swiftly from one side, so that by day's end the entire forest would be cleared.
At that very moment, Maharaj Surendrasingh and Jeetsingh also arrived there. They approved of cutting down the jungle and said, "It will be very good if we all—"
Let us become completely free from worry about the jungle."

How long could it possibly take to clear this small forest? Due to the king's vigilance, there was not a single person to be seen here who was not engaged in cutting down the trees. By midday, the jungle had been cleared away, but no trace of anyone was found. In fact, just as with Indrajit Singh, it had to be concluded that Anand Singh too had disappeared. However, at the edge of this forest, the body of a young, beautiful woman, adorned with exquisite and priceless jewelry and garments, was found—her head missing.

This corpse was brought before Maharaj Surendra Singh. Now everyone's anxiety increased, and all sorts of thoughts began to arise. Helpless, they returned toward the city, taking the body with them. Jeet Singh said, "We will go and send Tara Singh to summon all the ayyars who had gone in search of Shivdutt, and send them to look for Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh. But you, go at once wherever your heart guides you, in search of them."
Tej Singh was already prepared with his equipment. He saluted and immediately set off in one direction, while the Maharaj, wiping his eyes with a handkerchief, departed for Chunar.

Saddened and grieving the separation from his grandsons, Maharaj Surendra Singh returned home. Chandrakanta too heard the news of both young men's disappearance. Poor girl, she had come to understand the joys and sorrows of the world all too well, so she could only suppress her anguish. She did not wish to weep and wail openly, but by restraining herself, her delicate heart suffered an even greater blow—her appearance changed within moments. How much Chapla and Champa loved Chandrakanta, you all know well; there is no need to write it. The grief of the two young men's disappearance struck these two even more deeply than it did Chandrakanta, and both resolved that, when the opportunity arose, they would try to find out what had happened to Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh.

Hearing of Maharaj Surendra Singh's arrival, Virendra Singh went to meet him. Dev Singh was also present there. In Virendra Singh's presence, the Maharaj recounted everything to Dev Singh and asked, "Now what should be done?"
Dev Singh: "First, I would like to see the body that was found in the forest."
Surendra Singh: "Yes, you must see it."
Jeet Singh (to the attendant): "Tell them to bring here the body that was found in the forest."

"Very well," said the attendant, and went outside, but soon returned and said, "On the way here with the Maharaj, somehow that body disappeared. Several men are searching for it in distress, but it cannot be found!"
Virendra Singh: "Now the time has come for us to be vigilant once again."
When the corpse disappeared from among thousands of people, it became clear that much more trouble was yet to come.
Jeetsingh: "I had thought that whatever little life remains would now pass in peace, but no—no one should ever hold such hopes."
Surendra Singh: "Well, whatever will happen, we shall see. For now, think about what is best to do at this moment."

Jeetsingh: "My thought was to send Tarasingh to Badrinath and the others, so that they might free Bhaironsingh and not get entangled in any other affair, and come straight here. But even so, my heart does not wish to do this. For today, let us wait and be patient; after careful thought, I will give my opinion tomorrow."
chapters.summary: Upon Indrajit Singh's mysterious disappearance and the discovery of a headless corpse, Maharaj Surendra Singh, Jeetsingh.

chapters.title: The Rescue Mission to Shivdattgarh
paragraphs: Pandit Badrinath, Pannalal, Ramnarayan, Chunnilal, and Jagannath Jyotishi set out towards Shivdattgarh to rescue Bhaironsingh Aiyar. According to orders, Commander Kanchansingh had sent spies after the lion-clad Babaji and had discovered that Bhaironsingh Aiyar had been taken inside the fort of Shivdattgarh. Therefore, there was no need to search for these Aiyars; they went straight to Shivdattgarh and, changing their appearances, began to roam about the city. The five of them parted ways, but had agreed that after wandering about, they would all gather at a certain place.

After spending the day searching for Bhaironsingh, all the Aiyars gathered on a hill outside the city, and spent the night in counsel, forming a plan. The next day, they again entered Shivdattgarh, each in a different disguise. Ramnarayan and Chunnilal took on the appearance of the local palace guards and went to the place where Bhaironsingh was imprisoned. Having been in captivity for several days, Bhaironsingh had revealed his true identity, and in his real form, he was locked in a cell with iron bars on three sides. Next to his cell was another of the same kind, in which an old warden sat on a cushion, and several soldiers, naked swords in hand, patrolled back and forth on guard.
Ramnarayan and Chunnilal went and stood at the door of the cell and began to converse with the old warden.
Ramnarayan: "The Maharaj has summoned you."
Old Warden: "Why, what is the matter? Come inside, sit, let us go."
Ramnarayan and Chunnilal entered the cell and said—
Ramnarayan: "I do not know why you have been called, but the order is to bring you quickly."
Old Man: "It hasn't even been an hour since someone came and said that the Maharaj himself was about to come. Was that a lie?"
Ramnarayan: "Yes, the Maharaj was about to come, but now he will not."
Old Man: "Very well, you two sit right here and guard the prisoner. I am going."
Ramnarayan: "Very well."

After seating Ramnarayan and Chunnilal inside the cell, the old jailor stepped outside and, with cunning, quickly shut the door of the cell and called out from outside, "Greetings! I have recognized you both as ayyars! Now tell me, are you not trapped in our prison? How cleverly I found out! I asked, 'It was just learned that the Maharaj himself was coming,' and you immediately admitted, 'Yes, he was about to come, but now he will not.' You did not realize I was deceiving you. Is this the cleverness with which you practice ayyari? Well, now you can enjoy the air of this prison, and know that I, Baqar Ali Ayyar, have been placed here precisely to teach people like you a lesson."

Hearing the old man's words, Ramnarayan and Chunnilal fell silent, lowering their heads in shame. The old jailor left the place and went to Shivdutt, reporting the capture of these two ayyars. The Maharaj, pleased, rewarded Baqar Ali and, in his happiness, came himself to see Ramnarayan and Chunnilal.
Badrinath, Pannalal, and Jyotishiji also learned that two of their companions had been captured. Now, instead of rescuing one, they had to think of freeing three men.

Late at night, as these three ayyars were wandering and heading toward the outskirts of the city, a man, his body wrapped and hidden in black cloth, came running up behind them. He threw a small folded paper in front of them and, gesturing with his hand for them to follow, hurried ahead.

Badrinath picked up the slip and, by the light of a burning lamp at a shop on the roadside, read it. Only one word was written—"Bhaironsingh." Badrinath understood that Bhaironsingh had escaped by some trick and that it was he who had just passed. Badrinath also recognized Bhaironsingh's handwriting.
After tossing the slip, Bhaironsingh had signaled for the three to follow and, after moving ten or twelve steps ahead, now waited for them to catch up.

Badrinath and the others, delighted, moved forward and reached the spot where Bhaironsingh, his body concealed in black cloth, stood hidden by the roadside. There was no opportunity for conversation; Bhaironsingh led the way, with Badrinath, Pannalal, and Jyotishiji following behind.
They quickly walked out of the city.

The night was dark. Out in the open field, Bhaironsingh removed his black cloth disguise. In the moonlight, the three recognized Bhaironsingh—overjoyed, each of them embraced him in turn, and then they all sat down upon a stone slab to talk.
Badrinath: "Bhaironsingh, seeing you at this moment has gladdened my heart!"
Bhaironsingh: "I managed to escape somehow, but Ramnarayan and Chunnilal have gotten themselves into quite a fix."
Jyotishi: "Did they fall into the same trap as you?"
Bhaironsingh: "I am also thinking of rescuing them."
Pannalal: "How so?"
Bhaironsingh: "Well, we have the whole night to talk about everything, but right now I am terribly hungry. If you have anything, please give me something to eat."
Badrinath: "There are a few peda sweets—if you wish, you can eat them."
Bhaironsingh: "What good are just a few pedas? Anyway, at least there should be some arrangement for water."
Badrinath: "Then what should we do?"

Bhaironsingh (gesturing with his hand): "Look there, do you see that lamp burning at the edge of the city? We just saw it—it's a sweet-seller's shop, and he is making fresh puris right now. We can get water from him as well."
Pannalal: "Alright, I'll go."
Bhaironsingh: "We should all go together—it's better for everyone to stay together. What if you get caught and we are left waiting for you?"
Pannalal: "Getting caught—is this a game?"
Bhaironsingh: "Well, what harm is there if we all go together? Three of us can stand aside, and one can go forward to make the purchase."
Badrinath: "Yes, yes, that's best. Let's all go together."

The four ayyaars set off together and reached the sweet-seller, whose solitary shop stood at the city's edge. Badrinath, Jyotishiji, and Bhaironsingh lingered a little way off, while Pannalal went to the shop to buy provisions. Before he went, Bhaironsingh said, "Be sure to make the sweet-seller promise to give you water in an earthen vessel first, otherwise he'll argue about it later."
Pannalal went to the sweet-seller's shop and asked for two seers of puris and a seer of sweets. The sweet-seller himself asked, "Do you need water as well?"
Pannalal: "Yes, yes, you must give us water."
Sweet-seller: "Do you have a vessel?"
Pannalal: "There is a vessel, but it is small. You yourself pour water into some earthen pot."
Halwai: "For a whole pitcher of water, you'll have to pay eight annas more."
Pannalal: "Such extortion! Well, we'll pay."
chapters.summary: After Bhaironsingh escapes imprisonment and reunites with his friends, he suggests a late-night trip to a sweet shop, which might lead to more trouble.

chapters.title: Ayyars Pursued in the Wild
paragraphs: Taking the puris, sweets, and a pitcher of water, the four ayyars set off from there, but none of them knew that a little distance behind, the halwai was stealthily following them with two men. In the open field, the four sat upon a large stone slab, ate their meal, drank water, and after washing their hands and faces, sat back, content, and began to converse quietly among themselves. Barely half an hour had passed when all four fell unconscious and lay sprawled upon the rock. At that very moment, the halwai, accompanied by his two men, appeared over their heads.

The two men who had come with the halwai quickly bound Badrinath, Jyotishiji, and Pannalal, and, after making Bhaironsingh smell something to revive him, said, "Well done, Ajay Singh! Your cunning has served us well! Now all five of those worthless fellows who came to Shivdattgarh are in our hands! Of all, you have earned the greatest reward from the Maharaj!"

After enduring many hardships, Maharaj Surendra Singh and Virendra Singh, and thanks to them, Chandrakanta, Chanla, Champa, Tejsingh, and Devisingh, and others, enjoyed days of great happiness for a while—but those days are gone now. Indeed, joy and sorrow keep changing places. The days of happiness passed in the blink of an eye, so quickly that I found nothing worth writing about them. But now, the hours of misfortune drag on endlessly for these people. Who could have known that the fallen Shivdatt would rise again like a calamity? Who could have guessed that the two promising sons, raised in the lap of poor Chandrakanta, would be separated from her in such a way? Who could have said for certain that as much as their dynasty and kingdom advanced, just as suddenly, even greater calamities would befall them? Well, they endured the days of happiness—now, who will bear the hour of misfortune? Yes, poor Jagannath Jyotishi did say this much: that Virendra Singh's kingdom and lineage would flourish greatly, but always with adversity. Well, what will happen next remains to be seen, but for now, all are caught up in their troubles. See, in his private chamber, Maharaj Surendra Singh sits deep in worry, and to his left, pressing the corner of the throne, Raja Virendra Singh gazes anxiously at Jeet Singh, who sits before him. Both father and son—Devisingh and Tarasingh—sit nearby, on the upper dais, leaning toward the elder and revered Jeet Singh, waiting in hope to see what his final...

What is the command? Except for these people, there is no one else in this room; a deep silence prevails. Who knows what discussions have already taken place before this, but at this moment, Maharaj Surendra Singh broke the silence only by saying, "Well, we should accept what Champa and Chapla have suggested."
Jeet Singh: "As you wish, but what is your command regarding Devi Singh?"
Surendra Singh: "Nothing else, only this concern: how will Chunar be protected at such a time?"
Jeet Singh: "I believe Tara is quite sufficient for the defense here, and if the need arises, even in my old age, I will do whatever I can."
Surendra Singh (smiling slightly and looking at Jeet Singh with hopeful eyes): "Well, do as you think best."
Jeet Singh (to Devi Singh): "Here you are, sir, now you too are given a chance to make up for old shortcomings. Let us see what you do. May God grant you success in this endeavor."
As soon as Devi Singh heard this, he stood up, saluted, and left the room.
chapters.summary: Devi Singh receives a chance to redeem himself amidst rising tensions and whispered strategies, as Maharaj Surendra Singh grapples with Chunar's defense and uncertain futures.

chapters.title: Anand’s Search and the Vanishing Women
paragraphs: Tormented by separation from his brother Indrajeet Singh, Anand Singh left the jungle at that very moment and, standing in the open field, began to look around. To the west, he saw two women riding horses, moving slowly. He hastened in that direction, and in hopes of catching up to them, followed them for two kos, but his hope was not fulfilled. For, as soon as they reached the foot of the hill, the two women stopped, looked back at Anand Singh following them, and then suddenly spurred their horses, disappearing around the side of the hill.

Because it was a bright, moonlit night, Anand Singh could see the two women and mustered the courage to pursue them. But when they vanished near the hill, he was greatly distressed. He stood there, pondering what to do next. Leaving him thus bewildered and lost in thought, the pitiless moon too slowly made its way home, and, seeing its enemy depart, the darkness seized the opportunity to assert its dominion on all sides. Anand Singh became even more sorrowful. What should he do? Where should he go? Whom should he ask who had taken Indrajeet Singh?
In the distance, a light appeared. Upon closer inspection, it seemed to be coming from a hut...

Ahead, a fire was burning. Anand Singh walked in that direction, and in a short while, upon reaching near the hut, he saw that in front of a green bower made of leaves, eight or ten men were seated on rugs spread upon the ground. From their beards and attire, they were clearly Muslims. In the center, two wax candelabra were burning. One man was reciting Persian couplets aloud, while the rest were exclaiming "Wah! Wah!" in appreciation. To one side, a fire was burning, and two or three men were cooking some food. Anand Singh went and stood near the rug.

The moment they saw Anand Singh, all of them stood up and, with great respect, seated him upon the rug. The man who had been reciting Persian verses rose and, in a florid tongue, said, "Thanks be to God, that the Prince of Chunar has graced our gathering and elevated our honor to the 'Falak-e-Haftum.' In this desolate wilderness, what hospitality can we offer, save to place your footsteps upon our eyes and present you with perfume and cardamom!"

With these words, he brought forward a perfume bottle and a box of cardamom and placed them before Anand Singh. Considering it proper to accept the hospitality of such learned and noble men, Anand Singh inhaled the perfume and took some cardamom. After this, with Anand Singh's permission, the man resumed reciting Persian poetry. The other men placed a couple of cushions on either side of Anand Singh.

The strange fragrance of the perfume intoxicated him; his eyelids grew heavy, and gradually, unconsciousness overtook him, laying him down upon the rug. When he awoke the next day at noon, he found himself lying upon a bed under a mosquito net in an entirely different house. Alarmed, he sat up and looked around.

Before him stood five young and beautiful women, one of whom, standing slightly ahead of the rest, seemed to be their leader. At the sight of her beauty and grace, Anand Singh was left speechless. Her large eyes and sidelong glances drove him out of his senses; her slightest smile struck his heart like lightning, and when she stepped forward, joined her hands, and said, "Are you angry with me?"—that was the final blow.

Anand Singh, forgetting his brother's separation, the events of the night, the deceptions of the ayyars—forgot everything entirely, and, intoxicated by her love, replied, "How could one so fairy-like as you ever bring me sorrow?"

The woman sat upon the bed, put her arms around Anand Singh's neck, and said, "By God, I swear it has been a year now that your love has made me useless. Except for thoughts of you, I have no care for food or drink, but for lack of opportunity, I was helpless."
1. In Muslim texts, there are said to be seven levels of heaven. The highest is called Falak-e-Haftum.
Anand Singh: "(startled) What! Are you a Muslim, that you swear by Khuda?"
Woman: "(laughing) Yes, and are Muslims so terrible?"
Anand Singh stood up, saying, "Alas! If only you were not a Muslim, I would have loved you with all my heart and soul. But for the sake of a woman, I cannot forsake my faith."
Woman (grasping his hand): "Do not be so unkind! I swear, I cannot bear your separation any longer!"
Anand Singh: "I too speak the truth: do not expect anything from me."
Woman (frowning): "Do you say this from your heart?"
Anand Singh: "Yes, I swear it!"
Woman: "You will regret this, and never will you find another who loves you as I do."
Anand Singh: "(pulling his hand away) Curse such love!"
Woman: "So, you will leave this place?"
Anand Singh: "Certainly!"
Woman: "Impossible."
Anand Singh: "How dare you try to stop me?"
Woman: "Do not even think of it."
"Let us see who can stop me!" Saying this, Anand Singh stepped out of the room, and those women, opening a window set in the wall of that very room, slipped away from there.
Anand Singh began to wander about, hoping to find some way out, but his hope was in vain.

The house was not very large or spacious. Besides this room and a small courtyard, there was nowhere else to go. High walls surrounded it on all sides, and there was no door leading outside. Helpless and distressed, he returned to the same bed and lay down, pondering—

"What should I do now? How can I escape this wretch? It is simply impossible for me to love or desire her. God forbid—love and Islam! Such a thing could never happen, not even in a dream. Then what should I do? I am powerless. If I see no other way out, I will use the dagger at my waist to end my life."
He reached for his dagger, only to find his waist empty. Then he thought—

"What a calamity! That wretch has left me with nothing. If an enemy were to appear, what could I do? If that shameless woman comes near me, I could strangle her. No, no, I am a warrior's son—how could I raise my hand against a woman? That I cannot do, so what now?"

Will I have to give up my life, starving and thirsty? How can I partake of food and water in a Muslim woman's house! Yes, that's right, there might be a way out. (Looking towards the wall) They all left through this very window. If this window opens again and she enters the room, I will force my way out through the same path.

A day passed in hunger and thirst, and as darkness began to fall, that same small window opened and the pishachi appeared, accompanied by the four women. One woman held a lamp, another carried water, the third brought a silver tray filled with various sweets, and the fourth had a jeweled betel box.
Anandsingh rose from the bed, and, hoping to escape, slipped inside the window. The women did not stop him at all, for they knew that simply passing through this window would not help him escape.

He passed through the window, but beyond it was darkness. He wandered around the small chamber, but found no way out. Yes, on one side he found a closed door, but it could not be opened in any way. Helpless, he returned to the same room.

The woman laughed and said, "I told you before, you cannot be separated from me. God created you just for me. Alas, you do not think of me, and are wasting your life for nothing! Sit, eat, drink, enjoy yourself—what are you worrying about?"
Anand: "Should I eat what you have touched?"
Woman: "Why not? What harm is there? God belongs to everyone; He created both you and me. If all are children of the same Father, why should there be any untouchability between us?"
Anandsingh (irritated): "God created the elephant, the donkey, the dog, the pig, and the rooster too—if all are children of the same Father, then why make distinctions?"

Woman: "Well, as you wish. Don't listen to me now, but you will regret it, you will feel sorry, and in the end, you will be forced to do exactly as I say. To die of hunger and thirst is no small thing—well, I am going."

Leaving the food, drink, and lamp behind, all four attendants slipped back through the window. Anandsingh tried to force his way through the window along with the demoness, thinking, "If I go with her, either I will get through or at least prevent her from leaving," but this approach too was unsuccessful.
The intoxicated woman sat on the edge of the window, her legs dangling inside, and began to speak with him.
Woman: "Fine, if you will not marry me, at least love me in this way."
Anandsingh: "Never, no matter what happens."
Woman (gesturing with her hand): "Fine, will you marry that woman who—"
Who is standing behind me? That's a Hindu woman!
"Where did another woman come from behind me?" Anand Singh turned around in surprise. In that instant, the wretch seized his chance, slipped inside through the window, and quickly shut the door.

Anand Singh was completely deceived; his courage failed him in every way—helpless, he lay down again on the same bed. His eyes bulged with hunger; food and drink were present, but they were more poisonous than any venom. He understood in his heart that his life was now forfeit. Sometimes he would rise, sometimes sit, sometimes step out into the veranda to walk, but as midnight approached, weakness from hunger left him unable to move. He returned to the bed and began to remember God.
Suddenly, there was a loud noise outside, as if someone had jumped down from the roof of the room. Anand Singh sat up and looked toward the door.

He saw a man approaching from the front, about forty years old. He wore a soldier's uniform, a tripund (three horizontal lines) on his forehead, a dagger and a curved sword at his waist, a coil of rope slung over his shoulder, a traveler's satchel at his side, and in his hand, a lota filled with milk. He came and stood before Anand Singh and said—

"Alas! You are a prince, yet you wish to do the work fit for spies, detectives, or lowly soldiers! The result is that you have become trapped here by this wicked woman. How many days have you been in this house? Do not be afraid, I am your friend, not your enemy!"
Seeing this soldier, Anand Singh was astonished and began to wonder who he could be, arriving at such a time to help him! Well, whoever he may be, he is certainly a well-wisher, not an ill-wisher.
Anand Singh: "As far as I can recall, this is my second day here."
Soldier: "You haven't eaten or drunk anything, have you?"
Anand Singh: "Nothing at all."
Soldier: "Oh! The beloved son of Raja Virendra Singh in such a state! Here, let me give you something to eat and drink!"
Anand Singh: "First, I must know that your caste is pure and you do not intend to deceive me and make me impure."

Soldier (pressing his tongue under his teeth): "Ram-Ram! Never even dream that I would deceive you and defile your caste. I had already thought you might suspect me, so I have brought only such things that you would have no qualms about eating or drinking. Get up from the bed, come outside."
Anand Singh went outside with him. The soldier set the lota on the ground, took some dried fruits from his satchel, handed them to Anand Singh, and said, "Here, eat this and (the lota...
(pointing towards it) "This is milk, please take it."

Anand Singh felt as if life had returned to his body. He had been on the verge of collapse from hunger and thirst; at such a moment, to receive a little dried fruit and milk—was it not a great relief? He ate the fruit, drank the milk, and felt restored. After this, thanking the soldier, he said, "Now please help me get out of this house somehow."
Soldier: "I will take you out of this house, but I should get paid for it as well."
Anand Singh: "Ask for whatever you want, I will give it."
Soldier: "What do you have with you that you can give me?"
Anand Singh: "Even now, I have goods worth thousands of rupees on my person."
Soldier: "I do not want any of that."
Anand Singh: "Then what?"
Soldier: "Give me whatever jewelry that wretched woman is wearing, and one thousand gold coins."
Anand Singh: "How is that possible? She is not here, and where will I get a thousand gold coins?"
Soldier: "Take them from her and give them to me."
Anand Singh: "Will she give them just because I ask?"
Soldier (laughing): "She is ready to give her life for you. What are a few coins compared to that?"
Anand Singh: "So, will you not free me from here today?"

Soldier: "No, but do not worry, no harm will come to you. Tomorrow, when that woman comes, tell her that you will only love her if she leaves all her jewelry and a thousand gold coins here. Tell her to come the next day, and you will do whatever she says. She will immediately send for the coins and remove some of her jewelry to give you. That wretch is very wealthy, do not underestimate her."
Anand Singh: "Very well, I will do as you say."

Soldier: "Until you do this, I will not release you from this captivity. Do not think you can deceive her or force your way out along the path she uses. That will never be possible; there are several routes for her coming and going."
Anand Singh: "What if she does not come for three or four days?"
Soldier: "No matter, I will keep checking on you and bring you food and drink."
Anand Singh: "Alright, so be it."
The soldier threw a rope, climbed up to the roof, vaulted over the wall, and left the house.

A little of the night remained, which Anand Singh spent in pondering who this person could be who had come to his aid at such an hour. She is very greedy. She seems to be an ayyār. The more expenses ayyārs have, the more greedy they become. Well, whoever she may be, now I must do whatever she has said.

The night passed, and morning arrived. That woman came again, bringing the same four maidservants with her. She saw Anand Singh lying on the bed, and the food and drink were untouched, lying exactly where she had left them.
Woman: "Why are you stubbornly starving yourself to death?"
Anand Singh: "I would rather die like this than love you. But if you agree to one thing, then I will do as you say."
Woman (happily, sitting beside him): "Tell me, I am ready to do whatever you wish, but do not be obstinate with me."
Anand Singh: "Take off all the jewelry from your body and bring me a thousand gold coins."
Woman (putting her arms around Anand Singh's neck): "Is that all you want? Very well, I will give it to you at once!"
She told two of the maidservants to fetch a thousand gold coins and removed all the jewelry from her body. In a short while, the two maidservants returned, carrying a bundle of gold coins.
Woman: "Here you are, are you happy now? You have no more complaints, do you?"
Anand Singh: "No, but I ask for one more day's respite! Come again at this same time tomorrow, and then I will be yours."
Woman: "What new excuse is this? If you spend another day hungry and thirsty, what will become of you?"
Anand Singh: "Do not worry about that. I am used to going without food and water for several days."
Woman: "If I must, then so be it. Wait here, I will return."

Saying this, she left Anand Singh where he was and went out of the room with the four maidservants. Even after an hour had passed, she did not return, so Anand Singh got up and went outside to look for her, but there was no trace. In the outer wall, he saw two small cupboards. He guessed that, like the window, these too might be some secret passage leading outside, and perhaps they had left through them.
He spent the whole day in thought and worry. As night approached, just as before, the same soldier arrived and gave Anand Singh milk and sweets.
Anand Singh: "Here you are, your request has been fulfilled."
Soldier: "Then now you must leave this house. One day's hardship..."
So much money has come into my hands. What harm is there in that?

After securing everything, the soldier stepped out of the room, and, reaching the courtyard, used a rope to help Anand Singh out of the house. Then he himself came out as well. The fresh air of the open field revived Anand Singh's spirits. He realized his life was now safe. From the outside, it became clear that this house was inside a hill, carved out by craftsmen who had hewn the stone. Several tunnels were also visible on either side of the house.

The soldier, taking Anand Singh with him, walked a little distance to where two strong, well-groomed horses were tied to a tree. He said, "Here, mount one horse, I'll take the other. Let's go, I'll escort you home."
Anand Singh asked, "How far is Chunar from here, and in which direction?"

The soldier replied, "Chunar is twenty kos from here. Come, I'll go with you. These horses are strong enough to get us to Chunar by dawn. Go home, and don't worry about Indrajit Singh; his whereabouts will soon be discovered, as your spies are already searching for him."
Anand Singh asked, "Where did you get these horses?"
The soldier answered, "Stolen from somewhere—who can say from where?"
Anand Singh pressed on, "Well, at least tell me who you are and what your name is?"
The soldier replied, "That I cannot tell you, nor is it proper for you to ask about it!"
Anand Singh said, "Well, if there's some harm in telling me, then…"

But Anand Singh had not even finished his sentence when something startling caught his eye. He saw someone dressed in black approaching them. Both the soldier and Anand Singh hid behind a tree, and that person passed right by them, muttering to herself, completely unaware that anyone was watching her from hiding.

They both heard her muttering as she went: "Now my heart is at peace. Now I can go home and sleep soundly, and tomorrow, jackals and crows will feast on the corpse of that bastard who thought to oppress me just because I am a woman, never realizing that the heart of this woman is braver than a thousand men!"
Anand Singh and the soldier stared after her, realizing from her words that she was a woman. She soon disappeared from sight.
The soldier said, "She has surely committed a murder."
Anand Singh replied, "And that too, somewhere nearby. If we search, we will surely find out."

Both men began searching here and there. They did not have to trouble themselves for long; after only ten steps, their eyes fell upon a writhing corpse. The soldier took a pouch from his side, struck a spark with a flint, and lit a candle to examine the dying man. It was clear that someone had driven a dagger or a knife straight through his heart. Blood was flowing steadily; the wounded man thrashed his legs and tried to speak, but no words would come.

The soldier took a small bottle from his pouch, filled with some kind of elixir. He poured a little of it into the wounded man's mouth. As soon as it slid down his throat, the man gained just enough strength to utter, in a very faint voice, a few broken words before breathing his last—
"Ah... alas, that beautiful witch... Tej Singh's... life... like mine... in her snare... oh! Indrajeet Singh too...!!"

However disjointed and incomplete these few words from the dying man's lips may have been, they were more than enough to send a shudder through the hearts of both listeners. The soldier, who possessed the ability to accomplish much, was even more agitated than Anand Singh. He knew that, at this moment, if anyone could extend a helping hand to Kunwar Indrajeet Singh and Tej Singh, it was he alone.

Soldier: "Kumar, now you should go home. Hearing these broken, disjointed yet meaningful words that escaped the dying man's lips, it is certain that your elder brother and the chief of the spies, Tej Singh, have fallen into some calamity—one that holds the power to destroy swiftly. In such a situation, I, who have the courage to do much, cannot possibly hold back. My purpose will only be fulfilled when I find that woman who has just wrought this disaster and is sure to cause many more troubles ahead."
Anand Singh: "What you say is quite right, but can you really think that, upon hearing such news, I would quietly go home and shirk from helping those I love more than my own life?"

Soldier: (after some thought) "Very well, there is no time to talk further. Let us go. But listen—do you have any weapon with you? What will you do if the need arises? I have a dagger and a nimcha; take whichever you wish."
Anand Singh: "Just hand me the nimcha, and let us be off."
Anand Singh fastened the nimcha at his waist and, together with the soldier, set off on foot in the direction where the murderous woman had gone, ranting as she went.
They followed the very same narrow path the woman had taken. Every so often, they would pause, holding their breath to listen for any sound; when nothing was heard, they would press on swiftly.

After about a kos, they reached the point where they had to descend the hill. There, the two stopped again and looked around in all directions. The sound of a small bell being rung reached their ears. The bell was being rung from inside some cave or pit, very close to where these two brave men stood, scanning their surroundings.

They turned in the direction from which the bell's sound had come. The sound rang out again, and now they found themselves at the mouth of a cave, which lay a little down the slope of the hill, off to the left along a narrow footpath. It was from within this cave that the bell's sound had emanated.

Without hesitation, both men entered the cave. Once again, the bell sounded, and at the same moment, a light flashed, illuminating the path inside the cave so clearly that they could see the way ahead. In fact, they saw that a short distance ahead stood a woman, who, as soon as the light appeared, stepped to the left and descended into another pit, the entrance to which was so narrow that only one person could pass at a time. The two men were now convinced that this was the very woman they had come searching for.

The light vanished, but by feeling their way, they too reached the mouth of the pit into which the woman had disappeared. A stone had been wedged across its entrance, but around that rough stone were several small holes, through which the two could observe what was happening inside the pit quite clearly.

They sat down right there and began to watch through the holes. Inside, there was ample light. Seated on a rock before them was the same woman, who had not yet removed the veil from her face and, exhausted, was breathing heavily. Beside her stood a young and beautiful Abyssinian girl, holding a large dagger in her hand. On the other side, an ugly-looking Abyssinian man was digging the ground with a spade. In the middle, hanging from the ceiling, was an inverted corpse; in one corner stood an earthen pot filled with water, a small lota, and some food items. That was all there was in the pit, as we have described.

After a while, the woman removed the veil from her face. Ah! What a beautiful, rose-like face, yet her eyes, burning with anger, were so red and terrifying that one felt fear just to look at her. The woman stood up, took the dagger from the girl beside her, and approached the hanging corpse. With the dagger, she drew a line, two fingers deep, across its back.

Alas! Such beauty, and such cruelty! Such mercilessness! She has just come from committing a murder, and here she is again displaying her demonic nature! Whose corpse is this? Could it be another well-wisher of Chunar, or a character from our novel?
As soon as the wound was inflicted on its back, the corpse twitched. Now it was clear that this was no dead body, but a living man, hung up to be tortured. Wounded, the hanging man...
The man writhed in pain and, with a groan, said—
"Alas, why do you torment me? I know nothing!"
Woman: "No, you must tell me! You know very well! (She drove the knife deep into his back again.) Speak, speak!"
Inverted Man: "Alas, why don't you just kill me at once? How should I know anyone's secrets? What have I to do with Indrajit Singh?"
Woman (cutting him again with the knife): "I know well enough, you are a great scoundrel; you know everything. Speak, or I shall slice your flesh off and throw it to the ground."
Inverted Man: "Alas, it is because of Indrajit Singh that I am in this state!"

Until now, Kunwar Anand Singh and the soldier had been watching everything from their hiding place, but when those words left the lips of the man hanging upside down—"Alas, it is because of Indrajit Singh that I am in this state!"—their eyes blazed with fury. They pushed the stone aside and strode boldly inside. Anand Singh confronted the merciless woman wielding the knife and shouted, "Beware! Put down that knife!"

Woman (startled): "Oh! Why have you come here? Well, if you are here, then stand quietly and watch the spectacle. Do not think that your threats will frighten me. (Looking at the soldier) Has dust clouded your eyes too? Do you not recognize your mistress?"
Soldier (looking closely): "Yes, it is true, all your ways are indeed strange."
Woman: "Very well, then both of you leave this place and do not interfere in my work."
Soldier (to Anand Singh): "Come, let them be. Let them do as they wish—what is it to you?"
Anand Singh (drawing his dagger from his belt): "Ha! What are you saying! How can I leave without freeing this man?"
Woman (laughing): "Wash your face and come to your senses!"

How could the brave Anand Singh, son of the valiant Virendra Singh, bear to hear such words? What were a handful of people to him? The moment he heard "Wash your face and come to your senses," his blood boiled. He leapt forward and, with a swift stroke of his dagger, cut the rope tied to the man's feet, by which he was hanging, and at the same time, caught the man deftly so that he did not fall heavily to the ground.
Now the soldier too became Anand Singh's enemy and, challenging him, said, "What childishness is this?"
We have already written above that there are two women and an Abyssinian slave in this tunnel. Now the soldier too joined them, and the four of them seized Anand Singh—
But oh, Anand Singh! With a single blow, he sent all four tumbling away. Just then, a voice called out from outside—
