Within just two watches, it became known that Queen Kalavati had fallen asleep—not just for today, but forever. Now, no one could ever awaken her again.

In the evening, when Maharaj Shivdutt returned to the palace, the letter written by the Maharani was handed to him. The moment he read it, Shivdutt rushed to the chamber where Kalavati lay sleeping. He removed the cloth from her face, checked her pulse, and immediately turned and walked out.

Now, all her companions and maids realized that Queen Kalavati had gone to sleep forever. Who knows what thoughts had passed through the poor woman's mind that made her deem it best to end her life. Her beloved friends, whom she cherished more than her own life, gathered around the bed and gazed upon her for the last time.

Bhimsain had already departed on his campaign four hours earlier. He had no inkling of his dear mother's death, and, fearing that grief and sorrow might hinder him in his task, Shivdutt did not let news of Kalavati's death reach his ears.

Except for the ayyars and a handful of warriors, Bhimsain set out toward Rajgriha, taking Naharsingh with him. His companion, Naharsingh, was truly formidable in the art of war. He was confident that no single man could ever defeat him in combat. Bhimsain too considered himself strong and clever, but ever since Naharsingh, lured by reward, had entered his service, and after they had sparred in mock battles two or three times, Bhimsain realized that before Naharsingh, he was but a child. As skilled and powerful as Naharsingh was in the art of war, he was equally noble and honest, and it was most fitting that he had resolved: on the day anyone bested him, he would accept that person's command from that day forth.
They first arrived at Rajgriha, and after setting up camp in a secret cave...

Bhimsen set his spies to gather information about the place. In just two days of effort, the spies had learned everything there was to know, and when Bhimsen heard that Madhavi was not present there, he decided to move towards Gayaji without causing any disturbance.

At that time, seizing Rajgriha would not have been a difficult task for Bhimsen, but considering that King Virendra Singh now held authority in Gayaji, capturing Rajgriha would be of no use, and it would be extremely difficult to defeat Virendra Singh in battle. Therefore, he abandoned the idea of taking Rajgriha. Besides, he could not possibly capture Kishori by revealing himself; he preferred to act stealthily and first lay his hands on Kishori without alerting anyone.

Upon reaching near Gayaji, they set up camp in a secret and fearsome mountain, and sent spies to gather news. Just as Bhimsen's spies roamed about gathering intelligence, so too did Madhavi's companion Tilottama, who would disguise herself and wander all around to accomplish her own tasks. By chance, Bhimsen's spies encountered Tilottama, and soon enough, news of Madhavi reached Bhimsen, and news of Bhimsen reached Madhavi.
Of all the warriors with Bhimsen, he left them behind in the cave and, along with only Naharsingh, was summoned by Madhavi to the house whose details we have already described above.

It is these very Bhimsen and Naharsingh who today have broken into Kishori's house and brought calamity upon it. With the help of their spies, Bhimsen entered the ruins adjacent to that house and broke through the wall, making an opening, and through that breach, Naharsingh entered and did what the readers already know.

After entering the house, Naharsingh brought Kishori out through that breach and, laying the poor girl on the ground, prepared to kill her as ordered by his master. But as soon as he resolved to commit such cruelty upon an innocent woman, the heart of that young man trembled. He set Kishori down on the ground, stepped away, and said to Bhimsen, who stood there with his face veiled, "Here, whatever is to be done next, you must do yourself. I do not have the courage! But I must tell you...!"

With dagger in hand, Bhimsen immediately stepped forward and mounted the chest of poor Kishori, who, at that moment, had fainted from terror. At the same instant, Kishori's unconsciousness left her, and she found herself caught in the jaws of death, as we have described above.
Bhimsen raised his dagger, and just as he was about to strike Kishori, someone seized his wrist from behind and rendered his strong hand, which held the dagger, powerless. Bhim—
Sen turned around and saw the figure of a sadhu. He immediately left Kishori and stood up, attacking the sadhu with the same dagger.

This sadhu is the very one who lives on the terrifying mound in the middle of the Phalgu river, in front of the Ramshila hill—the same ascetic to whom Madhavi and Tilottama had gone for help, and to whom Devsingh had also arrived, as we have already described. At this moment, the sadhu seemed determined to save poor Kishori from these villains by any means possible.

In the moonlit night, Naharsingh stood at a distance, watching this spectacle, but, considering Bhimsen stronger than the sadhu, he did not come closer to help. Bhimsen's dagger did not harm the sadhu in the least; the sadhu dodged the blow with agility, swiftly moved behind Bhimsen, grabbed his leg, and pulled so forcefully that Bhimsen could not keep his balance and fell heavily to the ground. As soon as Bhimsen fell, the sadhu stepped aside and said, "Get up and come fight again!"

Filled with rage, Bhimsen got up, threw his dagger to the ground, and grappled with the sadhu, for he considered himself highly skilled in wrestling. But he was no match for the sadhu. In just a short while, the sadhu had exhausted Bhimsen and said, "Go, I spare you. If you value your life, flee from here at once."
Bhimsen, astonished, stared at the sadhu's face, unable to utter a word.
Poor Kishori, lying on the ground, witnessed all this, but out of fear, she could neither get up nor cry out.

Seeing Bhimsen so utterly defeated, Naharsingh could not restrain himself. He rushed at the sadhu and challenged him, "If you claim to be brave, come here! I know you are no true sadhu, but a deceiver!"

The sadhu was ready to confront Naharsingh as well, but such a moment did not arise, for just then, searching their way through the breach, Kunwar Indrajitsingh and Tarasingh also arrived at the ruins, and right behind them came Kinnari and Kamla.
The moment Kunwar Indrajitsingh appeared, the sadhu withdrew and, leaping over the ruined wall, vanished—no one knew where.

Meanwhile, Naharsingh, who had been standing by a tree, seized his spear and faced Indrajitsingh. Tarasingh, with a leap, delivered such a kick to Bhimsen that he could not recover and immediately rolled to the ground. Bhimsen was not the sort to fall from a single kick, but after fighting the sadhu, he was already dazed and exhausted, so Tarasingh's kick overcame him. Tarasingh quickly tied Bhimsen's hands and feet, set him aside, and turned to watch the fight between Naharsingh and Indrajitsingh.
For half an hour, the battle between Naharsingh and Indrajitsingh raged on. Indra—

Jeet Singh's sword split Nahar Singh's spear in two, and as it struck Nahar Singh's shield, Prince Indrajeet Singh's sword slipped from his grasp. For a moment, both brave men paused. Seeing the valor of Prince Indrajeet Singh, Nahar Singh was greatly pleased and said—
Nahar Singh: Well done! I have never seen a warrior like you till today.
Indrajeet Singh: In God's creation, there are always greater men to be found; what are you or I in comparison!
Nahar Singh: You speak truly. Do you know what vow I have taken?
Indrajeet Singh: Tell me, if I do not know, I shall learn it now.
Nahar Singh: I have vowed that whoever defeats me in combat, I shall accept his command and serve him faithfully.
Indrajeet Singh: For a brave man such as you, this vow is not unfitting. Come, then, let us settle this with a wrestling match.
Nahar Singh: Very well, let us!
The two began to wrestle. In a short while, Prince Indrajeet Singh threw Nahar Singh to the ground and asked, "Tell me, what is your decision now?"
Nahar Singh: I accept your command.

Indrajeet Singh rose from his chest and began to look around. All about them was silence. There was no sign of Kishori, Kinnari, or Kamla. Nor was there any trace of Bhimsen and his companions (if any had been there). Even his own ayyar, Tara Singh, was nowhere to be seen.
Indrajeet Singh: What is this! Why has such silence fallen all around?
Nahar Singh: It is strange! There were several people here before; I do not know where they have all gone.
Indrajeet Singh: Who are you, and who was with you?
Nahar Singh: I am now your servant. With me was Bhimsen, the son of Shivdatt Singh, and at his side was his attendant. I hope you will also tell me who you are.
Indrajeet Singh: My name is Indrajeet Singh.
Nahar Singh: Ah!
At the mention of the name, Nahar Singh fell at his feet and said, "I thank God that He has placed me in your service! Had I been forced to serve another, it would have brought me great sorrow!"

Nahar Singh accepted the prince's command with a true heart. After this, the two brave men wandered for a long time, searching everywhere for the others, but found no trace of anyone. However, beneath a tree, they did see Bhimsen, whose hands and feet were bound with a rope.
They were tightly bound. Bhimsen called out, "Why, Naharsingh! Will you not help me?"
Naharsingh: "Now I am no longer your subordinate."
Indrajitsingh (to Bhimsen): "Who tied you up?"
Bhimsen: "I do not recognize him, but I can say this much: it was one of your companions."
Indrajitsingh: "And where did that Babaji go?"
Bhimsen: "Who knows?"
Just then, Tarasingh was seen coming, leaping over the wall of the ruins. Indrajitsingh, anxious, hurried toward him and asked, "Where did you go?"

Tarasingh: "When we arrived here, there was a Babaji present at this spot, but who knows where he went! I was tying up a man when, at that very moment (gesturing with his hand), several men hidden in that thicket emerged and forcibly carried off Kishori in that direction. Seeing them go, Kinnari and Kamla also rushed that way. Thinking that this man might attack you from behind by deceiving you during the fight, I quickly tied his bonds and then hurried after them in the direction they had gone. There, in a corner, I saw an open window. I thought to myself that surely they must have escaped through that way, so I went outside the window."
Indrajitsingh: "Did you find any trace after that?"

Tarasingh: "Nothing at all. Who knows where they vanished! I had left you fighting, so I returned at once. Now, let us go home; after I see you safely there, I will set out to search for them. (Pointing toward Naharsingh) What has been decided about him?"
Indrajitsingh: "He has accepted my service."
Tarasingh: "That is well, but the enemy's..."
Naharsingh: "Do not worry about any of that. If God wills, you will never find me a traitor!"
Tarasingh: "May God make it so!"

The darkness of night had completely faded, and morning had come in full. Several men from the neighborhood entered the ruins through that window and, finding their king there, stood astonished and watched. Kunwar Indrajitsingh, Tarasingh, and Naharsingh, taking Bhimsen with them, reached the palace, and Indrajitsingh recounted all that had happened to his younger brother, Anand Singh.

The events of the night had plunged both princes into great anxiety. The fact that Kinnari and Kishori, after being found, had once again disappeared together, left both of them more troubled than ever before.
became even more despondent and began to ponder what should be done now.

It was the middle of the night, and a chilling wind swept through the silence. The moonlight, which sparkled like crystal and always seemed delightful to lovers, had been subdued by tonight's cold; even the most ardent hearts dared not venture out to bask in its beauty. Yet, what use was there in sitting indoors, gazing at the door, sighing endlessly? True manliness is something else entirely; love is a thing of a different nature. Still, those struck by love think it brave to let themselves be bitten by the serpentine tresses of their beloved, and consider it valorous to let their hearts be pierced by her sidelong glances. But those who are truly courageous do not sit at home sighing "Oh!"—when the time comes, they make the sword their beloved.
See, even in this cold and in such a dreadful place, a true warrior finds it distasteful to sit hidden behind a tree.

Now, less than a quarter of the night remains. Atop a hill—not so high that one could not climb it in a single run, but not so low as to be insignificant—a man, his face veiled, his entire body wrapped in black cloth, was pacing back and forth. All around was silence; there was no one here who might recognize him. Perhaps for this reason, he lifted his veil and, standing for a moment, gazed out toward the plain.

Beside this hill stood another, its base joined to the first. It seemed as if one hill had been split in two. Between them ran a path wide enough for bandits and robbers to pass through—a path that could rightly be called a fearsome chasm. The man's gaze kept darting toward that very fissure, and, finding only silence, would turn back to the plain, as if his eyes were searching for someone whose arrival he fully expected at this hour.

He had been pacing for a long time; now, in the east, the sky began to pale with the first hints of dawn. Seeing this, he grew somewhat anxious, stepped forward ten paces, and looked out over the plain. Suddenly, he started and murmured softly, "They have arrived."
The man blew a low whistle. From behind rocks and hidden crevices, ten or twelve men emerged. Seeing them, he spoke with authority, "Look, they have come. We must descend quickly now."

From his manner, it was clear that the man who had been pacing atop the hill was their leader. He now drew his veil back over his face and, gathering his companions, swiftly moved to block the pass below, where others were descending.
Several men, carrying a shrouded corpse and surrounded on all sides, entered the chasm. They walked briskly, never suspecting, even in their dreams, that—
There was no expectation that anyone would emerge from within this mountain to hinder our plans.

When those men, carrying the corpse, entered the crevice—indeed, when they had already traversed half the fissure—suddenly, several men who had been hiding all around sprang upon them and, by every means, rendered them helpless. The men could not take the corpse away; after three or four of them were wounded and one was killed, they were forced to abandon the body right there and flee.

Once the enemies had fled, the chief—who, as we have mentioned, was already present atop that hill—called out to his companions, "There is no need to pursue them; our purpose has been served. But we must make sure—whether this is indeed Kishori or not!"
One of them took a candle from his pouch, lit it, and after removing the cloth from the face of the corpse, said, "It is indeed Kishori." The chief placed his hand upon Kishori's pulse and said:
Chief: "Oh! She has been given a very strong dose of unconsciousness. Look, you too, see for yourselves!"
One (feeling the pulse): "Indeed, she has been given far too much. In such a state, life often slips away!"
Second: "It should be lessened a little."

The chief took a vial from his pouch, opened it, and after making Kishori inhale its contents, placed his hand on her pulse again and said, "That will do; if we lessen it any more, she will regain consciousness. Come, pick her up, it is not wise to stay here any longer."

Lifting Kishori, they retraced their steps through the fissure and crossed over the mountain, disappearing in an unknown direction. After they had gone, from the very spot where the fight had taken place, a man who had been hiding emerged and looked around. When he saw no one present, he softly spoke:

"How fortunate that I arrived here beforehand! I know well those who fought and took the poor Kishori away. Well, what does it matter? Where can they escape from me? It is all the same to me—whether those others had taken her, or these men have, I would have had to exert myself equally in either case. Well, as fate wills, now I must find Babaji. He too had promised to meet at this very place."

Saying this, the man began to search all around for Babaji. If Madhavi had seen this man at that moment, she would have recognized him at once, for he was the very sadhu who lived on the mound before the Ramshila mountain, whom Madhavi had visited, and who had saved Kishori's life from Bhimsen's hands when, in the ruins...
He was about to drive the dagger through his heart, straddling his chest.

It was already clear morning, and indeed, the crimson glow of the rising sun had claimed a quarter of the eastern sky. The sadhu wandered here and there, then halted at one spot, pondering where he should go or what he should do. Just then, from ahead, another babaji appeared, bearing the same face and form as himself. At the sight, he hastened toward him and said, "I have been searching for you for a long time, for we had agreed to meet at this very place!"

The newly arrived babaji replied, "I too have come to fulfill the promise (laughing) — how remarkable! If anyone were to see us at this moment, he would surely be dumbfounded and exclaim, 'Where have two babajis of the same color, face, and form sprung from?' Well, come along behind me."
The two babas took a path to one side, and in the blink of an eye, vanished — who knows where, or into what cave they disappeared.

When Kishori opened her eyes, she found herself lying on a beautiful bed draped with a fine mosquito net, and saw several women adorned in splendid clothes and jewelry standing nearby. At first, Kishori thought they must be daughters of wealthy nobles and chieftains, but soon, from their conversation and manners, she realized they were maidservants. Even as she wept over her helplessness and misfortune, Kishori was seized with a keen curiosity to know in which emperor's palace she had landed, for the servants themselves displayed such grandeur and splendor.
Seeing Kishori regain consciousness, two or three of the maidservants slipped away somewhere, though Kishori understood well enough that they had gone to inform someone of her awakening.

With eyes full of wonder, Kishori gazed all around. Ah, what a beautiful chamber this was! The walls on all sides were adorned with enamel work, and the ceiling, with its golden vines and inlaid jeweled flowers, was enough to astound the mind. Who knows how much money must have been spent in its creation! From the ceiling hung crystal lamps, their glass bowls strung with pendants of rubies; on the jeweled garlands, priceless wall sconces displayed their brilliance. On the arches of the doors, grapevines had been crafted, and upon them, tiny, exquisite birds perched — the artistry and labor that must have gone into their making was beyond reckoning. In those grape clusters, where the ripe grapes should be, rubies had been set, and in place of unripe grapes, emeralds had been used. Besides all this, if one were to describe the entire decoration of that chamber, our true purpose would be lost, and our promise of brevity would be broken. Therefore, we shall write no more on this subject.

Seeing this mansion, Kishori was utterly astonished. It is very difficult to describe her state of mind. Wherever her gaze fell, she became absorbed in that direction, but she had not even managed to properly take in the splendor of the place when, just as before, several more maidservants arrived and announced, "The queen is coming, accompanied by the king!"

At that moment, the queen entered the room with the king by her side. Poor Kishori had no idea who these two were or which kingdom they ruled. Yet, the instant she beheld their appearance, she was overawed. The king appeared to be around fifty years old—tall, with a round face, large eyes, a broad forehead, and upward-curling mustaches; bravery radiated from his countenance. The queen seemed about thirty-five, yet the grace and beauty of her figure would humble even the most youthful of fairies. Her large, sparkling eyes still held the same allure they must have possessed in her youth. There was no sign of any decline in the luster of her limbs. At this moment, a precious greenish gown enhanced her beauty, and her body was adorned with exquisite jeweled ornaments, though any onlooker would say she had no need for jewels—she seemed weighed down by her own loveliness alone.

The majesty of their presence did not allow Kishori to remain lying on the bed. She stood up and gazed at them. No matter how beautiful the queen might be, or how much pride she might have had in her own beauty, the moment she saw Kishori, she was left speechless and all her vanity vanished. At this time, Kishori was utterly disheveled and forlorn, with not a trace of adornment on her person, yet the queen's heart testified that there could be none more beautiful in the world than her. Kishori had not stepped down from the bed out of awe for the queen's beauty, but rather out of respect, and with the thought that if such grandeur adorned this ordinary room, what must their private chambers be like, and how great must be their wealth and dominion.
Both the king and queen looked at Kishori with eyes full of affection, and the king stepped forward, placed his hand on Kishori's back, and said, "Indeed, she is worthy to be my daughter-in-law."
This final word affected Kishori as salt does to a wound, as fire to a thatched hut, as an arrow to the heart, as wine to religion, as greed to faith, and as a lightning strike to the body.
chapters.summary: King Shivdutt orders Bhimsen to murder Kishori, while Queen Kalavati takes a drastic step, and Bhimsen, accompanied by Naharsingh, sets a treacherous plan in motion.

chapters.title: Princes in Distress
paragraphs: Kunwar Indrajit Singh returned home accompanied by Naharsingh and Tarasingh, and recounted everything to his younger brother. He too, upon hearing it all, became very distressed and began to ponder what should be done next. Both princes were deeply troubled. If they sent Tarasingh to investigate, there would be no ayyār left in Gaya, and if their father were to hear of this, he would be greatly grieved—which was their greatest concern. The two brothers remained in great anxiety until well past noon; only after midday did their worry lessen somewhat, when Pandit Badrinath, Bhaironsingh, and Jagannath Jyotishi arrived.
The arrival of these three brought great relief to the two princes, who felt certain now that their work would not be hindered.
Kunwar Indrajit Singh, Anand Singh, Tarasingh, Pandit Badrinath, Bhaironsingh, and the Jyotishi—all of them withdrew to the garden's outer pavilion, seeking solitude, and began to converse.
Anand Singh: "Well, sir, now even here the enemies have become numerous."
Jyotishi: "No matter, there is no harm in that."
Indrajit Singh: "Bhaironsingh, first tell us of your own situation—what happened after you left here?"
Bhaironsingh: "I realized on the way itself that Kishori was not there."
Indrajit Singh: "I too had learned that much."
Bhaironsingh: "Indeed, the same man who brought me the news must have come to you as well."
Indrajit Singh: "Well, what happened then?"

Bhaironsingh: "Nevertheless, I went there (gesturing towards Badrinath and the Jyotishi) and joined forces with these gentlemen. They were already present there with two hundred brave men. In the end, the result was that Diwan Agnidatt and two or three of his companions were arrested and sent to Chunar. As for Madhavi, no one knows where she has gone. All the people there were displeased with Agnidatt, so it was very easy for us to take control of the royal residence. I have now left Pannalal there with those two hundred men."
Badrinath: "Now tell us what has happened here. I have heard that some very strange affairs have taken place!"
Indrajit Singh: "You must have heard the account of this place from Bhaironsingh, but after that, a most peculiar incident occurred last night."
Tarasingh then recounted all the events of the night to them, which, upon hearing, left them all greatly
They became absorbed in these preparations.

While these people were still conversing, a chobdar came and announced, "Akhadnath Babaji is standing outside and wishes to come in." Upon hearing the name Akhandnath, they began to wonder who he was and where he had come from. At last, Indrajit Singh summoned him, and the moment he saw his face, he recognized him.

Reader, this Akhandnath Babaji is the very same who lived upon the fearsome mound in the middle of the Phalgu, opposite Ramshila, whom Madhavi used to visit, and who had saved Kishori's life at that time when, in the ruins, Bhimsen was about to plunge his dagger into her chest as he sat astride her. We have already recounted his story in the third chapter above. Tarasingh also recognized this Babaji, for he too had been with Indrajit Singh the previous night.

Indrajit Singh rose and bowed respectfully to Babaji. Seeing him rise, everyone else also stood up. The prince seated Babaji beside him and, glancing toward the ayyaars, said, "I have already told you about him—he is the one who saved Kishori's life in those ruins."
Babaji said, "It is God who saves lives; what can I do? But tell me, do you know what happened after that incident?"
Indrajit Singh replied, "Nothing at all. At this very moment, we are all pondering over it."
Babaji said, "Well then, listen to me. As for the two other women who were in that house, I do not know where they went in search of Kishori, but I know well what happened to Kishori herself."
Babaji's words drew everyone's hearts toward him, and all listened to him with rapt attention. Babaji began to speak:

"When you, Kumar, were fighting with Naharsingh, Bhimsen's companions, who were hiding nearby, found their chance. They seized Kishori and fled toward Shivdattgarh. But they could not take her far, for on the way, the ayyaars of the king of Rohtasgarh were lying in wait. They fought and snatched Kishori away, taking her to Rohtasgarh. Upon hearing of Kishori's beauty, the king of Rohtasgarh had resolved to marry her to his son, and for many days his ayyaars had been obsessed with the thought of capturing her. Now, finding the opportunity, they accomplished their task. If you do not quickly devise a plan to rescue her, all hope for the poor girl's safety will be lost."

1. Rohtasgarh is a renowned place in the region of Bihar. It is a fortress atop a mountain. In those days, the length and breadth of this fort would have been about ten kos. Even great kings did not dare to conquer it. Today, the structure is almost entirely in ruins, yet it is still worth seeing.

It is very difficult to conquer the fort of Rohtasgarh by force, even if you surpass them in army and wealth. Entering that magnificent fort atop the mountain is no easy task. Still, whatever happens, do not lose heart. Even if you do not think of Kishori, you must strive, considering that this mighty fort nearby is truly worthy of you. God will grant you victory, and as far as possible, I too shall aid you."

Hearing all this from Babaji, Kunwar Indrajit Singh was greatly pleased. On one hand, he was delighted to have news of Kishori; on the other, the prospect of fighting a great battle against the king of Rohtasgarh, proving his youthful valor, and establishing his claim over such a famous fort filled him with joy. With a voice brimming with enthusiasm, he spoke to Babaji:

Indrajit Singh: "The souls of great warriors will peer down from heaven to witness how the battle for Rohtasgarh is fought, and how we conquer that fort. We know well the state of Rohtasgarh, but without a proper cause, we could not resolve to attack."
Baba: "Very well, bring me a lota of water."
At once, water was brought. Babaji plucked off his beard and washed his face. Now everyone recognized him as Dev Singh.

Reader, you must not have forgotten Dev Singh's meeting with Babaji, who lived on the fearsome mound before the Ramshila hill. You will also remember that Babaji had told Dev Singh, "Tomorrow, we shall leave this place." After Babaji's departure, it was Dev Singh who, in Babaji's guise, sat upon that seat and carried out all the deeds you are aware of. On the day Madhavi came and said, "Bhimsain has come to help us," it was Dev Singh in Babaji's form. The real Babaji had already met Dev Singh on that hill, where we have written that two Babajis of the same appearance had gathered, and he had told Dev Singh the story of his youth and the matter of Rohtasgarh.
Dev Singh recounted all his adventures to the two princes, and in the end said, "Now we must certainly march upon Rohtasgarh."
Indrajit Singh: "That is excellent! Only then will our courage be revealed! But tell me, how should we treat Naharsingh?"
Dev Singh: "Who is Naharsingh?"

Indrajit Singh: "The one who fought me in those ruins! He is truly brave. He had vowed that whoever defeated him, he would become that man's follower. Now he has left Bhimsain's side and is ready to stay with us."
Dev Singh: "Such a brave man surely deserves our favor, but today we—"
We will test him. You arrange a fine house for him, and make every provision for his comfort.
Indrajit Singh: "Very well."

At once, Prince Indrajit Singh summoned Naharsingh to his side and received him with great kindness. He gave him a house, bestowed upon him the rank of commander of his army, and ordered Bhimsen to be kept in captivity.

Seeing such favor bestowed upon him by the prince, Naharsingh was greatly pleased. He conversed for a while, then saluted and departed to his quarters, and began to fulfill the duties of commander with utmost honesty.

Midnight had long passed. Silence reigned all around. From the streets and alleys came the cries of the watchmen, "Stay awake, be alert!" Naharsingh lay upon his bed in his house, reading a book, with a lamp burning at his bedside.

The book in Naharsingh's hand was not some scripture or ancient text, but a book of pictures, whose pages he turned slowly, gazing intently at each illustration. These pictures depicted famous battles of great kings and warriors, and portrayed the valor of wrestlers and the bravery of heroes. As he looked upon them, the blood in Naharsingh's veins surged with excitement, and he longed for a chance to prove his courage in such battles.
He spent a long time looking at the pictures, and at last, his sleep-laden eyes began to close. Finally, he shut the book and set it aside, and soon after, he fell into a deep sleep.

Somewhere in a corner of the house, a man had been hiding for who knows how long. Seeing Naharsingh asleep, he entered the room and stood by the bed, observing him closely. We do not know this man, for his face is covered by a mask. After a while, he took a small packet from his pocket and, taking a pinch of powder, brought it near Naharsingh's nose. With his breath, the powder entered his brain, and with a sneeze, Naharsingh fell unconscious.

The man untied a rope from his waist and, binding Naharsingh's hands and feet tightly, waited for him to regain consciousness. Then, drawing his sword and removing the mask from his face, he stood before him. As soon as Naharsingh regained his senses, he found himself helpless, with his hands bound, and Maharaj Shivdutt standing before him, sword in hand.
Shivdutt: "Well, Naharsingh, was it right for you to abandon my son at such a critical moment and let him fall into the hands of our enemies?"
Naharsingh: "As long as the brave Indrajit Singh had not defeated me, until then—"
I have always been your son's companion. When the prince won me over, I accepted his service according to my word. You already know my oath!
Shivdutt: "I'm here now to punish you for what you have done."
Naharsingh: "Well, as God wills."
Shivdutt: "Even now, if you agree to join me, I can let you go."
Naharsingh: "That cannot be. I cannot leave such a brave master to join someone as treacherous as you!"
Shivdutt (sternly, raising his sword): "Are you willing to give up your life?"
Naharsingh: "I gladly accept death, but I will never abandon my master!"
Shivdutt: "Look, I am warning you once more. Think it over and join me."
Naharsingh: "Enough of this useless talk. Do whatever you can. I do not wish to hear any more of this."
Shivdutt tried his utmost to persuade and threaten him, but the brave Naharsingh's resolve did not waver. At last, helpless, Shivdutt threw his sword aside and, patting Naharsingh on the back, said—
"Well done, brave man! If the heart of a youth like you were not so steadfast, whose would be? I am not Shivdutt—I am Kumar's ayyār, Dev Singh. I came here to test you!"

Saying this, he untied Naharsingh's bonds and left at once. Dev Singh recounted the whole incident to both princes and praised Naharsingh, but the brave Naharsingh never spoke of this test to anyone for the rest of his life.
The next day, Dev Singh left for Chunar, saying, "I will soon return after making arrangements for the assault on Rohtasgarh."

Upon learning that Kishori had been taken by the people of Rohtasgarh, Kunwar Indrajit Singh's restlessness grew beyond all bounds. He could not find peace even for a moment; in just a few hours, his appearance changed. Anyone calling him or asking him anything seemed like poison to him. Seeing him in such a state, Bhairav Singh could not restrain himself and began to counsel him in private.
Indrajit Singh: "No amount of your advice can change my condition, nor can it lessen the danger I feel for Kishori's life."

Bhairav Singh: "If Kishori had been taken to Shivduttgarh, her life would certainly be in danger, for Shivdutt, in his rage, would not have spared her. But now she is in the hands of the king of Rohtasgarh, and he intends to marry her to his son."
How could he possibly be an enemy of Kishori's life in such a situation?
Indrajit Singh: But what if they forcibly marry off Kishori? What then?
Bhairon Singh: Yes, if that happens, it would indeed be a cause for grief. But do not worry; if God wills, I shall settle this entire matter within five or seven days.
Indrajit Singh: Will you bring Kishori back from there?

Bhairon Singh: To break into the fortress of Rohtasgarh and rescue Kishori is not the work of two or three days. Besides, do you think the fortress of Rohtasgarh will be empty of spies and tricksters?
Indrajit Singh: Then what will you accomplish in five to seven days?
Bhairon Singh: I shall certainly do something to halt Kishori's marriage.
Indrajit Singh: What is that?
Bhairon Singh: By whatever means possible, I shall capture Prince Kalyan Singh of that place and bring him here. Once our decision is made, I will release him.
Indrajit Singh: Ah, if you do that, it would be splendid!
Bhairon Singh: Do not worry. I am setting out at once, but please do not tell anyone about my departure.
Indrajit Singh: Are you going alone?
Bhairon Singh: Yes, I am.
Indrajit Singh: Wonderful! If you get caught somewhere, I'll be left waiting for you with no one to bring me news!
Bhairon Singh: Do not expect such a thing.

Having made this promise to Kunwar Indrajit Singh, Bhairon Singh set out towards Rohtasgarh. Yet, Indrajit Singh was not pleased with Bhairon Singh going alone. At that moment, he kept silent due to Bhairon Singh's insistence, but after his departure, the prince told everything to Pandit Badrinath and ordered him to go and assist his friend. Upon receiving the command, Pandit Badrinath also set out for Rohtasgarh and met Bhairon Singh on the way.
After traveling for two days, these two men reached Rohtasgarh¹ and climbed the mountain.

¹ Raja Shivprasad Sitare-Hind has written in his book 'Jaan Jahanuma': "About seventy-five miles southwest of Arrah, upon a mountain a thousand feet high, stands a very strong fortress called 'Rohtasgarh', whose real name is 'Rohitashm'. It lies desolate on the left bank of the Son River, covering an area of ten square miles. There is only one narrow path of two kos (about four miles) ascent by which to enter; on all other sides, the mountain, forests, and rivers surround it so completely that it is impossible for anyone to pass through. Inside the fort, two ancient temples still stand, but all other buildings, palaces, gardens, ponds, etc., of which only traces remain, were built by the Muslim kings."
(The Author)—However, from the accounts written about 'Bihar' during Akbar's reign, it appears that this place existed even before the rule of the Muslims.

They entered the fort. This was a very large fort, built with exquisite craftsmanship atop a mountain, and within it lay the city itself, bustling with the commerce of great merchants, bankers, traders, and jewelers, all displaying their wealth and splendor. There is no need to describe here the beauty and ornamentation of this city, nor is there time; indeed, at the appropriate moment, after reading a few passages, the reader will come to know of its magnificence. Within this fort, there was yet another, smaller fort, where the Maharaja and his close ones resided, and among the people, it was famous as the palace.

On this mountain, there were many small waterfalls and ponds. There was only a single path leading upward, and that too was very narrow. On all sides, a dense forest surrounded it in such a way that if a person was even slightly careless and lost the path, he could wander for days. For enemies, or anyone else, it was extremely difficult to ascend this mountain, and even that narrow path was not wide enough for more than five or seven people to climb together at once.
Disguised, our two ayyars reached Rohtasgarh, and upon seeing the place, understood well that conquering this fort would be no easy task.

Bhaironsingh and Pandit Badrinath, disguised as Mathuria Chaubes, began to wander about Rohtasgarh, carefully observing everything. At noon, they arrived at a Shiva temple, which was very beautiful and grand. The assembly hall was so large that a hundred or a hundred and fifty people could sit comfortably within it. All around it was an open courtyard, where several Brahmins and priests sat, basking in the sun. Approaching these people, our two ayyars stood and declared in a loud voice, "Victory to Mother Yamuna!"
The priests welcomed the two Chaubes and began conversing with them.
One priest asked, "Tell us, Chaube ji, when did you arrive?"

Badrinath replied, "We have just come, Maharaj! Climbing the mountain has tired us, our throats are parched. Kindly give us a grinding stone and roller so we may prepare some bhang and settle our minds."
Priest: "Here, take the stone and roller, take the ingredients, take sugar—prepare as much bhang as you wish."
Bhaironsingh said, "We have our own bhang and spices with us; why should we trouble you Brahmins?"
Priest: "No, no, it's nothing. Here, everything is provided by the Maharaj's order. Any Brahmin or traveler who comes is to be given all he needs."
Badrinath: "Splendid, splendid! Then let us sing the Maharaj's praises!"

The priest gave them all the necessary items, and the two of them prepared the bhang, drank it themselves, and offered it to the priests as well. Through their conversation and playful banter, the two ayyars soon won over the priests. The chief priest was very pleased and said—

"Chaubeyji Maharaj, by great fortune we have had the honor of your company. Please, do stay here for two or four days! We will arrange for you to meet Maharaj Kumar right here, and you shall receive many favors. Our Maharaj Kumar is very cheerful, virtuous, and wise. You will be most pleased to meet him!"
Badrinath replied, "Wonderful, Maharaj! With such kindness from you, we shall certainly stay, and also meet your Maharaj Kumar. When does he come here?"
The priest answered, "He comes here both in the morning and evening, and performs the evening worship in this very temple!"
Bhaironsingh asked, "Then will we see him today as well?"
The priest replied, "Certainly."

This temple stood right beside the fort's wall. At its rear was a small iron window, through which one could go out into the jungle beyond the fort. At the priest's command, after drinking bhang, both ayyaars went out into the jungle by that path and returned across the field. The priests too went out into the jungle and field by the same way.

At dusk, Maharaj Kumar also arrived, and after shutting the temple door from within, performed his evening worship for more than an hour. At that time, only the chief priest remained in the temple, staying until Maharaj Kumar completed his daily rituals. The two ayyaars also got a good look at Maharaj Kumar, but had already told the priest not to mention to him that two Chaubeys had come; instead, they asked for an introduction to be arranged the following evening.

The two ayyaars spent the night in the temple, entertaining the priest greatly with their antics, and at the same time convincing him that a great Mahatma had arrived at the foot of the mountain, whom he must meet, for the Mahatma was especially kind to them.

In the morning, after rising, both of them ground and drank bhang again, and after serving it to everyone, went out into the field by the same window. The two ayyaars were absorbed in their own plans, thinking of how to spirit Maharaj Kumar away from here, and had already considered escaping by that very window. So, as they went into the jungle, they carefully observed the area, seeking how they might reach the main road directly from there. They spent the whole day on this task, and after thoroughly understanding the way, returned to the temple by evening.
The priest asked, "Tell me, Chaubey Maharaj! Where did you go?"
Badrinath replied, "Oh Maharaj, don't ask! We had barely gone a little ahead when we found ourselves in hell. We lost our way so badly—only we know what we suffered!"
Bhaironsingh added, "It is only by God's grace that we have returned at this hour; otherwise, there was little hope of ever making it back here."
Priest: Ram-Ram! This forest is truly terrifying. Many times, we have lost our way in it and wandered for two days straight. You poor fellows are new here. Come, sit down, have some refreshments.

Bhaironsingh: Oh, what food or drink! I can barely think straight. I'll just drink some bhang and sleep soundly. We're so exhausted from wandering that our whole bodies ache. Kind sir, please, don't inform the prince about us today—we're in no state to meet him. Tonight, we'll sleep deeply!
Priest: Very well, as you wish! (laughing) Come, at least sit down.

Both ayyaars drank bhang and offered it to the others as well. After resting for a while, they went out to explore the bazaar, looked around carefully, and then returned. At bedtime, they once again brought up the subject of the Mahatma to the priest—the very Mahatma they had promised to introduce him to—and praised him so highly that the priest became eager to meet him and said, "Tell me, will you take me to see him tomorrow or not?"

Badrinath: Certainly. As soon as the prince returns from his evening prayers, we'll go. But you must come alone, otherwise the Mahatma will be very displeased if too many people come. He's not one to meet just anyone.
Priest: Why would I bring anyone else? I'll go with you alone.
Bhaironsingh: That's best.

The next day, when the prince had finished his evening prayers and returned, Badrinath and Bhaironsingh set off with the priest. After descending the mountain, Badrinath said, "Let's prepare some bhang here. That's why I brought the cup."
Priest: Why not? Go ahead and prepare it.
Badrinath: Shall I make some for you as well?
Priest: Why would you offer bhang at this hour? I'm not used to it, but thanks to you fellows, I've been drinking quite a bit these past two days.
Badrinath: No harm in having a little.
Priest: As you wish.

Our brave ayyaars ground the bhang on a stone slab and drank it, and, taking care not to be seen, mixed a little sleeping potion into the priest's cup as well. In no time, the priest let out a faint sound and fell into a deep stupor. The two ayyaars picked him up and hid him in a thicket.
Badrinath: Now, what should we do?
Bhaironsingh: You stay here. I'll go and bring the prince using the same trick.
Badrinath: Very well. I'll disguise you as the priest myself.
Narsingh: "Proceed."

Disguised as the priest, Bhaironsingh left Badrinath at the same spot and returned. Before evening fell, he reached the temple. The people there asked, "Tell us, priestji, did you meet the Mahatma or not? And why have you returned alone, where is Chaubeji?"

The false priest replied, "I met the Mahatma. Ah, what a marvel he is! The Mahatma is truly accomplished! He holds both Chaubes in high esteem. He did not allow them to return, but I managed to come back. Chaubeji will return tomorrow."

At the appointed hour, Maharajkumar also arrived and entered the temple to perform the evening rituals. As usual, the false priest—Bhaironsingh in disguise—remained inside the temple in place of the real priest, and upon the prince's arrival, closed the doors from within. What the priest would do inside the temple during the prince's evening prayers, these two ayyars had already learned through casual conversation. The priest would not perform any special tasks inside; he would simply arrange the items for worship before the prince and then sit quietly in a corner. When it was time to leave, he would offer a garland as prasad to the prince, who would smell it, touch it to his eyes, and leave it there before departing. Today, all these tasks were performed by our ayyar disguised as the priest.

This temple had four doors on all sides. In front, several people and guards would always be seated. At the door on the left, there was a fire pit for the hom ritual. On the right, several pots of flowers were kept, and the rear door was always deserted.

Inside the temple, after closing the door, the prince began his evening prayers. Seizing the opportunity during the pranayama, the false priest mixed a powder of unconsciousness into the garland of flowers meant to be given as a blessing. When the prince was about to leave, the priest placed the garland around his neck. The prince removed it, smelled it, touched it to his forehead, and placed it back in its place.

No sooner had the prince smelled the garland than his head spun, and he fell unconscious to the ground. Bhaironsingh quickly bundled him up and, taking the route through the rear door, slipped outside. Then, through the small window, he exited the fort and took the path into the forest. In just two hours, he reached the spot where he had left Pandit Badrinath.
These two ayyars, taking Kumar Kalyansingh with them, set off in the direction of Gaya.
chapters.summary: After Akhandnath Babaji arrives with news of Kishori's capture, Indrajit Singh is eager to fight for her rescue and capture Rohtasgarh fort.

chapters.title: The Torment of Love
paragraphs: Ah, what a terrible affliction love is! Alas, whomever this wretch has pursued, it has left them ruined, rendering all the good things of the world useless and turning them bitter.

The scattered moonlight kindles sparks upon his body; the cool evening breeze feels like a scorching wind; the sight of lovely flowers pricks his heart with thorns; strolling along the garden's pathways blisters his feet; lying upon a soft bed seems to break his bones, and even after turning from side to side, he finds no rest.

Food and drink become forbidden, a lump of sugar tastes like poison, his belly fills with the bitterness of sorrow, and a few drops of tears are enough to quench his thirst. Even after enduring a thousand torments, the soul entangled in a beloved's tresses finds no chance to escape. The advice of friends tears his heart to pieces; the fire of separation roasts his very core; the blood in his body turns to water, and thus both hunger and thirst abandon him. The face that is hidden in his eyes appears everywhere—in the walls and doors, in dreams he sees only that beloved, swaying gracefully. Words once heard from her lips echo in his ears day and night; the pearly teeth glimpsed in laughter become a necklace around his neck, impossible to forget. The memory of those magical glances unsettles his soul; the embrace, arms entwined around his neck, weighs heavily upon his body, so that leaning to one side in remembrance, he cannot even straighten himself.

Day and night, with closed eyes, he wanders in the garden of beauty. His cold sighs work like a storm, scattering dry leaves, and slowly he himself withers, until he gathers the courage to be swept away with the wind. The master of love, whip in hand, is ever at his heels, never allowing his disciple to pause, nor to utter any word but the beloved's name.

Not only people, even the wind teases such lovers—knocking at the door, reminding them of the beloved's arrival, pinching them with memories, and sometimes leaning close to whisper, "I have come from the lane where your darling lives."

While strolling in the garden, the branches of trees, swayed by the breeze, beckon him closer, and when he approaches, they drop two flowers in laughter and fall silent, making his heart all the more restless, so that he sits clutching his chest with both hands. His dear relatives, seeing his condition, sigh in pity, and taking his soft fingers in theirs, ask, "Why have you let your nails grow so long?"

His restlessness increases to such an extent that he cannot fix his mind on anything for even half an hour, nor can he sit comfortably in one place for a moment. Even the sleep that used to hide in his eyes seems to have vanished, leaving in its place a wakefulness that, moment by moment, paints and erases countless images.
Such is the state of our Kunwar Indrajit Singh and his beloved Kishori. At this moment, both are far from each other, yet the ghost of love, taking on myriad forms...
dance before her eyes and do nothing to lessen her growing sorrow and restlessness.

All the women living in the palace of Rohtasgarh, despite their constant efforts to comfort Kishori, could not diminish her sadness in the least. Although she suffered no hardship here, she could not, even for a moment, forget the heart-rending words she had heard from the Maharaj's lips as he stroked her back upon her arrival: "She is fit to be my daughter-in-law!"

Though, compelled by the insistence of the noble ladies, Kishori had to stroll in the women's garden, nothing there could soothe her poor heart. At the sight of a blooming rose, she would wither within; at a glance toward the narcissus, her shy eyes would hide behind the veil of her lashes; approaching the cypress, she would bend under the weight of her sorrow, and the winding vines laden with cheerful blossoms would remind her of Kunwar Indrajit Singh's wavy tresses, in which her soul was so entangled that she had no hope of ever being freed in this life.

She saw the garden paths as fields of separation from her beloved, the flowerbeds filled with tiny, colorful blooms as dense jungles, and the humming of bees echoed in her ears like the incessant chirring of cicadas, which, heedless of the seasons, sing all year round in the forest and, by chance, shake the hearts of delicate souls who wander there.

At the sight of the soft breezes rustling the beautiful, multicolored leaves, she would shiver; reaching the artificial stream, clear and sparkling like pearls, her heart would sink; at the sight of the cascading fountains, her heart would leap to her mouth, and tears would fall in a steady stream from her eyes. Witnessing this, the delicate birds of the garden, who delighted hearts with their melodious songs, could not remain silent and would cry out, "Alas! This poor girl's heart has been bled by separation, and that blood, turned to water, flows out through her eyes."
The few young, delicate, and lively women assigned to keep her company pitied her condition, but they were helpless, for their own lives were dear to them.

At night, when Kishori found herself alone, she would think of many things. Sometimes she would devise plans to escape, but, deeming them impossible, she would turn her thoughts to her beloved Indrajit Singh and wonder, "Will he not help me and rescue me from here?" No, surely he will rescue me—but when? When he learns that Kishori is imprisoned in such and such a place. Alas! What if, by the time he hears, I am forced to leave this world, and the desires of my heart remain forever unfulfilled?

I will have to be taken away. No, if anyone tries to force me, I will certainly do so, and except for the one to whom I have already given my heart, I will not belong to another. Before such a situation arises, I will leave this body and go to join him. There is no power that can stop me from doing so. Oh God! Will you not show the way here to those brave ayyars who are always ready to lay down their lives for the prince?

One night, she was lost in such thoughts when morning arrived, and from outside her room, a voice reached her ears that made her cry out. Her scattered thoughts gathered at once, and a glimmer of happiness appeared on her face. The voice was—
"This is certainly the work of Virendra Singh's ayyars."
Kishori immediately stood up, and upon stepping outside her room, she learned within an hour that Prince Kalyan Singh had been spirited away by Virendra Singh's ayyars.
Now Kishori began to feel some hope of her own release, and she spent the entire day immersed in thoughts of what might happen next.
chapters.summary: Love torments Kunwar Indrajit Singh with longing, while Kishori, held in Rohtasgarh, finds a glimmer of hope when she hears news of Prince Kalyan Singh.

chapters.title: Kishori’s Sleepless Night
paragraphs: It is well past midnight. Kishori is lying on her bed under the mosquito net in her room, lost in thoughts unknown. Yes, her tear-filled eyes certainly reveal that some kind of turmoil is raging within her heart. There is no sleep in her eyes; she keeps turning from side to side and sighing deeply.

Suddenly, a heart-wrenching sound from outside the room reached her ears, making her restless at once. She could not remain lying down any longer. She got down from the bed, opened the door, and began to look around outside. The sound was of someone sobbing and weeping.

Outside the room was an eight-doored veranda, where, leaning against a pillar, stood a young woman, sobbing and crying bitterly. The moonlight was falling clearly on both the pillar and the woman. Coming closer, Kishori realized that the woman was shivering from the cold, for she wore no heavy garment to protect herself.
Kishori's heart was already wounded. How could she bear to see someone weeping so bitterly? She immediately went up to the woman, took her hand, and asked—
"What calamity has befallen you, that you are weeping so bitterly?"
Woman: "Alas, a calamity has befallen me that cannot be averted in any way!"

Kishori brought her into her own chamber and, seating her beside her on the carpet, began to converse with her. This woman could not have been more than eighteen years old. She was beautiful and delicate in every way; the jewelry she wore made it clear that she must be the daughter of a noble family.
Kishori: "I hope you will tell me your heart's story plainly, and, considering me your sister, hide nothing from me."
Woman: "Sister, I will certainly tell you my tale, for you too are ensnared in the same misfortune as I am."
Kishori (startled): "Have you, too, suffered injustice as I have?"
Woman: "Without a doubt."
Kishori (with a deep sigh): "O God! I have wronged no one, then why must I endure such sorrow?"
Woman: "But I cannot remain in this place any longer!"
Kishori: "Why is that? Do you feel some kind of fear?"
Woman: "No, no, I am not afraid of anything, but at this moment I have hope of escaping with someone's help, and that is why I left my room and came here."
Kishori: "Has some plan been devised?"
Woman: "Yes, and if you wish, you too can escape from here with me. A powerful man of this very kingdom will help us tonight."

Hearing this, Kishori was overjoyed. She quite forgot to ask who this woman was, what her name might be, or what sorrow had befallen her; in her eagerness to escape, she clasped the woman's hands in her own and, gazing at her with affection, asked, "With your help, can I too be freed from here?"
Woman: "Certainly you can, but we must not delay any longer."

Kishori was about to reply when the door before them opened, and a beautiful woman entered. She appeared to be about twenty years old, her complexion fair as wheat, her stature neither tall nor short, her body graceful and well-formed, her face charming, her eyes full of sweetness. Aside from a diamond stud in her nose and a few simple ornaments, she wore little jewelry, yet she was worthy to sit among the highest ranks of beauties. At the sight of her, the woman sitting beside Kishori started, looked at her, and exclaimed, "Lali, your coming here at this hour astonishes me!"
Lali: "But you will be even more astonished to learn that I have come to save poor Kishori from your clutches."
At these words, the other woman's entire demeanor changed. On her face appeared...

The gloom that had lingered until now vanished completely, replaced by a sudden flush of anger. Her eyes, which had been brimming with tears, dried up at once, and a crimson fury began to burn within them. She looked at Lali with such a commanding gaze, as though she held some authority over her.
Kishori, too, recognized Lali, for she was one of those beauties appointed to entertain Kishori and ensure her safety.
After fixing Lali with that imperious look for several moments, the woman spoke again—
"Lali, have you gone mad today, that you dare to speak so disrespectfully in my presence?"
Lali replied, "And who are you, that I should treat you with respect?"
The woman (standing up): "Do you not know who I am?"
Lali: "Kundan, I know you very well. But you do not realize that your reins are in my hands, and you can do nothing to me. Nor can you ensnare poor Kishori in the web of your deceit!"

No sooner had Lali spoken these words than the woman—whose name was Kundan—turned red with rage, unable to contain her fury. She drew a dagger, hidden at her waist, and lunged at Lali to strike. But Lali swiftly produced an orange from beneath her arm, held it up, and asked, "Have you forgotten how many segments are in this?"
At the sight of the orange, and upon hearing Lali's words, Kundan's anger melted away. Fear and panic drained the color from her face, and with a shriek, she collapsed to the ground.
chapters.summary: Kishori, sleepless and distressed, encounters a weeping woman who promises escape, but the arrival of Lali reveals a dangerous deception and hidden power dynamics.

chapters.title: The Gathering Before Rohtasgarh
paragraphs: At some distance from the hill in front of the fort of Rohtasgarh, Virendra Singh's army was encamped. Soldiers could be seen everywhere, each busy with his own task. Some troops had already arrived, and more continued to pour in. In the center stood the richly decorated tent of Raja Virendra Singh, resplendent in its grandeur. On either side were the tents of Kunwar Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh. In front and to the rear, the camps of great sardars and brave warriors were pitched. Preparations for the bazaar were underway, and such a vast array of war equipment was being assembled that the mere sight of it would chill the hearts of their enemies.

On the second day after the camp was established, Kunwar Indrajit Singh, Anand Singh, Tej Singh, Devi Singh, Pandit Badrinath, Bhairon Singh, Tara Singh, Jagannath the astrologer, and Fateh Singh (the old

The general who had been stationed at Naugarh, along with Naharsingh and others, also arrived with King Virendra Singh, and everyone settled into their respective camps. Pannalal was kept at Gayaji, while Ramnarayan and Chunnilal were held at Chunar Fort. For this battle, the rank of commander was bestowed upon Naharsingh. On the third day, as more troops arrived, five standards—signifying an army of fifty thousand—were raised. The faces of the brave warriors shone with joy. Everyone was preoccupied with the hope that the battle would commence as soon as possible, and indeed, it was expected that within a day or two, the fighting would begin. However, a sudden calamity befell Virendra Singh's army, causing the battle to be delayed for several days. No one had even dreamt of such a disaster, the details of which we shall recount further ahead.

An ayyār of King Digvijay Singh arrived at King Virendra Singh's camp, bearing a letter from his master. Virendra Singh took the letter and handed it to his munshi to read aloud. The gist of its contents was as follows:

"There has never been enmity between us, yet for some unknown reason, you have resolved to wage war or sow discord. Well, whatever the cause may be, we cannot say, but you should remember that even if you fight for fifty years, you will not be able to take this fort from us. Even if we sit quietly, you can do us no harm. Still, we shall fight you and come forth onto the battlefield to display our valor. If you are so proud of your bravery and manliness, why endanger the lives of your soldiers? Let us settle this one-on-one. After witnessing the actions of the brave, let there be a duel between you and me. If you defeat me, this kingdom shall be yours; if not, you will be considered our subordinate. Alas, my son is not present at this time; had he been here, he alone would have faced both your sons."
In response to this letter, King Virendra Singh wrote the following, the summary of which we present below:

"You entered our kingdom and took away Kishori—was this not an act of force? Can this not be called the foundation of this war? If you return Kishori to us with honor, we shall certainly return to our home. Otherwise, remember this: we shall tear down every brick of this fort you are so proud of. We are also ready for single combat; let any man test his courage one-on-one. Your son is a prisoner here with me. If you send Kishori back to us, we are prepared to release him."

In reply to this letter, a single cannon shot rang out from the fort of Rohtasgarh. Now, there was no longer any doubt about the impending battle. The ayyārs on both sides readied themselves to display their skills, and what deeds they performed will be revealed as the story progresses.
Within the fort of Rohtasgarh, upon the terraces of the royal palace, many women had gathered...

The women were looking in the direction where Virendra Singh's army was camped. With Kunwar Kalyan Singh having been captured, Kishori felt a certain kind of relief, for her greatest fear had been the prospect of being married to him; she cared not a whit for her own death. Yet, not for a single moment could she forget Kunwar Indrajit Singh, whose image was etched upon her heart. Upon hearing of Virendra Singh's advance, she was filled with joy, and she too climbed up to her attic, gazing longingly in the direction where Virendra Singh's forces lay. Even though it was far from here, Kishori's eyes seemed to reach all the way there, searching through the crowd, striving to pick someone out.

At this time, Lali was with Kishori—the same Lali who, several days earlier, had frightened Kundan in Kishori's chamber by showing her the orange. Lali had been appointed to watch over Kishori, yet she showed her kindness. Kishori had tried several times to uncover the secret of the orange, but to no avail. Since that day, she had met Kundan many times, but when questioned, Kundan never said anything that would dispel Kishori's suspicions. Though they lived together daily in the same house, no further enmity appeared between Lali and Kundan, which only increased Kishori's amazement.

At this moment, besides Lali, there was no other woman with Kishori. Both were intently watching towards Virendra Singh's camp, when suddenly the memory of the orange incident returned to Kishori. After pondering for a while, she began to question Lali.

Kishori: "Lali, when I remember that day, or think upon it, Kundan's treachery becomes clear as day. If Kundan had been true, she would not have lunged to strike you, or if she had truly been planning to escape that day, she would have been distressed at her plan being foiled. Yet, instead of sorrow, she seemed pleased."
Lali: "No, she is not entirely false."
Kishori: "Was there some truth in what she said?"
Lali: "Certainly, there was."
Kishori: "What was it?"
Lali: "That she too was brought to this fort for the same purpose as you."
Kishori: "You mean, to be married to your prince?"
Lali: "Yes."
Kishori: "Very well, and what else did she say that was true?"
Lali: "What will you gain by asking all these things? The revelation of this secret will..."
Great trouble will arise.

Kishori: "No, no, my dear Lali, no one else can ever hear such a thing from my lips, and I hope that you will tell me everything clearly! Since that day, I have come to trust that you share in my sorrows. So, if my suspicion is correct, you must tell me the truth, so that I may always remain alert."
Lali: "Now she will never do you any harm."
Kishori: "Still, please be kind and..."
Lali: "Very well, I will tell you. But beware, never mention this to anyone else!"
Kishori: "I could never do such a thing, and you yourself know that in this palace, there is no one but you with whom I speak even two words."

Lali: "All right, then except for what I have already told you above, everything else she said was a lie. She never wanted to escape from this house; in fact, she is happy in the hope of marrying our prince. But ever since you arrived, she has been troubled, because she considers you far superior to herself in beauty and honor—and truly, it is so. She is tormented by the thought that Kishori will marry the prince before she does, and then I will be second, and in such a case, Kishori will be called the chief queen, and her children will be considered heirs to the throne. That is why she was plotting to kill you, but in such a way, and at such a place, that no suspicion would fall upon her."
Kishori: "Oh, shame! Shame!"
Lali: "But now she cannot do you any harm."
Kishori: "And what is the secret of the orange?"
Lali: "That I cannot say. But why don't you ask her yourself? Now she is always trying to please you."
Kishori: "I have already asked her."
Lali: "What did she say?"

Kishori: "She said that Lali showed her an orange and gave her this advice: "Look, there are many segments in this, but because they stay together and are covered by a single peel, it is counted as one. No one can tell how many segments are inside. In the same way, we too should remain united."
Lali: "She spoke rightly."
Kishori: "Well, well! You are taking her side! You are trying to fool me like a little girl!"
Lali (laughing): "Well, don't worry, slowly you will come to know everything."

Just then, the sound of someone ascending the stairs was heard, and both of them turned to look in that direction. Kundan arrived, greeted them, and, glancing at Lali with a smile, said, "A man has come here searching for you. He says that Lali has stolen his book—the book that was written in someone's blood."

There was some hidden meaning in Kundan's words, for as soon as Lali heard them, the color drained from her face. Terror seized her entire body, and it seemed as if someone had drawn all the blood from her veins. For a while, she lost all sense of herself. At last, folding her hands, she pleaded with Kundan—
Lali: "Kundan, I have made a grave mistake. Have mercy on me! I will spend my whole life as your servant!"
Kundan: "Will you inscribe the deed of your servitude upon the hem of my veil?"
This second remark from Kundan left Lali utterly distraught. This time, she could not compose herself at all—her head began to spin, and she staggered and collapsed to the ground.

Seeing Lali in this state, Kundan quietly left the place. Yet, from her expression, it was clear that she was pleased with her own actions, or perhaps she felt she had established her authority over Lali. The way she pursed her lips and shook her head seemed to say that she intended to inflict even greater torment upon Lali.

Poor Kishori was in a strange state herself. She had already been troubled in her quest to uncover the secret of the orange, and now this new mystery twisted her heart even further. With great difficulty, she composed herself, left Lali as she was, and descended from the terrace. From her own room, she brought a glass of water and sprinkled it on Lali's face. After a short while, Lali regained consciousness and, without saying a word, weeping, went away to her own quarters. Kishori too made her way toward her room.

The room where Kishori lived was situated in the very heart of a beautiful garden. In each of the four corners of this garden stood a small building. In one of these lived all the women who had been appointed to guard Kishori. Lali was the chief among these women. In the second building, Lali lived with two or three maids. The third building, furnished in luxurious style, was allotted to Kundan. The fourth, which was the smallest, was kept locked, but from time to time, several women, armed with naked swords, would stand guard at its door.
This garden was within the women's palace, and it was exceedingly difficult for any outsider to enter or for anyone inside to escape.
chapters.summary: Kishori questions Lali about Kundan's treachery and the orange, but a cryptic exchange about a blood-written book sends Lali into a terrified collapse.

chapters.title: Warriors in Restless Slumber
paragraphs: It is the middle of the night. Silence reigns all around. Except for the sentries in King Virendra Singh's camp, all are sunk in deep, restful sleep. Yet, the sleep of a few soldiers is of a peculiar kind—one can neither call them fully awake nor count them among the truly sleeping. These men, numbering no more than a thousand, lie clad in battle attire, their fine weapons strapped to their bodies. It is winter, yet none wears any garment that might truly ward off the cold, and so the chill, carried by the sharp wind, keeps them from falling into a deep slumber.

Fatehsingh is keeping watch over King Virendra Singh's tent. He himself sits on a stool before the entrance, while his subordinate soldiers patrol around the tent, naked swords in hand. Kanchansingh stands guard over Prince Indrajit Singh's tent, and Naharsingh, with his men, protects Anand Singh's tent.

When more than half the night had passed, a man approached the entrance of Prince Indrajit Singh's tent. He saluted Kanchansingh and stood silently by his side. This man was tall and strong, with a turban wound about his head and a black Kashmiri cloak draped over his shoulders.
Kanchansingh: Who are you, and why have you come?
Man: I am a resident of the fort of Rohtasgarh, and I have brought a message from Kishoriji.
Kanchansingh: What is the message?
Man: I have orders to speak only to the prince and to no one else.
Kanchansingh: The prince is asleep at this hour!
Man: If you deem my arrival important, then take me inside the tent, or awaken the prince and inform him.
Kanchansingh: (after some thought) Indeed, in such a case, I must wake the prince. Tell me, what is your name?
Man: I cannot tell you my name, but the prince knows me well. Take me inside with you. The moment he opens his eyes, he will recognize me, and you will not need to say a word!

Kanchansingh led the man into the tent. Kanchansingh walked ahead, the man followed behind. When they reached the center of the tent, the man drew a dagger from beneath his cloak and, taking advantage of Kanchansingh's unsuspecting state, struck him so forcefully from behind on the neck that with a single blow, the head was severed and fell far away, and from the poor man's lips...

Not a sound could escape. After this, he wiped his dagger, tucked it back into his belt, and came to stand beside the deeply slumbering Kunwar Indrajit Singh. He took out a small vial from his waistband and, with great care, held it to the prince's nose. The vial contained a powerful sleeping potion. Once the prince was unconscious, he untied a cloth from his waist, wrapped the prince in it, and went to the door, peering out from behind the curtain to see if the way ahead was clear.

At that moment, the guards, making their rounds, had passed to the rear of the tent. Finding the path ahead deserted, he lifted the bundle containing the prince, slipped out of the tent, and, keeping himself hidden, moved away from the camp. Some distance from the camp, a chariot stood ready, harnessed to two strong, dusky-colored horses. The coachman sat waiting. He unwrapped the bundle, laid the prince upon the chariot, climbed in himself, and ordered the coachman to drive.
The chariot had not gone far when the coachman realized that a rider was following them. Alarmed, he said to the man inside, "Someone is riding alongside the chariot."

The chariot was urged on faster, but the rider did not give up the chase. By dawn, the chariot had traveled far and reached a place where dense forest lined both sides of the road. Then the rider spurred his horse forward, drew level with the chariot, and called out, "Enough! Stop the chariot now!"
Coachman: "Who are you, that we should stop at your command?"
Rider: "I am your father! Beware—let the chariot go no further!"

The rider held a spear in his hand. When the coachman ignored his words, the rider, having no choice, hurled his spear. Struck, the coachman fell to the ground. The startled horses bolted, running even faster, and the wheel of the chariot passed over the coachman's body.

The rider threw his spear at one of the horses. One horse, wounded, collapsed; the other also came to a halt. The man sitting inside the chariot leapt out, drew his sword, and confronted the rider. In a flash, the rider struck him down as well and dismounted. This rider was masked.

Planting his spear in the ground, the rider tied his horse to it and, with great care, lifted Kunwar Indrajit Singh from the chariot. On either side of the road, the forest was thick. Carrying the prince, he entered the jungle and laid him beneath a sal tree, then returned to his horse. After reaching the same spot again, he sat beside the prince and began to try to revive him.
The cool morning breeze roused the prince, who sat up in alarm. The rider drew his sword and stood before him. The prince, regaining his composure, stood and said:
Prince: "Is it you who brought me here?"
Rider: No, it was someone else who was taking you away. I rescued you.
Kumar: (Looking around on all sides) If you saved me from the hands of an enemy, then why do you stand before me with a sword drawn?
Rider: I have heard much praise of your bravery and valor. I have a desire to fight.
Kumar: Even though I have no weapon, I am ready to fight. Strike if you wish.

Rider: The man who was carrying you away in the chariot—I have brought his shield and sword. (Gesturing with his hand) Look, they are right beside you. Pick them up and face me. I do not wish to fight you empty-handed.

Kunwar Indrajit Singh picked up the shield and sword, and, taking a fighting stance, stood ready to face the masked rider. For a short while, the battle continued. Kumar realized that this was not a fight born of enmity. Challenging him, he said, "Are you fighting or merely playing?"
Rider: I bear you no enmity!
Kumar: Then why did you challenge me to a fight?

Rider: So that your body might regain some agility. After lying unconscious for so long, your limbs must have grown sluggish. If I were your enemy, why would I have saved you from the hands of another foe?
Kumar: Then are you our friend?
Rider: I cannot say that either.
Kumar: Surely you are our friend, if you saved us from an enemy.
Rider: Do you doubt that I saved your life?
Kumar: Of course I doubt it. How can I be sure it was you who brought me here, and not someone else?
Rider: For that, I will give you three proofs. First, if I were your enemy, I would have killed you while you were unconscious.
Kumar: Indeed. And what are the other two proofs?
Rider: Wait a moment, I will return and give you the other two proofs as well.

Saying this, the masked rider swiftly mounted his horse and rode to where the chariot stood, the one in which Kumar had been brought. One horse lay dead, the other stood apart, tied by its reins. The corpse of the ayyār who had rendered Kumar unconscious and carried him away was also lying there. A short distance behind, the charioteer's body was sprawled.

The masked rider dismounted and, with some effort, managed to overturn the chariot, which until then had been standing upright. Then he paused, pondering what to do next. His gaze fell upon the charioteer's corpse; he went over and began to drag the body...

He brought it near the chariot, set it down, and after thinking for a moment, said softly, "Now the prince cannot guess where his army is, nor from which direction he has been brought. By deceiving him, I must test both his and my own fate."
After this, the rider mounted his horse again and went to where the prince was waiting for him.
Prince: Where had you gone?
Rider: I went in search of a man, but could not find him.
Prince: Never mind, you were about to give further proof of your honesty!

The rider dismounted and said to the prince, "Please mount the horse and come with me." But the prince refused. The rider then took hold of the horse's reins and, leading the prince on foot, brought him to the chariot, explained everything, and said, "Look, it was in this very chariot that you were brought. This is the villain who brought you, and here is the second charioteer. By chance, I was coming to meet you, and so was able to be of service. Now, of the two horses of this chariot, one remains. You may ride it and return to your army!"
Prince: Indeed, you have saved my life. I shall never forget this favor.
Rider: Do you truly consider this a favor?
Prince: Certainly.
Rider: Then relieve yourself of this debt by giving me something in return.
Prince: Gladly, I am ready to do so. Ask for whatever you wish.
Rider: At this moment, I can take nothing from you. But promise me that, should I ever need something, I may ask you for it and receive your help.
Prince: I promise, whatever you ask, I shall give, whenever you wish.
Rider: See that you do not go back on your word.
Prince: Never. That is not the way of a Kshatriya.
Rider: Very well. Now let me give you one more proof: I shall leave for my home without causing you the slightest trouble.
Prince: At least remove the veil from your face, so that I may know you.
Rider: That too is necessary.
Saying this, the rider lifted the veil from her face, astonishing the prince—for she was a beautiful and youthful woman.

Indeed, except for Kishori, the prince had never seen such a lovely woman. With her sidelong glance, she captured the prince's heart, and, paying no heed to his fixed, admiring gaze, she left him as he was, descended from the road, and took the path into the forest.
After she had gone, the prince continued for some time to gaze in the direction she had disappeared...

She had mounted the horse. After this, she looked towards the chariot and the road, then went to the horse among the two chariot horses that was still alive.
