She unfastened whatever baggage was on its back, leaving only the bridle, and, mounting its bare back, took the path in the same direction in which that veiled woman had disappeared before their eyes. Hungry and thirsty, they kept riding the horse until noon, but found no trace of that woman—where she had gone or what had become of her. Tormented by hunger and thirst, they were preoccupied with the thought of finding some cool water to quench their thirst. But in this forest, there was no sign of any spring or stream. Helpless, they continued onward, and by evening, reached such a meadow, which was surrounded on all sides by dense forest, but in the middle, there was a unique pond, rippling with beautiful, clear water.

Kunwar Indrajit Singh was greatly astonished to see this strange pond and gazed at it intently. In the very center of the pond stood a small, beautiful house, surrounded on all sides by a courtyard, and at each of the four corners stood four women, armed with bows and arrows, ready and alert. It seemed as if they were about to shoot their arrows at any moment. On the roof of the house, on a small platform, another woman could be seen, her head hanging down and her feet pointing towards the sky. After watching for a long time, it became clear that these women were not living beings, but artificial—more aptly called dolls. A small dinghy was also tied to the same platform with a rope, indicating that someone surely lived in this house, for whom the dinghy was kept for coming and going.

The prince fastened the horse's bridle to a stone and descended to the edge of the pond. After washing his hands and face and drinking some water, he rested for a while, then again gazed towards that house, for the prince intended to swim across to the house and see what was inside.

As the sun was setting, a woman emerged from within the house and stood in the courtyard, looking towards the prince. Then, with a gesture of her hand, she signaled him to leave. The prince recognized her clearly—she was the same veiled rider who had rescued him from the hands of the ayyār while he was being taken away in the chariot.
chapters.summary: After being abducted, Prince Indrajit is rescued by a mysterious veiled woman who then challenges him to a duel.

chapters.title: Kishori’s Lonely Vigil
paragraphs: Some of the night had already passed. Inside the Rohtasgarh fort, in her own chamber, poor Kishori sat, lost in some unknown thought, pondering over something. No other woman was with her. At last, hearing the sound of footsteps, Kishori, lost in her reverie, lifted her head and looked towards the door. Lali entered, greeted her, and said, "Forgive me, I have come into this room without your permission."
Kishori: I have already ordered the maidservants that no one is to enter this room, and along with that, I also told them that if Lali wishes to come, she should not be stopped.
Lali: Indeed, you have shown me great kindness.
Kishori: But I do not know why you do not show the same compassion towards me! Come, sit.
Lali: (Sitting down) Please do not say such things. I am ready, with all my heart and soul, to be of service to you.

Kishori: These are all empty words. If that were truly the case, then why do you hide from me the secret concerning yourself and Kundan? I was already troubled by the matter of the Narangi, but ever since Kundan has managed to influence you with her words, my anxiety has only increased.

Lali: Certainly, you must have been greatly surprised. I can swear that what Kundan told me at that time, or the things she said that frightened me, she herself did not know beforehand. If she had known, then when I tried to threaten her by showing the Narangi, she would have taken her revenge on me right then. Now I am convinced that someone from outside has indeed entered this house, someone who has revealed our secrets to Kundan and made her aware. Alas, now my life seems destined to be lost for nothing, for Kundan is a most merciless and wicked woman.
Kishori: Your words only increase my anxiety. For mercy's sake, tell me something—what is the secret?
Lali: I will tell you everything, and I will relieve your worries, but tonight, please forgive me once more and help me with something right now.
Kishori: What is it?

Lali: I am now certain that my life cannot be saved by any means, yet I will still try whatever I can to escape. I wish, before my death, to rid this world of Kundan, but I am caught in such a dilemma that I cannot even resolve to do so. However, I do wish to know something particular about Kundan, and after that, I want to enter that house at the corner of the garden—the one that is always locked, with two women standing guard at the door in turns, each holding a naked sword. I need your help with these two things.
Kishori: Do you know what is inside that house?

Lali: Yes, I know something, and I wish to learn the rest of the secret. I am certain that if you come inside that house with me, and if both of us manage to escape safely, then you too will be freed from this captivity. But—
Entering it and coming out safely—that is the real difficulty.
Kishori: You have said something even more astonishing. Well, I would rather die than live such a life. Do whatever you must, and take whatever help you need from me.

Lali: (Taking a small picture from her waistband and handing it to Kishori) After a little while, Kundan will certainly come to you as usual. At that time, show her this picture in such a way that she does not realize you are showing it to her deliberately. Then, whatever expression appears on her face, or whatever she says, tell me about it. For now, this is the only task.
Kishori: I can do this task very well.

Kishori took the picture from Lali's hand and looked at it herself first. In this picture, a cave was depicted, in which a man was hanging upside down, and a woman, holding a dagger, was wounding him. Nearby stood a young woman, and in the corner, the earth was being dug up.

Reader, this picture was exactly of that moment whose account we have already written in the eighth chapter of the first part. But Kishori did not yet know about that incident. Kishori was deeply astonished upon seeing the picture and wanted to ask Lali something about it, but after handing over the picture, Lali did not stay there—she immediately left.

Shortly after Lali's departure, Kundan arrived. But at that moment, Kishori was so absorbed in looking at the picture that she did not even notice Kundan's arrival until Kundan came close, stood for a while, and then asked, "Well, sister, what are you looking at?"
Kishori: (startled) Oh! How long have you been standing here?
Kundan: For a little while. What is it about this picture that you are examining so intently?
Kishori: Have you seen this picture before?

Kundan: Hundreds of times. I suppose Lali gave you this picture especially to show me. You may tell Lali that I am not frightened by seeing this picture. I will never rest until I have taken my revenge, because on the very first night I met you, all my arrangements for leaving this place were perfectly in order. It was this very Lali who ruined all my efforts and trapped my helpers as well. Well, we shall see. I was pleased to meet you, but alas, she fabricated lies and turned your heart away from me. Still, I will not do you any harm, and as far as possible, I will warn you against her tricks. Whether you believe me or not is your choice.

Kishori: "Nothing makes sense to me; I cannot understand what is happening. Oh God, what crime have I committed that dangers have surrounded me from all sides? Alas, I cannot even tell who here is my friend and who my enemy."
Saying this, Kishori began to weep. She tried hard to compose herself, but could not. Sobs choked her throat. Kundan sat beside Kishori, took her hand in both of hers, and said—

"Dearest Kishori, it is very difficult to discern who your friend is here. To trust someone merely because they speak kindly is a mistake—especially in the house of an enemy. Still, I can certainly prove to you that Lali bears enmity towards you. Lali must have told you that, like you, I too have been brought here to be married to the prince. But that is not true at all; it is a complete lie. The truth is, Lali does not know me at all, nor do I know who Lali is. Yet, from the way Lali has been behaving lately, I am convinced she is plotting against you. It would not be surprising if, one day, she takes you to that house whose door is always locked and guarded by a naked sword, for lately she has been befriending the women who stand guard there and is preparing a key to open the lock. Her enmity will reach its end the day she gets you inside that house, for then your life cannot be saved by any means. To do such a thing is not only to act against you, but also to betray the king and this very kingdom. Surely, she will try to send you into that house, but you must never set foot across that threshold."
Kishori: "What is inside that house?"
Kundan: "I do not know."
Kishori: "Does anyone here know?"
Kundan: "No one. In fact, as far as I can imagine, not even the king knows what lies within."
Kishori: "Is the house never opened?"
Kundan: "Never, at least not in my presence."
Kishori: "Then how can you say that no one who enters can ever return?"

Kundan: "That is not hard to guess. First, consider that the door is always locked. Even if someone were to sneak inside, it would be nearly impossible to find a way out. And what benefit would there be for any of us to enter? You must have seen, above the door it is written: 'Whoever enters, his head will fall off by itself!' Be that as it may, despite all this, Lali will surely try to send you into that house."
Kishori: "Well then, if you know the story behind this picture, tell me."

Kundan: "I will tell you, listen—when Kunwar Indrajit Singh was deceived and taken away by Madhavi, his younger brother Anand Singh set out in search of him. A Muslim woman tricked him, captured him, and wanted to marry him, but he refused. For three days, he remained imprisoned at her place, hungry and thirsty. In the end, it was their own ayyār, Devisingh, who rescued him from that captivity, though Anand Singh still does not know that it was Devisingh who set him free."
After that, Kundan recounted everything Anand Singh had seen and heard about the picture, up to the point when Anand Singh, rendered unconscious, was taken out of the cave and even brought home.
Kishori: "How did you come to know all this?"
Kundan: "Devisingh told me."
Kishori: "What is your relation to Devisingh?"
Kundan: "We are acquainted. Have you ever heard anything from Lali about this picture?"
Kishori: "Nothing at all."
Kundan: "Ask her, let's see what she says. Well, I must go now, I'll see you again."
Kishori: "Wait a moment!"
Kundan: "Don't stop me now, it would be untimely. I'll return very soon."

Kundan left, but Kishori fell into even deeper thought than before. At times, her heart leaned toward Lali, considering her a companion in sorrow; at other times, when doubts about Lali's words crept in, she believed Kundan to be the truthful one. Her heart was torn between the two, helpless in the pull from both sides. She could not decide whether to make Lali or Kundan her confidante, for both Lali and Kundan were hiding their true secrets from Kishori.

That day, Lali came again and asked Kishori, "What happened to Kundan when she saw that picture?" To this Kishori replied, "Kundan paid no attention to the picture at all, and when I asked her myself, she said she didn't know what kind of picture it was, nor had she ever seen it before."

Hearing this, Lali's face grew somewhat sad, and she rose and left Kishori's side. Kishori called after her, "At least you could tell me what this picture is about!" But Lali gave no answer and went away.
Several days passed in this manner. The news of Kunwar Indrajit's disappearance from the camp spread everywhere, and as Kishori heard it, her melancholy deepened even more.
One night, as she lay on her bed, Kishori's mind wandered through many thoughts...

She was thinking, pondering over Lali and Kundan as well. Suddenly, she sat up and softly murmured to herself, "Now I must do something myself; lying here like this will not accomplish anything. But alas, I do not even have any weapon at hand."

Kishori climbed down from the bed and began pacing back and forth in the room. At last, she stepped outside. She saw that the guard-maids were deep in slumber. More than half the night had passed, darkness enveloped everything. Moving quietly, step by step, she made her way toward Kundan's house. As she drew near, she saw a man dressed in black hurrying in that direction—indeed, he had already reached the veranda of the room where Kundan lived. Kishori hid herself behind a tree, perhaps thinking that if the man returned, she would advance further.

After a short while, Kundan too emerged with that man, and together they slowly made their way toward the part of the garden where the trees grew thickest. When the two reached the tree behind which Kishori was concealed, the man stopped and spoke softly:
Man: "Now you go, there is no need to escort me any further."
Kundan: "Still, let me tell you, there will be no need for 'Narangi' for the next five or seven days."
Man: "Very well, but continue to show mercy to Kishori!"
Kundan: "There is no need to say that."

The man walked off toward the cluster of trees, and Kundan returned to her room. Kishori, too, did not linger there any longer and went back to her own room, lying down on her bed, for the conversation between the two—which Kishori had overheard quite clearly—had disturbed her, and she began to ponder over many things. But to whom could she confide the state of her heart? There was no one there worthy of such trust.

At first, Kishori had considered Lali to be more sincere and virtuous than Kundan, but now that belief was shaken. Kishori kept recalling the words spoken by that man: "Continue to show mercy to Kishori!"

Who was that man? It was exceedingly difficult to enter or leave this garden, so how had he come? The man's voice seemed familiar. Surely, I have spoken to him several times before, but when and where, I cannot recall, nor can I remember his face. Kundan had said, "There will be no need for Narangi for five or seven days." From this, it appears that the matter of Narangi is somehow connected to that man, and Lali knows the secret. For now, it is certain that Kundan is my well-wisher, and Lali wishes me harm. Yet, even this cannot be believed with certainty. Some secrets have been revealed, but this has only increased my confusion. Well, if I try, perhaps I will...
...will also be revealed, but for now, I must find out what has become of Lali.

For a while, Kishori pondered all these matters. At last, she rose from her bed and stepped outside her room. The maids assigned to guard her were still deep in slumber. Pausing for a moment, she made her way toward the corner of the garden where Lali's house stood. Concealing herself behind the trees, she moved cautiously, pausing now and then to listen for any sound from around her. When she reached near Lali's house, she heard the faint murmur of voices and stopped behind a grapevine bush, straining her ears to listen. She caught only these words: "Do not worry. As long as I live, Kundan cannot harm Kishori, nor can anyone else take her away. Kishori belongs to Indrajit Singh, and she will surely be delivered to him."

Kishori recognized Lali's voice. Though Lali had spoken very softly, Kishori was so close that she heard and recognized her well. However, she could not discern who the other person was. Lali was right by her room; as soon as she finished speaking, she quickly climbed a few steps and slipped inside. From that very spot, a man emerged, hiding himself among the trees as he made his way toward the back of the garden, where there was a house whose door was always kept locked. But at that very moment, loud cries of "Thief! Thief!" rang out. Kishori recognized the voice and realized it was Kundan, who was trying to trap that man. At once, Kishori hurried back to her own room, while the cries of "Thief! Thief!" grew louder and louder.

Back in her room, Kishori lay down on her bed and began to reflect on the events she had witnessed and overheard in the past two or three hours. She thought to herself, "I have now been to both Kundan and Lali, and it is clear that each of them is acquainted with a man who comes secretly to this house. From what I overheard from the man who met with Kundan, it seems that Kundan bears me no ill will; rather, she wishes to treat me kindly. Then, when I went to Lali, the conversation there revealed that Lali is truly my ally, and perhaps it is Kundan who regards me with enmity. Yes, that must be it. Now I understand—surely it is so. No, no, I must not trust Kundan's words! Very well, we shall see. Kundan raised the alarm of 'Thief! Thief!' without reason—what if poor Lali is made to suffer for it?"

Turning all these thoughts over in her mind, Kishori spent the remaining hours of the night awake, and as the first light of dawn spread, she stepped outside her room, for her heart was restless to uncover the truth of the night's happenings.
As soon as Kishori reached the veranda, she saw Kundan approaching from the front. Kundan...
He came closer, saluted, and asked, "Do you know anything about what happened last night?"
Kishori: "I know everything! It was you who made all that commotion!"
Kundan (in surprise): "What are you saying?"
Kishori: "Your voice was clearly recognizable."
Kundan: "I had only gone there after hearing the cries of 'thief, thief!' and, just like the others, I too began shouting."
Kishori (laughing): "Perhaps that's how it was."
Kundan: "Do you doubt me?"
Kishori: "Certainly. Look, here comes Lali as well."
Kundan (a little flustered): "Whatever happened, it was all her doing."
Just then, Lali also arrived and, looking at Kundan, said, "Your attack missed its mark."
Kundan (nervously): "What did I..."
Lali: "Enough, let it be. Perhaps you haven't seen much of my work, but two hours ago I had already learned all about your actions."
Kundan (distraught): "You can swear..."
Lali: "Yes, yes, I remember well; I never forget."
Kishori: "Whatever the case, I won't need any oranges for the next five or seven days."

Kishori's words startled both Lali and Kundan. There was a hint of a smile on Lali's face, but all color drained from Kundan's, for now she was convinced that Kishori had overheard everything that had happened during the night. Kundan's anxiety and confusion grew so much that she could no longer compose herself, and without saying a word, she got up and walked away toward her own chamber. Now, a conversation began between Lali and Kishori—
Lali: "It seems you too were engaged in some ayyari last night!"
Kishori: "Yes, I was secretly watching Kundan."
Lali: "Then you must have realized that Kundan intends to deceive you."

Kishori: "At first, it wasn't entirely clear, but when I came to your side and heard you speaking with someone, I became convinced that in this palace, you alone are the one from whom I can expect any kindness."
Lali: "That's right. You didn't hear everything about Kundan, but from me as well… (pausing) well, let it be. Yes, now the time has come for you and me to leave this place. Do you trust me?"
Kishori: "Certainly, I expect goodness from you. But Kundan seems to have gone completely astray."
Lali: "She cannot harm me in any way."
Kishori: "What if she tells someone about your situation?"
Lali: "She cannot say it with her own tongue, because she is just as caught in my snare as I am in hers."
Kishori: "Alas! Even after being so kind, you do not share that secret with me!"
Lali: "Do not worry! Little by little, everything will be revealed."
After this, Lali whispered something to Kishori, explained a few things, and, promising to meet again in two hours, left from there.
chapters.summary: Lost in thought, Kishori receives a mysterious picture from Lali and then faces Kundan's arrival, unsure of who to trust amidst hidden secrets.

chapters.title: The Locked Chamber’s Secret
paragraphs: We have mentioned several times above that in the garden where Kishori lived, on one side there was a building whose door always remained locked and was guarded by a naked sword.

It is midnight. Darkness has enveloped everything. The strong wind rustles the leaves of the tall trees, breaking the silence. At this moment, Lali, holding a rope in her hand, cautiously protecting herself from all sides and looking around carefully, is heading toward the back of that very building. She reaches the wall, fastens the rope, and climbs up onto the roof. All around the roof was a wall three cubits high. With great cunning, Lali broke open a hole in the roof, just large enough for a person to descend through comfortably, and she herself went down inside with the help of the rope.

After two hours, Lali emerged carrying a small chest and, using the rope, descended from the roof and set off in another direction. She entered the baradari on the eastern side, from where there was a way into the palace, slipped inside the gate, and reached the palace.

This palace was very large and magnificent. The queen herself resided here with two hundred maids and companions. Passing through several halls and doors, Lali reached the door of a small room and gently knocked on the latch.

An old woman got up, opened the door, let Lali in, and closed it again. The old woman must have been about eighty years of age, and goodness and compassion radiated from her face. The small room, the few necessary items, and the simple cot all indicated that the old woman was living her life in helplessness. Lali touched her feet in reverence, and the old woman stroked her back and asked her to sit.
Lali (placing the box in front): "Is this the one?"
Old Woman: "Did you bring it? Yes, that's right, this is certainly it. Now, whatever you do next, be very careful! Let it not be that, at this final moment, I am stained with disgrace."
Lali: "I will do the work as cleverly as possible. Please bless me, so that my endeavor may succeed."
Old Woman: "May God reward you for this good deed. Did you feel any fear there?"
Lali: "With a firm heart, I brought it here; otherwise, what I saw there is not something I could ever forget while alive. I will have to see it once more yet. Oh, my heart still trembles."
Old Woman (smiling): "Indeed, wondrous things are gathered there, but there is nothing to fear. God will help you."
Lali picked up that little chest and, returning to her own room, placed it safely and lay down on her bed. In the morning, she rose and went to Kishori's chamber.
Kishori: "All night I kept thinking of you, and again and again I got up and went outside, wondering if any sound of commotion might be heard."
Lali: "By God's grace, nothing hindered my task."
Kishori: "Come, sit by me! Now you must have hope that my life will be saved and I will be able to leave this place."
Lali: "Certainly, now I have full hope."
Kishori: "Did you find the chest?"

Lali: "Yes, thinking that there would be no opportunity during the day, I showed it to old Dadi right then. She recognized it and said that this is certainly the one. There were several chests of the same color there, but seeing the special mark that old Dadi had described, I took only this one!"
Kishori: "I too wish to see that chest."

Lali: "Of course, I could take you to my room and show you the chest, but seeing it would be of no benefit to you. Rather, your going there would arouse Kundan's suspicion, and she would wonder why Kishori went to Lali's room. There is nothing remarkable about the chest either; it is just a small, ordinary box, with no place for a lock, and so strong that it cannot be broken by any means."
Kishori: "Then how will it be opened, and how will we get the key from inside, the one we need?"
Lali: "We will file it with a rasp and make a hole in it."
Kishori: "That will take time!"
Lali: "Yes, it will take two days, because except at night, there will be no opportunity during the day."
Cannot be found.
Kishori: For me, even a single moment passes like a hundred years.
Lali: Well, after so many days, what are two more!
They continued talking for a while. After this, Lali rose and went to her own quarters, busying herself with her usual chores.

On the third night after this, at midnight, Lali stepped out of her house and came to Kishori's quarters. The maidservants assigned to guard Kishori were deep in slumber, snoring loudly, but there was not a trace of sleep in Kishori's eyes. She lay on her bed, gazing toward the door. Just then, Lali entered the room, carrying a small bundle in her hand. Seeing her, Kishori immediately stood up, and with great affection, took Lali's hand and seated her beside herself.
Kishori: Oh! These two days have passed with great difficulty. Day and night, I was filled with fear.
Lali: Why?
Kishori: Because I was afraid someone might go up to that roof and see that a hole has been made.
Lali: Hmph! Who goes up there, and who would see! Come, now there is no time to delay.
Kishori: I am ready. Is there anything I need to take?
Lali: I have everything necessary with me. You just come along.

Lali and Kishori set out from there, hiding behind trees as they made their way to the back of the house whose roof Lali had breached. Throwing up a rope, both climbed to the top, then pulled the rope up after them. Using the same rope, they descended through the hole into the house. On seeing the wonders inside, Kishori was struck with amazement, but her attention soon shifted elsewhere. As soon as Kishori and Lali entered the house, a shout rang out from outside, and at once, ten or fifteen men swiftly climbed to the roof using ropes, shouting, "Catch them! Don't let them escape! Don't let them escape!"
chapters.summary: Lali and Kishori sneak into the locked chamber at night, but their exploration is interrupted by a sudden shout and pursuing men climbing the walls.

chapters.title: The Lady of the Lake
paragraphs: Kunwar Indrajit Singh stood by the edge of the lake, gazing at the strange building and the beautiful woman. He considered swimming across to the house that stood in the very center of the lake, but the young woman gestured with her hand to stop him.
With a gesture, she forbade him—not only that, but she signaled for him to flee from there. He understood her sign and stopped, but his heart would not allow it; once again, he entered the pond.

That beautiful maiden realized that the prince would not be satisfied without coming here, so she gestured for him to wait and also indicated that she would bring a boat. The woman untied a boat, boarded it herself, and, steering it in a peculiar manner, took it toward the far corner of the pond, signaling the prince to come that way as well. The prince went in that direction and, delighted, boarded the boat with the woman. She maneuvered the boat in the same winding way and brought it near a house. Both of them disembarked and went inside.

The prince was greatly pleased by the decoration of that small house. Everything needed was present there. The central large room was beautifully adorned, with priceless mirrors, Kashmiri carpets embroidered with various flowers and patterns, small but tall marble stools decorated with ornaments and vases. There were also instruments for music and singing; the paintings on the walls had been crafted with great artistry by the painters. Beside that room was another small, decorated chamber with a bed draped in a mosquito net for sleeping. Next to it was a bathing room, its floor made of white and black stones. In the center was a small pool, into which water from the pond flowed in from one side and out the other. Besides this, there were three or four more rooms for necessary purposes, but in that house, apart from that one woman, there was no other lady, nor any servant or maid to be seen.

Seeing the house and finding no one there except that young, beautiful woman, the prince was greatly astonished. The house was such that it could not possibly be kept clean or its things maintained without four or five people. Weary and sunburnt, Prince Indrajit Singh found the place exceedingly pleasant, and, enraptured by the supernatural beauty of that lovely woman, he forgot all else. With great grace and charm, the woman led the prince into the room, seated him on a cushion, and sat before him herself.
Prince: "For all the favors you have done for me, I can never repay you."
Woman: "That is true, but I hope you will never do anything that would bring disgrace upon me."
Prince: "No, no, never expect such a thing from me. But what is the reason you say this?"
Woman: "In this house, where I live alone, your coming in this manner and staying for long will certainly be the cause of my dishonor."

Prince (after some thought): "Why are you so beautiful? Alas! Every gesture of yours draws me toward you. (hesitantly) Be that as it may, I should leave this place now. If this was to be the case, then why did you bring me here on the boat?"

Woman: "I had already signaled you to leave, but when you began swimming toward this place, I was helpless and had to do this. I could not knowingly let a man fall into trouble, especially one whose life I myself had saved from a cruel, cunning enemy. Do not think that anyone can simply swim across this pond and reach here, for nets have been cast all around it. If anyone tries to swim here, he will surely get entangled in the nets and lose his life. That is why I had to bring the boat for you."

Prince: "Of course, for that too I must thank you. Forgive me, I did not know that my coming here would cause you trouble. Now I shall go, but please, at least tell me your name, so that I may remember that such-and-such woman helped me in my time of need."
Woman (laughing): "I do not wish to tell you my name, nor do I ask you to leave in this heat. Rather, I hope you will accept my hospitality."
Prince: "Well, well! At times you make me your guest, and at others you order me to leave. Do as you please."
Woman (laughing): "Well, let all that be for later. For now, please rise and have something to eat, for I know you have not eaten anything yet."
Prince: "I have not even performed my bath and evening prayers. But I am surprised that I see no maidservant with you here."
Woman: "Do not worry about that. I am your maidservant myself. Please sit for a moment; I shall set everything in order and return at once."

Saying this, without waiting for the prince's consent, the woman rose and went into an adjoining room. After she left, the prince began to pace the room, examining each object closely. Suddenly, his eyes fell upon a scrap of paper pressed beneath a bouquet. It would not have been proper to pick up and read that note, but he was compelled. Several letters of the note, left visible from being pressed under the bouquet, were clearly legible, and those very letters forced the prince to take out the note and read it. The letters were:
"Kishori"
Helplessly, the prince took out the note and read what was written:
"As per your instructions, all actions are proceeding well. Lali and Kundan are laying their traps skillfully. Kishori too has been thoroughly deceived. Kishori's lover…"

are also present here, and she has high hopes for Kishori. I too have done work worthy of a reward. At this moment, the situation is taking on a strange new color, but never mind, in two or three days I will write you a detailed account.
Your servant: "Tara"

The prince quickly read the note and put it away as before, then came and sat down on the cushion. Thoughts and worries closed in on him from all sides. This note had completely changed the state of his heart. At this moment, even a true friend could not have discerned his condition by looking at his face. However, after pondering for a while, the prince finally let out a long sigh and openly said, "Well, where can the wretch go! I am not one to leave without doing something."

Just then, the woman also arrived and said, "Get up, everything is ready." The prince went with her to the bathing chamber, where there was a cistern. A dhoti, towel, and all the items for worship were present there. The prince bathed and performed his evening prayers. The woman brought him some sweets and milk confections on a silver tray and left, then returned again to bring water for drinking. At that very moment, the prince heard two women talking in the adjoining room. He was surprised—where had these other women come from! The prince finished his meal, washed his hands and face, and was about to step outside the chamber when the door in front of him opened and two women appeared. At the sight of them, the prince started in surprise and exclaimed, "Ah! How did these two come here!"
chapters.summary: Kunwar Indrajit Singh finds himself in a strange house in the middle of a lake with a mysterious woman, Kishori, and a troubling note.

chapters.title: A Midnight Meeting on the Plain
paragraphs: In the dead of night, two young women walked together across a desolate plain, conversing quietly. Along the way, they had to cross small mounds, which they did with some difficulty, occasionally stopping to catch their breath before continuing. From this, it was clear that they were in urgent need of reaching a particular place or meeting someone at this very hour. Our readers are already well acquainted with these two women, so there is no need to describe their appearance—for one is Kinnari, and the other is Kamla.
Kinnari: "Kamla, look, this is what they call the twists of fate. By all accounts, we had completed our work in Gayaji, but alas!"

Kamla: "You did everything you could to help Kishori, with all your heart and soul. Surely Kishori will remember you all her life, and she will consider you her sister. Well, never mind, we must not lose courage, nor should we ever forget God."

I keep thinking of poor Anand Singh again and again. He truly loves you, but not knowing anything about your condition, who knows what thoughts must be arising in his heart. Yes, if he knew that the one his heart loves is safe and well, he would surely be happy.
Kinnari (sighing deeply): "As God wills!"
Kamla: "Look, the wall of that old building is coming into view."
Kinnari: "Yes, that's right, we've arrived now."

With this, the two of them reached a dilapidated building whose wide walls and grand gates spoke of the honor it must have once held in some bygone era. Even though the structure was now in a wretched state, besides the small chambers, several large halls and rooms still remained.

They both entered the building. In the middle, there was a heap of lime, mortar, and bricks, beside which the two circled around and reached a hall. In this hall, there was a small room to one side. Kamla went inside and lit a candle, then began to look around. Beside her, built into the wall, was a cupboard with two handles for pulling open the panel. Handing the candle to Kinnari, Kamla gripped both handles with her hands and turned them three or four times. Instantly, the panel swung open, revealing a small chamber within. Both of them entered the chamber and closed the panels behind them. On the inside of these panels, there were also handles for opening and closing them in the same way.
In this chamber was a cellar, with small steps leading down. The two descended and saw a man sitting there, a candle burning before him as he wrote something.

This man appeared to be about sixty years old. More than half the hair on his head and mustache had turned white, yet there was no sign of weakness in his body. His hands and feet were sturdy and strong, and his broad chest spoke of his valor. Though his complexion was dusky, his face was handsome and commanding. The brilliance of youth still shone in his large eyes, and the fitted mirzai he wore suited him well. His head was bare, but nearby on the ground lay a white turban, which, judging by its placement, he had removed due to the heat. In his left hand was a fan, with which he was trying to keep cool, though the dampness of sweat was still visible on his body.

To one side, in a clay vessel, a small fire burned, upon which some fragrant substance was smoldering, filling the cellar with a pleasant aroma. Hearing the footsteps of Kamla and Kinnari, he had already turned his attention toward the stairs, and as soon as he saw them, he said, "So, you both have come?"
Kamala: "Yes, indeed!"
Man (gesturing toward Kinnari): "Is her name Kamini?"
Kamala: "Yes."
Man: "Kamini! Come, my child, sit beside me. Just as I consider Kamala my own, I regard you the same."
Kamini: "Certainly, just as Kamala does, I too consider you my real uncle."
Man: "Do not worry about anything. As far as I am able, I will help you. (Looking at Kamala) Do you have any news from Rohtasgarh?"
Kamala: "I went there yesterday, but I could not find out much. I had promised to meet you here, so I returned quickly."
Man: "It has only been about a watch since I myself came from Rohtasgarh."
Kamala: "Then surely you must have learned a great deal about the situation there."

Man: "No one could know more about that place than I. For twenty-five years, I served the king there with honesty and honor. Even though now Digvijay Singh has become our enemy, still, I would never do anything to harm that kingdom. Yes, for your sake, I will certainly help Kishori."
Kamala: "Digvijay Singh became upset with you for no reason."

Man: "No, no, he did not act without cause. When he wishes to keep Kishori with him by force, and he knows that Kamala, the niece of Sher Singh the Aiyyar, is serving Kishori and is skilled in the arts of disguise, and that she will try every trick to rescue Kishori, then it was only prudent for him to be wary of me, no matter how loyal and upright I may be considered. His intention to imprison me was not unjustified. Alas! There was a time when Randhir Singh (Kishori's grandfather) and Digvijay Singh were friends, I served Digvijay Singh, and my younger brother—your father (may God grant him heaven)—lived with Randhir Singh. Look now, how everything has turned upside down. I fled, fearing wrongful imprisonment, but people will surely say that Sher Singh betrayed them."
Kamala: "When you do not speak ill of Rohtasgarh from your heart, what does it matter what people say? Why would they malign you?"

Sher Singh: "Yes, that is true. Well, let us leave these matters aside. Ah, poor Kundan was thoroughly outwitted by Lali. If I had not known one of Lali's secrets and warned Kundan, Lali would surely have ruined her. Kundan too made a mistake; if she had told Lali the truth about herself, they might have become friends."
Kamala: "Is there any news of Kunwar Indrajit Singh?"
Sher Singh – Yes, I know. He has been trapped by that very witch who lives in the Ajayabghar.
Kamla – Which Ajayabghar?
Sher Singh – The one built in the middle of the pond, which I have resolved to dig up and destroy from its very foundations. It is not far from here.
Kamla – Yes, I have heard of it. Many strange tales are told about that place.
Sher Singh – Indeed, everything about it is filled with wonder. Alas, who knows how many handsome young men have been mercilessly killed there!
Just then, the sound of footsteps was heard above, on the roof. The attention of all three turned to the stairs.
Kamla – Someone is coming.
Sher Singh – We were not expecting anyone here. Be on your guard.
Kamla – I am ready. Look, there he comes!

A tall man descended the stairs and came to stand before Sher Singh. Whatever his true age might have been, the weakness of his body, his thinness, and the sorrow etched on his face made him appear older than fifty years. On his once-handsome face were marks of sadness and grief. In his large eyes, the trace of tears was clearly visible; his gaze, full of longing, revealed the state of his heart and seemed to say that sorrow, worry, anxiety, and despair had drained his body of blood and flesh, leaving only bone. His clothes, too, were very old and tattered.

From this man's appearance, one could discern honesty and simplicity, yet Sher Singh, upon seeing him, trembled. Fear and astonishment choked his throat. He was suddenly as startled as one who beholds the face of a bloodthirsty executioner. Looking at him, Sher Singh stammered, "Ah... you...! Please... come..." But these words, broken and faltering, barely escaped his lips, so overcome was he with agitation.
The man gestured toward Kamla and said, "Is this girl...?"
Sher Singh – Yes... you... (glancing at Kamla and Kamini) You two, please go upstairs for a while. This is a very noble man, he has come to see me. I wish to speak with him alone.

Kamla and Kamini both left the cellar and went upstairs. The arrival of this man, and seeing her uncle in such a strange state, made Kamla anxious. Many thoughts began to stir in her mind. Why would her uncle, so skilled and lion-hearted in the art of disguise, be so shaken upon seeing such a weak, helpless, and poor man?

She was troubled, wondering why he had been so startled and frightened. Poor Kamini, too, was bewildered and afraid; so much so that even after an hour had passed, neither of them spoke a word to each other. After an hour, the man emerged from the underground chamber and, glancing at Kamini, said, "Now you two go down. I am leaving." With that, he left, opening the door in the same manner as Kamla had when she brought Kamini into this house.

Kamla and Kamini went down into the underground chamber and sat before Sher Singh. The fear and anxiety had still not left Sher Singh's face. With great difficulty, after a while, he composed himself and, looking at Kamla, said:
Sher Singh: "Well, what should we do now?"
Kamla: "We must do whatever you command. Who was that man, whom upon seeing you…?"
Sher Singh: "He was just a man. Do not try to learn anything about him, nor even think of him. In fact, forget him entirely."
Kamla wished very much to know more about that man, but receiving such a direct answer from her uncle, she could not press further and was forced to keep her curiosity buried in her heart.

Sher Singh: "Kamla, go to Rohtasgarh and return in two or three days to tell me all that has happened there. Meet with Kishori, give her courage, and tell her not to be afraid. Enter the fort by the same path I told you about, and come straight into the garden where Kishori resides. No one will ever know if you use that way."
Kamla: "Very well. But what are your orders regarding Kamini?"

Sher Singh: "I will take her with me and entrust her to a friend of mine. She will be quite safe and comfortable there. When all the troubles have subsided, I will bring her back, and then she, too, will attain her heart's desire."
Kamla: "As you wish."
The three of them left the underground chamber and, as described above, made their way through the rooms and corridors and out of the house.
Sher Singh: "Kamla, now you go, and do not worry about Kamini. This is the best place for us to meet."
Kamla: "Very well, I shall go. But at least tell me—how cautious should I be of the man who came to meet you?"
Sher Singh (in a stern voice): "I have already told you once to forget about him. There is no need to be wary of him, and you will never see him again."
chapters.summary: Kamla and Kinnari meet with Sher Singh in secret, where a mysterious visitor arrives, leaving Sher Singh shaken and Kamla curious about the stranger's identity.

chapters.title: Darkness Beneath Rohtasgarh’s Forest
paragraphs: All around the fort of Rohtasgarh lies a dense forest, where the thick shade of towering trees—sal, shisham, tendu, asan, and salai—casts a kind of perpetual gloom. Night is another matter altogether, but even by day, it was difficult to discern any path or trail, for the golden rays of the sun rarely found their way to the ground through the thick canopy of leaves. In some places, thanks to the smaller trees, the forest was so impenetrable that those who lost their way could hardly hope to escape. At such times, thousands of men could hide within it so completely that, even if one were to search and scour a thousand times over, it would be impossible to find them. Darkness reigned in this forest even during the day, but now we write of the night, when its shadows and the deep silence would seem to announce death itself to any lost traveler, and for the earth there, the nights of the new moon and the full moon were all the same.

On the right side of the fort, in the forest at midnight, we see three figures wandering—each cloaked in black robes and veiled, their identities concealed. Who knows what they seek, or what land they search for in such bewilderment? Among them are Kunwar Anand Singh, Bhairon Singh, and Tara Singh. After wandering for some time, the three arrived at a small walled enclosure, the surrounding wall of which was no higher than five cubits, and where the trees were less dense, the undergrowth thinner. Here and there, moonlight even touched the ground.
Anand Singh: "Perhaps this is the enclosure?"
Bhairon Singh: "Certainly, this is it. Look, there is a heap of bones at the gate."
Tara Singh: "Well, let us go inside and see what we find."
Bhairon Singh: "Wait a moment! The rustling of leaves suggests someone is coming this way!"
Anand Singh: (listening intently) "Yes, you are right. We should hide and see who it is, and why they come here."

All three, alert to the approach of the newcomer, concealed themselves behind the trees. Soon, they saw a woman dressed in white coming towards them. She paused at the gate, listened carefully for any sound around her, and then slipped inside. Bhairon Singh said to Anand Singh, "You two wait here; I will follow this woman and see where she goes." The others agreed, and Bhairon Singh, keeping himself hidden, set off after her.
Even within that enclosure, despite the dense forest, there were neither trees nor undergrowth—

It was indeed a matter of astonishment. Bhaironlil found the ground there to be very clean and tidy, though there were ten or twenty small wild jujube trees, which could neither cause any harm nor provide cover for anyone to hide behind. However, the abundance of dead animals and their bones made the place exceedingly dreadful. Inside that walled enclosure, there were many graves, some freshly dug, others made of brick, lime, and stone. In the garden stood the largest grave, made of marble.

As soon as Bhaironsingh set foot inside the gate, he saw the woman he had been following standing atop the large marble grave in the center, looking all around. But in just a moment, before his very eyes, she vanished. Bhaironsingh approached the grave and searched for her, but found no trace. He looked around the other graves and here and there as well, but found no sign. Helpless, he returned to Anand Singh and Tara Singh and said—
Bhairon: That woman has gone exactly where we wish to go.
Anand: Indeed!
Bhairon: Yes, exactly.
Anand: What do you suggest now?
Bhairon: Let her go. Come, let us also proceed there. Even if we meet her on the way, what harm can it do? That one woman cannot do us any damage.

The three men entered the walled enclosure and, reaching the large marble grave in the center, stood there. Bhaironsingh began to carefully feel the ground around the grave. In a short while, there was a clicking sound, and a small piece of stone, which must have been held in place by a spring, swung open like a door. The three men entered through it and closed the stone behind them in the same way before proceeding further. Now they found themselves in a tunnel, very narrow and long. Bhaironsingh took a candle from his pouch, lit it, and after carefully surveying the surroundings, led the way forward. Soon, the tunnel ended, and they reached a large hall. The ceiling of this hall was very high, and from beams hung several chains. On the other side of the hall was another door, through which they entered a small room. Beneath this room was a cellar, with marble stairs leading down. The three descended.

Now, the sound of a large bell ringing reached their ears, causing them to pause for a moment. It seemed that in a room adjacent to the cellar, a bell was being rung. The three suspected that there were several other people present there as well.

In this underground chamber, there was another door on the opposite side. As Bhaironsingh approached it, he extinguished the candle and quietly opened the door. Peering through, he saw a grand, imposing barahdari with marble pillars. In this pavilion, two torches were burning, their light illuminating every object clearly. By this light, ten or fifteen people could be seen, among whom were three women bound with ropes.

Bhaironsingh recognized that one of these women was Kishori, whose hands were tightly tied behind her back, her head bowed as she wept. The two women beside her were in the same condition, but neither Bhaironsingh, Anand Singh, nor Tarasingh recognized them. Behind the three women stood three men with drawn swords, whose appearance and attire revealed them to be executioners.

In the very center of the barahdari, upon a silver throne, sat an enormous statue of black stone—so large that even a man standing beside it could not lay his hand upon the statue's head. As for the features of the statue, it suffices to say that it resembled a demon, so terrifying that one felt fear simply to look upon it.
Bhaironsingh, Tarasingh, and Anand Singh stood there, watching to see what was happening in the hall. The sound of the bell now rang out loudly, though it was impossible to tell from where it came.

The three women, including Kishori, were firmly seized by six men and, one by one, brought before the black statue. Their heads were forced down at its feet before being pulled back and made to stand in front of it.

Then two men led forward one of the women—whom none of our three heroes recognized. The executioner with the drawn sword also stepped forward behind her. The two men shoved the woman so violently towards the statue that she fell helplessly to the ground. Instantly, the executioner struck with his sword, severing her head, which rolled away and began to convulse.
At this sight, the two remaining women—one of whom was poor Kishori—cried out in terror and collapsed unconscious to the floor.

Witnessing this scene, our two ayyars and Kunwar Anand Singh were seized by a strange agitation; they trembled with rage. After a moment, the captors lifted Kishori and led her towards the statue, the second executioner stepping forward as well. Now, the three could bear it no longer. Kunwar Anand Singh cried out to the ayyars, "Strike down these tyrants! There are only a few of them—what are they to us!"

The three men drew their daggers and were about to rush forward when several others came from behind and seized them as well, shouting, "These are the ones! These are the ones! They should be sacrificed first!"
Part Four
chapters.summary: Anand Singh, Bhairon Singh, and Tara Singh follow a mysterious woman into a hidden chamber where they witness a horrifying ritual and are subsequently captured.

chapters.title: The Chamber of Wonders
paragraphs: Now, let us resume our tale from the point where, inside the fort of Rohtasgarh, Kishori, accompanied by Lali, entered that chamber of wonders through a secret passage. The lock of this chamber was always kept shut, and there was always a guard posted at its door. As we have written earlier, the moment Lali and Kishori entered this building, several men climbed onto the roof and began shouting, "Catch them! Seize them! Do not let them escape!" Lali and Kishori heard these cries. Kishori was frightened, but Lali at once reassured her, saying, "Do not be afraid. These people can do us no harm."

Descending from the roof, Lali and Kishori reached a small room that was completely empty. On three sides of this room, there were three doors. One was the main door, outside of which the guard was usually stationed. The second door was open, and seemed to lead to a corridor or another room. In haste, Lali only said that she had once gone through this way to fetch the key. On the third side, there was a small door, its lock embedded directly into the panel itself. Using the very key she had taken from this chamber of wonders, Lali unlocked the door, and both of them slipped inside. Lali then locked the sturdy door from the inside with the same key. The lock was set in such a way that the same key could be used from both outside and inside.¹ Lali performed this task with great speed, so much so that after they had entered, those who were pursuing them—coming down through the broken roof—could only then descend into the small room below. Locking the door from within, Lali said, "Now we are safe. The only fear is that someone might come by another route and trouble us, but—
1. Wherever in this building Lali unlocked a door, she did so with this very key and in this very manner.
As far as I know, and from all that I have heard, I am certain that there is no other way to enter this House of Wonders."

Lali and Kishori now reached a room whose ceiling was so low that one could touch it simply by raising a hand. The room was completely dark. Lali opened her bundle, took out some things, and lit a candle. It became clear that this was a small chamber, with walls of stone all around—very smooth and solid. Lali began searching to see if there was any passage or door leading from this place to another.

She found a door set into the floor, which she opened, and, candle in hand, descended. After going down some twenty or twenty-five steps, both of them entered a tunnel that stretched far into the distance. They had gone perhaps three hundred paces when a voice reached their ears—
"Ah! Kill me at once! Why torment me so?"
Hearing this, Kishori trembled and stopped, asking Lali, "Sister, what is this voice? It is thin, and seems to be that of a woman!"
Lali replied, "I do not know what this voice is, nor did old Manji ever tell me anything about it."
Kishori said, "It seems someone is tormenting a woman. What if that person torments us as well? We are both unarmed, not even a dagger between us."

Lali answered, "I have brought two daggers with me—one for myself, and one for you." (She drew a dagger from her waist and handed it to Kishori.) "Here, you keep one. I well remember that once you said you would rather die than stay here—so why be afraid? Look, I am ready to give my life with you."
Kishori said, "Indeed, I did say that, and I still mean it. Come, let us go on. There is no harm now; we have daggers in hand, and God is our protector."

They moved forward again. After another twenty or twenty-five steps, the tunnel ended and they found themselves in a hall. Here, a lamp was burning, containing at least a whole seer of oil, its light spreading all around so that every object was clearly visible. In the very center of this hall stood a pillar, and tied to it was a beautiful young woman, no more than twenty years old. Beside her, on a small stone stool, sat an old man in clean, light clothing, cutting something with a knife. His face was turned toward the direction where Lali and Kishori stood, observing the scene. There was also a lamp burning before the old man, by whose light his features were clearly visible. The old man must have been about seventy years old; his white beard reached down to his navel, and both his beard and mustache—
had covered most of his face.

Seeing the strange state of that veranda, both Kishori and Lali hesitated, and they wished to turn back. But where could they go if they turned around? This thought rooted their feet to the spot. The old man, too, heard the sound of their footsteps, raised his head, looked at them, and said, "Well, well! Lali and Kishori have come too! Come, come, I have been waiting for you for a long time!"
chapters.summary: Venturing into a hidden tunnel beneath the fort, Kishori and Lali hear a woman's cries and discover a mysterious old man torturing a captive young.

chapters.title: Chaos After Kanchan’s Death
paragraphs: The killing of Kanchan Singh and the disappearance of Kunwar Indrajit Singh caused great commotion in the camp. Spies were sent out in all directions to gather information. The ayyaars also spread out here and there, striving with all their might to quell the unrest. With the permission of Raja Virendra Singh, Tej Singh too set out, and, changing his disguise, entered the fort of Rohtasgarh.

There was strict security at the main gate of the fort, but no one suspected Tej Singh in his fakir's guise. Disguised as a sadhu, Tej Singh wandered inside Rohtasgarh fort for seven days. In this time, he thoroughly observed and understood every neighborhood, market, alley, road, temple, and dharamshala. Several times, he even attended the court, paying close attention to Raja Digvijay Singh, his ministers, and the ayyaars—their ways and conversations. He also discovered whom Raja Digvijay Singh favored, whom he honored, and whom he considered trustworthy. During these seven days, Tej Singh also had to disguise himself as a chobdar and as a woman several times, entering fine houses to observe and listen to their conditions and affairs.

Once, Tej Singh even went to that very Shiva temple where Bhairon Singh and Badrinath had performed their ayyari, or from where Kunwar Kalyan Singh had been captured. Tej Singh found the residents and priests of that Shiva temple in a peculiar state. Ever since Kunwar Kalyan Singh had been arrested, such fear had taken hold of their hearts that they startled and trembled at every little thing. At night, even the rustling of a leaf made them suspect the arrival of an ayyaar. They had grown to detest the appearance of any sadhu or Brahmin; at the mere sight of a sanyasi, Brahmin, or sadhu, they would immediately declare, "He is an ayyaar!" Even if a laborer was found standing before the temple, they would at once take him for an ayyaar, and would not rest until they had seized him by the neck and thrown him out of the gate.

By chance, today Tej Singh too, in the guise of a sadhu, entered the Shiva temple. The priests, upon seeing him, immediately began to shout, "Ayyaar! Ayyaar! Catch him, don't let him escape!" Poor Tej Singh was greatly alarmed and astonished.

They began to wonder how these people had found out that they were ayyars, for Tejsingh had not even the slightest suspicion that even the dogs and cats of this place would recognize them as ayyars. However, he did not think it wise to suddenly flee from there, so he stayed and said—
Tejsingh: "How do you know that we are ayyars?"

A priest replied, "Oh, we know very well! No one except an ayyar could stand before us! It was you people who captured our Kunwar Sahib, wasn't it? Or was it someone else? Enough, enough—leave this place at once, or we'll grab you by the ears and eat you alive!"

Upon hearing "Enough, enough—leave this place," and so on, Tejsingh understood that these people were fools. If they were truly convinced that he was an ayyar, they would never have simply told him to leave; instead, they would have tried to arrest him. Clearly, Bhaironsingh and Badrinath had frightened them, nothing more.

Tejsingh was still standing there, deep in thought, when suddenly a lame beggar arrived, leaning on a stick and carrying a broken clay bowl, loudly singing the priests' praises. At the sight of him, one of the priests cried out, "Look, another ayyar has arrived! This time the devil has come disguised as a cripple! Don't you know we can see right through you? Get lost, or I'll break your head!"

Now Tejsingh was completely certain that these people had lost their wits. Whoever they saw, they immediately took for an ayyar. Tejsingh turned away from there and, pondering as he went, slipped through a window in the wall and made his way into the jungle, thinking that now he should meet the ayyars of this place and see what kind of men they were, and how skilled they were in the art of ayyari.

Inside this fort, there were several shops selling hemp drinks, which the locals called "addas." As soon as the lamps were lit in the evening, the ganja-smokers would gather there, and the owner of the adda would prepare and serve the ganja, collecting payment in return. There, all sorts of wild tales were spun, mixing truth and falsehood, so that people would learn all the news of the city.

Before evening fell, Tejsingh returned from the jungle. Disguised as a hermit, he entered the fort alongside some woodcutters and went straight to the adda, where the ganja-smokers were taking puff after puff, filling the air with clouds of smoke. Here, Tejsingh found much useful information. He learned that the Maharaj had only two ayyars: one named Ramanand, the other Govindsingh. Govindsingh had gone to Chunar to rescue Kambar Kalyansingh, while Ramanand was still here. The next day, Tejsingh—

[1. All around the great outer wall of the Rohtasgarh fort were many small windows, each fitted with strong iron doors, guarded at all times by two soldiers. Fakirs, beggars, and poor townsfolk would often use these windows (small doors) to go out into the jungle to gather dry wood, pick wild fruits, or attend to necessary business. But as soon as the lamps were lit in the evening, these windows would be closed.]

In the court, Tejsingh observed Ramanand closely and made up his mind: tonight, he would perform ayyari with Ramanand, for Ramanand's build greatly resembled his own. It was also well known that the Maharaj trusted Ramanand above all others and considered him his most loyal confidant.

At midnight, when all was silent, Tejsingh scaled the wall of Ramanand's house with a rope. He saw that on the topmost floor, Ramanand lay snoring atop a mosquito net. Instead of a curtain, a mesh hung at the door, adorned with tiny bells. At first, Tejsingh took it for an ordinary curtain, but being both clever and cautious, he did not deem it wise to touch it carelessly. He examined it closely and soon realized that the fool had hung many bells on this mesh curtain. Tejsingh thought, "What a simpleton! He believes these bells will protect him—that if anyone enters, the sound will wake him. But he does not understand that ayyaars are not so easily thwarted."

Tejsingh took a pair of scissors from his pouch and, with great care, began to cut off the bells one by one. In a short while, he had removed all the bells and set them aside. He then lifted the curtain and entered. Ramanand was still snoring. Tejsingh held a drug of unconsciousness beneath his nose; with a single light breath, it took effect upon his mind. Ramanand sneezed once, which assured Tejsingh that the stupor would not leave him for many hours.

Tejsingh then took a razor from his pouch and shaved off Ramanand's beard and mustache, carefully storing the hair in his pouch. He then affixed a new beard and mustache of the same color, which he had prepared earlier that day in the forest outside the fort. This was the sole purpose of Tejsingh's visit to Ramanand's house; having accomplished it, he descended by rope and made his way toward the dharmashala.

When Tejsingh had entered the fort of Rohtasgarh in the guise of a vairagi sadhu, he had rented a small room in the house of a caretaker near the dharmashala¹, and from there he conducted his work. The room had a door opening onto the street, which he kept locked, always carrying the key with him. Thus, day or night, he could come and go as he pleased.

After finishing his task at Ramanand's house, Tejsingh descended while a quarter of the night still remained. He went to his room near the dharmashala, and before dawn, transformed his appearance to resemble Ramanand's. He carefully affixed the very beard and mustache he had shaved off, then stepped out of his room and began to patrol the city. As dawn broke—
¹ There was only one dharmashala in Rohtasgarh.
They set off towards the royal palace and, after sending word ahead, arrived before the Maharaj.

As we have mentioned earlier, in Rohtasgarh there were only two real ayyars: Ramanand and Govindsingh. It is necessary to elaborate a little about these two. Of the two, Govindsingh was extremely skilled and clever in the art of ayyari, and he practiced it day and night. Ramanand too was well-versed in the craft, but he was very fond of his beard and mustache, so he only undertook those ayyari tasks that did not require him to shave them off. For this reason, the Maharaj had also entrusted him with the duties of a minister. There is no doubt that Ramanand was very cheerful, witty, and intelligent, and by his cleverness, he had won the Maharaj's heart completely.
Disguised as Ramanand, Tejsingh arrived before the Maharaj. Seeing Ramanand arrive much earlier than usual, the Maharaj assumed he brought some new information.
Maharaj: "You have come very early today! Is there some new news?"
Ramanand (in a confidential tone): "Maharaj, three guests arrived at our place yesterday."
Maharaj: "Who are they?"
Ramanand: "First, a cough, which has troubled me greatly; second, Kunwar Anand Singh; and third, his four ayyars, who claim they will take Kishori away from here within a day or two."
Maharaj (laughing): "These are delicate guests indeed. Has any arrangement been made for their hospitality or not?"

Ramanand: "That is precisely why I have come to you, Your Majesty. Their ayyars were present in the court yesterday. First and foremost, we must make arrangements for Kishori; there should be no lapse in her protection."
Maharaj: "As far as I understand, they will not be able to take Kishori away by any means. However, Virendra Singh's ayyars, by whatever means possible, must be captured."

Ramanand: "Virendra Singh's ayyars will not escape my grasp now. They will certainly come to the court in disguise, and if fate allows, I will capture one of them today itself. But they are extremely cunning and clever. They often manage to escape even from prison."
Maharaj: "Well, if they manage to escape from our underground cells, then we shall admit they are truly clever and cunning."

From this brief conversation, Tejsingh realized that there was some underground cell here where prisoners were kept. Now he became determined to learn as much as possible about this cell. With this thought, Tejsingh, through his artful and engaging conversation, so entangled the Maharaj that, even beyond the usual time, for half an hour...

It had grown quite late. By doing this, Tejsingh's intention was that, with the delay, the real Ramanand would surely come to the Maharaj, and upon seeing me, he would be startled. At that very moment, I would accomplish the task for which I have brought his beard and mustache! And in the end, Tejsingh's thinking proved correct.

When Tejsingh, in the guise of Ramanand, had come to the Maharaj, all the guards stationed at the palace gate were replaced, and new guards, according to their turn, took up their posts at the entrance. These new guards were completely unaware that Ramanand had gone into the palace to meet the Maharaj.

At the appointed time, the court was convened. High-ranking officials, deputy diwans, revenue officers, clerks, administrators, and other courtiers gathered in the hall. The real Ramanand took his seat upon the diwan's cushion, but he was entirely unaware of the state of his beard. He knew nothing of Tejsingh's scheme, yet he was deeply troubled, trying to discover who had cut the bells from the latticed curtain at the door. He questioned everyone in the household and made inquiries, but could not find out. This led him to suspect that some ayyār had indeed entered the house, but what he had done after coming in was not known. However, the ayyār had certainly destroyed his belief that no one could enter his room silently through the latticed curtain adorned with bells. Now it was clear that someone could indeed enter that way. Surely, it was his mistake to place so much trust in that curtain. But had the ayyār come only to prove this point?

Pondering all these matters, Ramanand finished his necessary tasks, dressed himself in courtly attire, and set out for the court. Indeed, he was somewhat late today and thought that the Maharaj must already have arrived in the court. But upon reaching there, he found the royal seat empty, and upon inquiry, learned that there was still no news of the Maharaj's arrival. Not only Ramanand, but all the courtiers were astonished as to why the Maharaj was delayed today.

The Maharaj held Ramanand in high regard; he was a favorite of the king. Therefore, everyone asked him to go and find out the situation. Ramanand himself was anxious and wished to learn of the Maharaj's condition. Thus, after sitting for a short while, he departed and went to the palace gate to make inquiries.

Meanwhile, Tejsingh, in the guise of Ramanand, was sitting and conversing with the Maharaj when a servant arrived, folded his hands, and stood before them. From his demeanor, it was clear that he was anxious and wished to say something, but no words would come from his mouth. Tejsingh understood that something was about to happen. At last, looking at the servant, he spoke—
Tejsingh: "Well, what is it you wish to say?"
Attendant: With some trepidation, I must report, with astonishment, that Diwan Sahib (Ramanand) is present at the gate.
Maharaj: Ramanand!
Attendant: Yes, Your Majesty.
Maharaj: (Looking towards Tejsingh) What is the meaning of this?

Tejsingh: (Smiling) Maharaj, now the matter is about to be resolved. What I have already stated remains true. Some ayyār has come in my likeness and wishes to deceive you. Allow me, I shall arrest this wretch at once, and then we shall see. Please order that he be admitted first, and then watch the spectacle I shall create. Allow me to hide for a moment; once he is seated, I shall expose his disguise.
Maharaj: What you say is right; surely, it must be an ayyār. Very well, go and hide, and then I shall summon him.

Tejsingh: Excellent, I shall hide. But, Your Majesty, please pay close attention to his beard and mustache. I shall leap out from behind the curtain and tear off his beard, for a false beard needs but a single jerk to come away.
Maharaj: (Laughing) Very well, very well! (Looking at the attendant) Listen, say nothing else to him—simply convey the order to present himself.

Tejsingh went and concealed himself in another room, and the real Ramanand slowly made his way to where the Maharaj was seated. Ramanand was puzzled as to why the Maharaj had delayed in admitting him, and so his face bore a trace of anxiety. The beard was the same one Tejsingh had affixed. When crafting the beard, Tejsingh had deliberately introduced a slight difference, which Ramanand had not noticed, but which now caught the Maharaj's eye. The Maharaj began to regard his Diwan Sahib with the same suspicious gaze one reserves for a masquerader, without uttering a word. Seeing this, Ramanand grew even more uneasy, wondering why there was such a change in the Maharaj's demeanor at this moment.

As the color of Ramanand's face shifted with anxiety and astonishment, so too did the Maharaj's suspicion that he was an ayyār grow firmer in his heart. Several moments passed, yet neither did Ramanand dare to speak, nor did the Maharaj bid him to sit. Tejsingh saw this as a most opportune moment, and at once emerged from his hiding place, laughing, and offered Ramanand a deep, formal salute. Astonishment, anxiety, and fear drained the color from Ramanand's face, and he stared fixedly at Tejsingh.
Ayyāri is indeed a difficult art. The greatest requirement in this craft is courage. The more timid an ayyār, the sooner he will be caught. Look at Tejsingh, how courageous he is—

What kind of an ayyār is he, that he dares to enter the enemy's house without the slightest fear, and in broad daylight tries to turn the truth into a lie! At such a time, if even the faintest sign of fear or anxiety appears on his face, it would be no wonder if he himself gets caught.

Tej Singh did not give Ramanand even a moment to speak. Smiling, he looked at him and said, "Well, you there! Do you take the court of Maharaj Digvijay Singh for some ordinary place? Do you think you can use your ayyāri here as well? Your tricks will not work here. Watch now, how I flatten the thickness of your donkey-like face!"

With a swift motion, Tej Singh grabbed Ramanand's beard, showed it to the Maharaj, and gave it a sharp tug. The jerk was forceful, but he did it in such a way that to the Maharaj it seemed only a light pull. Ramanand's fake beard came off.

This spectacle drove Ramanand nearly mad. All sorts of thoughts began to swirl in his mind. Realizing that this ayyār was trying to make a liar out of him, though he was innocent, anger flared within him, and he drew his dagger and lunged at Tej Singh. But Tej Singh dodged the attack. The Maharaj's suspicion of Ramanand deepened even further. Rising from his seat, he firmly seized Ramanand's wrist, the one holding the dagger, and struck him with his fist right in the face. The powerful blow from the Maharaj's hand made Ramanand's head spin, and he collapsed to the ground. Tej Singh quickly took out a vial of knockout medicine from his pocket and forced Ramanand to inhale it.
Maharaj: "Why did you make him unconscious?"

Tej Singh: "Maharaj, in his anger and seeing himself trapped, who knows what foolish things this ayyār might have blurted out. That's why I rendered him unconscious. After taking him to the prison, we can see to him again."
Maharaj: "Very well, that's fine. Now take the key from me and, after taking him to the underground cell, hand him over to the jailor."

Hearing the Maharaj's words, Tej Singh grew anxious and began to think that things had taken a bad turn. Where should I go after taking the key to the underground cell from the Maharaj? How am I to know where the underground cell is, or who the jailor is! This is a real problem! If I hesitate even a little, suspicion will fall on me. After some thought, Tej Singh said—
Tej Singh: "It would be best if Maharaj himself comes along."
Maharaj: "Why?"

Tej Singh: "If the jailor sees this ayyār and me together, he might get nervous and all sorts of suspicions may arise in his mind. If this scoundrel regains consciousness, he will surely try to make up some story. If you are present, the jailor will have no reason to doubt anything."
Maharaj: (laughing) "Very well, let us go together."
Tej Singh: "Yes, Maharaj, besides, it will be difficult for me to unlock and lock the cell while carrying this heavy body on my back."

The Maharaj took a key from his pen case and, having summoned a lantern from a servant, took it along with him. Tej Singh hoisted Ramanand's bundle onto his back. With Tej Singh in tow, the Maharaj proceeded to his bedchamber and unlocked a cupboard set into the wall. Tej Singh saw that the wall was hollow, and from that spot, a passageway led downward. Carrying Ramanand's bundle, Tej Singh followed the Maharaj down the steps. After passing through a corridor, they entered a small room, where the Maharaj opened a door and they found themselves in a vast baradari.

Tej Singh saw that in the very center of the baradari, upon a small cushion, sat an old man, writing something. As soon as he saw the Maharaj, the old man rose to his feet, folded his hands, and came forward.
Maharaj: "Daroga Sahib, see here—today Ramanand has ensnared one of the enemy's ayyars. Keep him under your protection."
Tej Singh (removing the bundle from his back and opening it): "Here, take charge of him now. He is your responsibility."
Daroga (in astonishment): "Was he impersonating the Diwan Sahib?"
Tej Singh: "Yes, indeed. He thought he could fool even me."
Tej Singh (laughing): "Well, let's go. Now Daroga Sahib will take care of him."

Tej Singh: "Maharaj, if you permit, I would like to stay and bring this wretch to his senses, to extract some information for our purposes. I would have asked Your Majesty to stay as well, but if you delay or forgo the court session, all manner of suspicions will arise in the hearts of the people, and at such a time, that would not be wise."

Maharaj: "You are right. Very well, I shall go. I will take my key with me and lock the door as I leave. You come out by the other way with the Daroga. (Turning to the Daroga) You too, come along, and bring your daily register."

Leaving Tej Singh there, the Maharaj departed. The Daroga, taking Tej Singh—still in the guise of Ramanand—came to his own cushion, seated Tej Singh in his place, and sat below him. For half an hour, Tej Singh kept the Daroga thoroughly entangled in conversation. Then, rising, he said, "Well, now it is time to bring this ayyar to his senses and find out who he is." He approached the ayyar. Reaching into his pocket, he began searching for his bottle of smelling salts, and finally exclaimed, "Oh dear! I left the bottle of smelling salts in the audience chamber. What shall I do now?"
Daroga: "I have a bottle of smelling salts. Shall I fetch it, if you command?"

Tej Singh: "Bring it, but your smelling salts may not revive him, for the potion that rendered him unconscious was of my own new concoction, and its antidote is different. Still, bring it—I might be able to make do."
"Very well," said the Daroga, and went off to fetch the smelling salts. Left alone, Tej Singh took another small bottle from his pocket (in which was a red powder)...

He (Tej Singh) took a pinch of his own special smelling salts and, with a deep breath, held it up to Ramanand's nose. Then, assured, he sat back. Now, except for the one concocted by Tej Singh, no other smelling salts could bring him to his senses (though, yes, perhaps if left lying for a day or two, he might regain consciousness on his own).
In a moment, the Daroga Sahib arrived, holding a box of smelling salts. Tej Singh said, "Go ahead, try it yourself and see if your smelling salts have any effect."
The Daroga Sahib held the box of salts under the unconscious Ramanand's nose, but what effect could it have? Helpless, he looked at Tej Singh.

Tej Singh said, "Why waste your effort? I told you before that your smelling salts won't work. Come, let's go to the Maharaj. Leave him as he is; when we return with my own smelling salts, it will be effective."
Daroga: "As you wish. These salts are of no use."

The Daroga Sahib tucked his daily logbook under his arm, took up his ring of keys and lantern, and set off. Entering a small room, the Daroga Sahib opened another door. Stairs leading upward appeared. The two of them climbed up and, passing through two or three more chambers, reached a tunnel. After walking some distance, their heads bumped against the ceiling. The Daroga inserted a key into a hole and pressed a hidden latch. A piece of stone shifted aside, and both of them stepped out. Here, Tej Singh found himself in a cemetery.

In the fourteenth chapter of the third part of this series, we have already described this cemetery. It was by this very route that Kunwar Anand Singh and Tara Singh had entered that underground chamber. The events we are now narrating took place before Kunwar Anand Singh entered the chamber. To maintain continuity, we have had to return to an earlier point in the story.
