Every door of the underground chamber used to be locked, but ever since Tej Singh had taken control of it (the details of which will be revealed later), the locks had been removed, and only the secret latches remained in use.

Tej Singh looked around and realized that he had come to this jungle several times before while conducting investigations, and had even reached this cemetery, but had never known what it truly was or for what purpose it had been built. Now Tej Singh thought, "Our work is done; the Daroga Sahib must be trapped here, so he cannot escape."
Tej Singh said, "Daroga Sahib, you are truly a scoundrel."
Daroga (looking at Tej Singh in astonishment): "What crime have I committed that you are scolding me now? This has never happened before!"
Tej Singh: "And you dare growl at me! I'll grab you by the ears and tear them off!"
Daroga: "Even the Maharaj himself has never insulted me like this!"

Tej Singh delivered such a kick to the Daroga that the poor fellow fell to the ground with a thud. Tej Singh climbed atop his chest and forcibly stuffed a dose of knockout medicine into his nostrils. The poor Daroga lost consciousness. Tej Singh untied the sheet from the Daroga's waist as well as his own, bundled up the Daroga's belongings in it, placed the bunch of keys and the diary inside, slung the bundle over his back, and swiftly set out toward his own camp. By midday, he reached the tent of Raja Virendra Singh. At first, seeing Ramanand's face, Virendra Singh was startled, but when Tej Singh revealed himself with a secret sign, he was overjoyed.
chapters.summary: Tej Singh, disguised as a sadhu, infiltrates Rohtasgarh fort, navigating suspicious priests and gathering crucial information about the Maharaj's trusted ayyaar, Ramanand.

chapters.title: Tej Singh’s Triumph and Worry
paragraphs: Raja Virendra Singh was overjoyed at Tej Singh's return, and his happiness grew even greater when Tej Singh recounted in detail all that he had accomplished at Rohtasgarh. Hearing of Ramanand's capture, he laughed so hard that he nearly rolled on the ground. But at the same time, upon hearing that there was no trace of Kunwar Indrajit Singh at Rohtasgarh, and that it seemed he was not there at all, Raja Virendra Singh became despondent. Tej Singh did his best to reassure and console him. After a short while, Tej Singh shared all the thoughts that weighed on his heart and the plans he wished to carry out. Virendra Singh was much pleased with his counsel and said—
Virendra: "Is there any plan of yours that I could possibly dislike? Now tell me, which ayyars will you take with you this time?"

Tej Singh: "I actually needed several ayyars for this task, but only four are present here; the rest have gone to search for Kunwar Indrajit Singh. No matter, it cannot be helped! Let Pandit Badri Nath remain here in the camp—I do not think it wise to send him elsewhere, for this task requires a very clever and experienced ayyar. As for the rest, I will take Jyotishi Ji, Bhairon, and Tara with me."
Virendra: "Very well. Will these three suffice for your purpose?"

Tej Singh: "No, I do not intend to keep all three ayyars with me. Rather, I will have Bhairon and Tara show me the way there and then send them back. Afterwards, they will bring a few fighters to me, and then either you or Kunwar Anand Singh will come to me as well. At that time, we will carry out all the actions I have already discussed with you."
Virendra: "And what of this Daroga's book you have brought—what will become of it?"
Tej Singh: "I will take it with me again another time, and when the opportunity arises, I will read it from beginning to end. This is the one thing we have managed to obtain."

Virendra:—Indeed, it is a remarkable thing. (Taking the book from Tejsingh's hand.) You will learn all about the underground chambers of Rohtasgarh from this, and in fact, you will discover many more secrets of that place as well.
Tejsingh:—Yes, in this, the daroga has written the daily happenings. I believe there must be several more such books there, written by previous darogas before him.
Virendra:—There must be, and from this, we can also deduce the location of the treasure in that underground vault.

Tejsingh:—Indeed, now that treasure too is about to become ours! We must not delay here any longer and should reach there as soon as possible, for Digvijaysingh had summoned both me and the daroga to his presence. If we are late, he might return to the vault, and if he finds no one there, all our plans will be ruined.
Virendra:—You are right. Go now, do not delay.

After taking some refreshments, Tejsingh set out towards Rohtasgarh, taking with him Jyotishiji, Bhaironsingh, and Tarasingh. With two hours of daylight remaining, they reached the underground vault. Tejsingh was still in the guise of Ramanand. After showing the way to the vault, Bhaironsingh and Tarasingh were sent back, while Jyotishiji was kept with him. This time, Tejsingh did not lock the door leading out of the vault; he merely left it secured with the latches.

From reading the journal of the vault, Tejsingh learned many things, which need not be detailed here, for they will become apparent in due course. However, one matter is necessary to mention. In the hall where the daroga resided, there was an iron wire fastened to a pillar, the other end of which passed through a hole in the ceiling and extended upward. From reading the book, Tejsingh learned that pulling or shaking this wire would ring the bell that hung in Digvijaysingh's private audience chamber, for the other end of the wire was attached to that very bell. Whenever the daroga needed assistance, he would tug at this wire.

In a small room adjacent to that hall, there was also a large bell, to which another iron wire was attached, the other end of which led to the Maharaj's audience chamber. When the Maharaj wished to alert those in the vault or had some need, he too would ring the vault's bell in the same manner as described above. But this was a privilege reserved for the Maharaj alone, for the affairs of the vault were kept extremely secret. The nature of the vault and what transpired within it was known only to a select eight or ten individuals. All its secrets were guarded as closely as sacred mantras.
As we have written above, Maharaj Digvijaysingh, suspecting the real Ramanand to be an ayyār, brought him into the vault, and upon returning—at the time of departure—the false Ramanand, that is…
Tejsingh told the Daroga, "You both find some free time and come to me."

But the Maharaj's order could not be carried out, for Tejsingh took the Daroga, having arrested him, to his own camp, and most of the day passed there, as we have written above. When Tejsingh returned to the underground chamber, he explained many things to Jyotishiji and, making him the Daroga, seated him on the throne. At that very moment, a noise came from the rooms in front. Tejsingh understood that the Maharaj was coming. He had Jyotishiji lie down and said, "You cry out in pain, I will speak with the Maharaj." After a short while, the Maharaj entered the chamber by the same path along which he had brought Tejsingh.
Maharaj (looking at Tejsingh): "Ramanand, I had ordered you both to come to me. Why did you not come? And what has happened to this Daroga who is groaning in pain?"
Tejsingh: "Maharaj, it is because of him that we could not come. Suddenly, the poor man was seized with stomach pain. After trying many remedies, he is now somewhat at ease."
Maharaj (after expressing regret for the Daroga's condition): "Has anything been learned about the ayyār?"
Tejsingh: "No, he has not revealed anything. But it is no matter; within a day or two we shall surely find out. Ayyārs are stubborn by nature."

After a short while, Maharaj Digvijay Singh left that place. After the Maharaj's departure, Tejsingh too left the underground chamber and went to the Maharaj. He remained in attendance for two hours, then, under the pretext of patrolling the city, took his leave. A little past the first watch of the night, Tejsingh again went to the Maharaj and said—
Tejsingh: "Maharaj, you must be surprised to see me return so soon, but I had to come to deliver an urgent message."
Maharaj: "What is it?"

Tejsingh: "I have learned that several ayyārs have come to arrest me. Maharaj, be on your guard. If I manage to escape their hands through the night, I will certainly devise some plan tomorrow. If I am caught, then so be it."
Maharaj: "Then why do you not stay here tonight?"
Tejsingh: "Should I hide myself out of fear of them, without taking any action? That cannot be."
Maharaj: "Well done! That is the right course. Go, then; whatever happens, we shall see."
Tejsingh returned home—not to Ramanand's house, but to his own camp. Thus, by this pretext, he saved himself and departed. In the morning, when...
When Ramanand did not appear in the court, the Maharaj became convinced that Virendra Singh's spies had ensnared him.
chapters.summary: Tej Singh, disguised as Ramanand, deceives Maharaj Digvijay Singh while learning the secrets of the vault, setting the stage for a daring plan to unfold.

chapters.title: The Corpse in the Dungeon
paragraphs: After completing his task, Tej Singh thought that now the real Ramanand should be taken out of the dungeon with such finesse that the Maharaj would not suspect anything, nor would he imagine that Virendra Singh's spies had entered the dungeon or that anyone else had learned its secrets. This could only be accomplished if a fresh corpse could be found.

Leaving Rohtasgarh, Tej Singh returned to his camp and, after telling Virendra Singh everything, dispatched several spies with the instruction that if they found a fresh corpse—one that had not yet decomposed or bloated—they should bring it and keep it somewhere near the camp, then inform him. By coincidence, that very day, a destitute beggar had died, unclaimed, on the banks of a river two or three kos from the camp. By evening, the spies had brought the body and, placing it a little distance from the camp, informed Tej Singh. Taking Bhairon Singh with him, Tej Singh went to the corpse and began his work.

Tej Singh fashioned the corpse to look exactly like Ramanand, and with Bhairon Singh's help, carried it into the dungeon of Rohtasgarh. There, he handed it over to the dungeon's warden (Jyotishiji), instructing him carefully about many details, and then brought the real Ramanand back to their camp.

After Tej Singh left, our new warden pulled the cord tied to the pillar, which caused the bell in Digvijay Singh's audience hall to ring. By then, two hours of the night had passed. The Maharaj, seated in the audience hall with several of his courtiers, was pondering many strategies to defeat his enemy. Suddenly, startled by the sound of the bell, they understood that their presence was required in the dungeon. Digvijay Singh immediately stood up and ordered the executioners to be summoned—those who, when needed, would enter the dungeon and, whether out of fear for their lives or loyalty, never revealed its secrets to anyone else.

The Maharaj went to another room. By the time he had changed his clothes and was ready, the executioners had also arrived. These executioners were exceptionally strong, powerful, and tall. Their skin was dark,
1. A corpse often stiffens and cannot be tied up in a bundle, so two men had to carry it together.

With their mustaches curled up, dressed only in a loincloth, a short jacket, and a hooded cloak, and wielding a heavy sword in hand, they appeared truly fearsome. The Maharaj took only four executioners with him and descended into the underground chamber by the usual route. Seeing the Maharaj approach, the jailor became alert and, folding his hands before him, said, "Forgive me, Maharaj, for having to trouble you."
Maharaj: "What is the matter?"
Jailor: "That ayyār who was arrested by Diwan Ramanandji has died."
Maharaj (startled): "What, he has died!"
Jailor: "Yes, he has died. It is not known what kind of poisonous stupefaction was administered to him, but its effect was such."

Maharaj: "This is very bad. The enemy will think that Digvijay Singh deliberately killed our ayyār, which is against the code. Now the enemy will become obstinate, and if they too begin to use poison instead of stupefying agents, it will be a great loss to us, and many men will lose their lives."
Jailor: "It is unfortunate, but what can be done now? The mistake is Diwan Sahib's."

Maharaj (growing agitated): "Ramanand is a complete fool! He has made himself out to be a renowned ayyār for nothing, and that is why a mere subordinate ayyār of Virendra Singh came and captured him. Well, it's over now!"

Hearing the Maharaj's words, Jyotishiji laughed inwardly and thought, "See how even such a clever and brave king has been fooled by such a small matter. Bravo, Tej Singh, you can do whatever you wish."

The Maharaj himself inspected Ramanand's corpse and ordered the executioners to take it elsewhere and bury it in the ground. The executioners took the body to a place in the same underground chamber where corpses were interred and buried it there. The Maharaj, lamenting, emerged from the underground chamber, pondering what revenge Virendra Singh's ayyārs would now take for this.
chapters.summary: Tej Singh cleverly replaces the real Ramanand with a corpse, fooling Maharaj Digvijay Singh into believing the spy has died.

chapters.title: The Jailor’s Midnight Alarm
paragraphs: On the third day after the above incident, the jailor was sitting on his seat, reviewing the daily register, and reading the old records of that underground chamber with amazement, when suddenly a noise came from the back room. Startled, he stood up and looked toward the rear. Again, the sound came. Jyotishiji opened the door and went inside, only to find that someone was fleeing through the second door of that room. The room was completely dark; Jyotishiji had barely advanced a few steps when, lying on the ground, a corpse—

She collided with their feet, causing them to stumble and fall, but they quickly regained their balance and pressed on. Yet they wondered in surprise, whose corpse was this? It seemed clear that a murder had taken place here, and it would be no surprise if the fleeing man was the murderer himself!

The man was running ahead through the tunnel, and behind him, Jyotishiji chased with a dagger in hand, but no matter how hard he tried, he could not catch him. Suddenly, a light appeared at the mouth of the tunnel. Jyotishiji thought, "Now he has escaped outside." In a moment, he too reached there and, stepping out of the tunnel, looked around in all directions.
The first person Jyotishiji's eyes fell upon was Pandit Badrinath. He saw Badrinath standing there, holding a woman captive, and less than half a ghadi of the day remained.
Badrinath said, "Daroga Sahib, look! Thieves have entered your place and you didn't even know!"
Jyotishiji replied, "If I hadn't known, why would I have chased all the way here?"
Badrinath said, "Still, the thief slipped right through your hands. Had I not arrived at this moment, you would not have caught her."
Jyotishiji admitted, "Yes, I concede this. Do you recognize who she is? I feel as though I have seen this woman somewhere before."
Badrinath replied, "You must have seen her. Now let's take her to the dungeon, then we shall see. It surprises me that she came out of the dungeon empty-handed."

Jyotishiji said, "She is not empty-handed, rather, she has come after cleaning out someone. While following her, a corpse struck my feet, but in my eagerness to pursue, I could not stop to investigate."

Pandit Badrinath and Jyotishiji, having arrested the woman, brought her into the dungeon and reached the hall or verandah where Daroga Sahib's seat was usually placed. They tied the woman to a pillar and, taking a lantern in hand, went to examine the corpse that had blocked Jyotishiji's path. At a glance, Badrinath recognized the body and exclaimed, "This is Madhavi!"

Jyotishiji asked, "How did she come here?" (Placing his hand on Madhavi's nose) "She is still breathing, not dead yet. Look, there's a wound on her stomach. The wound is not severe, she can be saved."
Badrinath, feeling her pulse, said, "Yes, she can be saved. For now, bind her wound and leave her as she is. We'll question her later. Yes, a little elixir should be poured into her mouth."

Badrinath bandaged Madhavi's wound and poured a little elixir into her mouth, then carried her to another room. In this dungeon, light and air entered from several places; the craftsmen had devised clever means for this.

Badrinath and Jyotishiji carried Madhavi to a chamber where cool air from the passageway was drifting in, and left her there. Then they returned to the barahdari, where the woman who had wounded Madhavi was tied to a pillar.

Badrinath quietly said to Jyotishiji, "Today, Kunwar Anand Singh will come here, and shortly after, I will arrive with twenty or twenty-five men. I must go now—there is much to do. I only came to tell you this. After I leave, you should interrogate this woman and find out who she is. But there is one thing I fear."
Jyotishiji: "What is that?"
Badrinath: "This woman has recognized us. Suppose you call His Majesty, and he comes, she might blurt out that the daroga sahib is actually an ayyār of Raja Virendra Singh!"
Jyotishiji: "That is bound to happen. We must make arrangements for that as well."

Badrinath: "No matter, it's not a problem. I have the remedy ready. (He took a small vial from his pouch and handed it to Jyotishiji.) Keep this with you. When the time comes, forcibly rub a little of this medicine on her tongue. In an instant, her tongue will stiffen. Then she won't be able to say anything clearly. After that, you may explain whatever you wish to His Majesty."

Badrinath departed. After he left, Jyotishiji tried to frighten and beat the woman into revealing her story, but to no avail. Hours of effort were wasted. At last, the woman said to Jyotishiji, "Jyotishiji, I know you very well. Do not think that I am the one who harmed Madhavi. Someone else wounded her. Anyway, none of this matters, for Madhavi is no longer in your custody."
Jyotishiji: "How could Madhavi escape from my custody?"
Woman: "She has gone where she could. Go and see for yourself the place where you left her—see if she is there."

Hearing this, Jyotishiji became very anxious and stood up. He went to the place where he had left Madhavi. The woman's words proved true—there was no trace of Madhavi. Lantern in hand, Jyotishiji searched everywhere for hours, but it was of no use. At last, he returned to the woman and said, "You spoke the truth, but now I will not rest until I have your life. However, if you tell me your story truthfully, I will let you go."

Jyotishiji pleaded with her a thousand times, but the woman said nothing. It was the sound of this woman's cries and voice that Kishori and Lali heard when they entered the underground chamber, as described in the earlier part of this volume, for at that very moment, Lali and Kishori had also arrived there.

Jyotishiji recognized Kishori, and even called out to her by name along with Lali's, but it was still not clear how and since when Jyotishiji had known Lali. However, both Kishori and Lali were surprised that the daroga had recognized them, for Jyotishiji was in the guise of the daroga.

Jyotishiji wanted to call Kishori and Lali to his side and speak with them, but he did not get the chance. Just then, the sound of a bell rang out, and Jyotishiji understood that the Maharaj was coming. But why would the Maharaj come at this time? Perhaps it was because Lali and Kishori had entered this underground chamber and the Maharaj had come to know of it.

In his haste, Jyotishiji could only manage two things. First, he looked at Kishori and Lali and said, "Alas, if I had even half an hour more, I would have gotten you out of here, for all this commotion is because of you." Second, he applied a potion to the tongue of the woman so that she would not be able to speak before the Maharaj. Just then, the Maharaj arrived, accompanied by torchbearers and several executioners, and, looking at Jyotishiji, said, "Kishori and Lali have come into this underground chamber. Have you seen them?"
Daroga (standing up): "No, Your Majesty, they have not arrived here yet."
Maharaj: "Search for them! Where are they? And who is this woman?"
Daroga: "I do not know who she is or why she has come. I arrested her here in this very chamber, but she will not answer any questions."

Maharaj: "Very well. She too must be offered as a sacrifice to Bhootnath along with Kishori and Lali, for such is the established rule here: that anyone, apart from those whose names are written, who sees this underground chamber, must be sacrificed at once."

Everyone began searching for Kishori and Lali. At this moment, Jyotishiji grew anxious and prayed to God that Kunwar Anand Singh and our other ayyars might arrive soon, so that Kishori's life could be saved.

Kishori and Lali were not far away; they were quickly captured and their arms were bound. Afterwards, the Maharaj questioned the woman whose tongue Jyotishiji had smeared with the potion, but she gave no answer to any of his questions. At last, she too was untied from the pillar, her arms were bound, and the three women were led through a doorway into another ominous, stone-walled chamber, where, upon the throne, sat that dreadful black stone idol whose story we have already told in the final account of the third part of this chronicle.

At that very moment, Anand Singh, Bhairon Singh, and Tara Singh arrived and saw with their own eyes the scene of that woman's execution, the one whose tongue had been rendered mute by the potion. When it came time for Kishori to be killed, Kunwar Anand Singh and the two ayyars could bear it no longer; they drew their daggers and rushed at the crowd...
...but they could not attack, because several men came from behind and seized all three of them.
chapters.summary: Jailor Jyotishiji chases a mysterious intruder through dark tunnels after a murder, only to find himself in a situation with a captured woman.

chapters.title: A Young Woman by the Ganga
paragraphs: Now, turning the thread of our tale in a new direction, we take our readers to the sacred city of Kashi, and draw their attention to the condition of a young woman sitting by the banks of the Ganga at dusk.

The sun has set, and darkness is gathering all around. The Ganga flows gently and serenely. In the sky, small clouds drift from the east and gather in the west. Right at the riverbank sits a young woman, who cannot be more than fifteen years old, resting her cheek upon her palm, gazing at the water, lost in thought. There is no doubt that this woman is beautiful and graceful from head to toe, though her complexion is dusky. Yet, this does not in any way diminish her beauty or delicacy. Every so often, she lifts her head and glances around, then resumes her thoughtful pose, resting her cheek upon her hand.
Before her, anchored in the Ganga, is a small barge on which four or five men can be seen, along with some travel gear and two or four palanquins.

After a little while, as darkness falls, the woman rises. At the same moment, two guards descend from the barge, help her up, and escort her onto the vessel. She goes up to the deck and sits by the edge, gazing out as if awaiting someone's arrival. Indeed, that was the case, for just then a man appeared, carrying a bundle in his hand. At the sight of him, two boatmen came ashore; one took the bundle from his hand and carried it up to the deck, while the other lightly supported the man as he climbed aboard. He too stood before the woman on the deck, and with a gesture, asked, "What are your orders now?" In response, the woman signaled with her hand to proceed to the opposite bank of the river. The newly arrived man called out to the boatmen to take the barge across, and then he and the woman exchanged a few more gestures, which we could not understand. However, it became clear that this woman was mute and deaf—she could not speak, nor could she hear.
The barge was cast off from the shore and began to move across. Four boatmen took up the oars...

began to look. The woman descended from the roof and went below, and the man too, taking the bundle he had brought, climbed down from the roof. There were two cabins below deck in the barge—one had a beautiful white carpet spread out, and in the other a cot was laid with some belongings scattered about. The woman, making a gesture with her hand, sat down on the carpet, and the man placed a wooden writing board and a small piece of chalk before her. He too sat down, and the two began to converse by writing on the wooden board with the chalk. Now, the conversation that took place between them we shall set down below, but the reader should remember that the entire exchange happened in writing.

First, the woman opened the bundle and began to see what was inside. Out came a brass pen case, which she opened. She took out five or seven letters and notes, read them, and put them back as they were, then began to look at other things. After examining two or four kinds of handkerchiefs and some old coins, she opened a large tin box, inside which was something astonishing. After opening the box, she first removed some cloth that was packed as padding, then peered inside to see the thing within.

Who knows what it was in that box, but the moment the woman saw it, her entire demeanor changed. At a single glance, she gasped and shrank back, drenched in sweat, her body trembling, her face drained of color, and her eyes closed. The man quickly replaced the padding cloth and closed the box, removing it from before her.
Just then, a voice came from outside the barge, "Nanakji!"

Nanakprasad was the name of the man who had brought the bundle. He was neither tall nor very short, stout in build, fair of complexion, and his upper teeth were somewhat uneven. At the sound of the voice, he rose and went outside. The boatmen had stopped rowing, and three soldiers stood alert at the door.
Nanak (to one of the soldiers): "What is it?"

Soldier (pointing across the river): "It seems to me that many people are standing on the far bank. Look, whenever the clouds part and the moonlight falls, it becomes clear that those people too are moving downstream, in the same direction as our barge."
Nanak (looking carefully): "Yes, that's right."
Soldier: "Who knows, perhaps they are our enemies."
Nanak: "It wouldn't be surprising. Well then, let the boat drift with the current, do not cross to the other side."
Saying this, Nanakprasad went inside. By then, the woman had regained her senses and was gazing intently at the tin box, which was now closed.
was. Seeing Nanak, she gestured and asked, "What is it?"
In response, Nanak wrote on a wooden slate with chalk and showed her:
"On the opposite bank, many men can be seen. Who knows, perhaps they are our enemies."
The woman (writing): "Let the barge drift with the current. Tell the soldiers to be ready with their guns. If anyone is seen swimming towards us in the water, by all means, shoot them."
Nanak: "Very well."

Nanak went out again, relayed the order to the soldiers, and returned inside. The woman, opening a key from her sari's edge, handed it to Nanak and signaled that he should place this tin box in their chest.

Nanak did as instructed, then went into another room. Here a bed was laid out, along with some belongings and a chest. Using the same key, he opened the chest, placed the tin box inside, locked it again, and returned the key to the woman. Just then, the sound of a gunshot rang out from outside.
Nanak immediately went out and asked, "What is it?"
Soldier: "Look, several men are swimming this way."
Another: "But hearing the gunshot, they have turned back now."
Nanak went back inside and wrote the situation on the slate to explain to the woman. She too stood up and came outside to look towards the opposite bank.

An hour passed in this manner, and now those men who had been visible on the far side, or who had been swimming towards the barge, had disappeared and were nowhere to be seen. Gesturing for Nanak Prasad to come with her, the woman went back inside the barge, and Nanak followed. The mute woman began to examine the other items in the bundle. Apart from three or four sets of valuable men's clothing, there was nothing else in the bundle. The bundle was tied up and set aside, and the two began to converse by writing on the slate.
Woman: "The letters in the pen case, where did you find them?"
Nanak: "They were in that very pen case."
Woman: "And where was that pen case?"
Nanak: "It was lying under his cot. The house was silent, no one was to be seen. I took whatever I could find in haste."
Woman: "Well, no matter. We only needed that tin box. Now that we have the pen case, these letters and notes will also be very useful."
Besides this, there were other conversations, which need not be written here. More than a quarter of the night had passed when the woman finally rose and, taking the candelabrum...
She extinguished the lamp and went to lie down on her cot. Nanak, too, slept on the floor in a corner, and the boat continued to glide smoothly through the night; nothing happened worth recording.

When only a little of the night remained, the woman rose from her cot and peered out through the window. The sky was perfectly clear at this hour; the moon, accompanied by the stars, shone with their appointed brilliance, and moonlight streamed into the boat through two or three windows. Indeed, the very cot on which the woman had slept was bathed in the moon's radiance. She quietly slipped down from her cot, opened the trunk in which Nanak had placed the tin box, took out the box, and set it on the cot. After closing the trunk, she opened another and took out a candle, then sat down again on the cot. Taking some wax from the candle, she carefully sealed all the seams and cracks of the tin box, pressing wax into every joint so that not even air could enter. This task completed, she leaned out the window, gazing toward the riverbank. Two boatmen were rowing slowly; when they grew tired, they would rouse the other two to take over, while they themselves rested.

By dawn, the boat reached a place where there was some habitation along the shore; in fact, right on the bank of the Ganga stood a tall Shiva temple, with steps built down to the river for bathing. The woman observed the spot carefully, and when the boat came directly opposite the temple, she threw the tin box—containing some mysterious object, its holes now thoroughly sealed with wax—into the water, then lay back down on her cot. No one else noticed what she had done. In a short while, the settlement was left behind, and the boat sailed on into the distance.

When morning had fully broken and the red glow of the sun appeared, the boat, on the woman's orders, reached the edge of a forest. She instructed the boatmen to follow the riverbank. This was the same side as Kashi, the very bank from which their journey had begun.

The boat moved along the shore, and the woman gazed intently at the trees lining the bank. The forest was dense and beautiful; in the pleasant freshness of morning, birds of many kinds were singing, and the breeze carried the sweet fragrance of wild fruits. The woman rested her head on a window and admired the beauty of the woods. Suddenly, her eyes fell upon something that startled her. She hurried outside and signaled for the boat to stop and draw up to the bank.
The boat was brought to shore, and the mute woman, after signaling to her guards, took Nanak with her and disembarked.
For an hour, she wandered through the forest. In that time, she attended to her necessary business...

After bathing and washing, she finished her ablutions and, after returning to the barge and taking a little food, she donned her masculine disguise. She put on tight-fitting pajamas, a chapkan reaching above her knees, a waistband, and wrapped a large turban around her head. Besides a shield, sword, and dagger, she also concealed a small pistol loaded with a bullet in her waist, and kept a little gunpowder and some bullets close at hand, preparing herself to disembark from the barge.

When Nanak saw her in such a state, he stood in her way and, by gesture, asked what they should do now. In response, the woman asked for a slate and chalk, and thus began a written conversation between the two.
Woman: You should return to your quarters on this very barge. I will come and meet you!
Nanak: I cannot leave you alone under any circumstances; you know well how much hardship I have endured for you, and how I have been ready to do even the lowest of tasks for your sake.

Woman: What you say is true, but your life cannot pass happily with a mute like me. Yet, in exchange for your love, I will make you wealthy, so that you may find the most beautiful woman and marry her.

Nanak: Alas, today you are bent on giving me such advice and have no regard for my true love. I care nothing for wealth, nor do I mind that you are mute. I do not wish to discuss this further—either accept me, or give me a clear answer so that I may end my life here before you and be free forever. I do not wish to hear people say, "Your love for Rambholi was not true, and you could do nothing."

Rambholi (the mute woman): I am not yet free from my tasks; when a person is carefree, then thoughts of marriage and happiness arise. Yet, there is no doubt that your love is true, and I value you for it.
Nanak: Until you are free from your tasks, keep me with you. I will help you in every matter and am ready even to give my life for you.
Rambholi: Very well, I accept this. Instruct the soldiers to take the barge away and keep all the things in it safe, for I am leaving even that iron box you brought yesterday in this boat.

Nanakprasad was so overjoyed that he swelled with pride. After coming out and giving the soldiers many instructions, he too armed himself in every way and prepared to accompany her. Rambholi and Nanak descended from the barge. At her signal, the boatmen set the barge adrift, and it once again began to move with the current.

Taking Nanak with her, Rambholi entered the jungle. After walking a short distance, she reached a place where there were many footpaths. Standing there, she looked around in all directions. Her gaze fell upon a felled sal tree whose leaves had dried and fallen to the ground.

She went and stood near that tree, looking all around as if searching for some sign. The ground in that place was very rocky and uneven. At a distance of about fifty yards, a pile of stones could be seen, which seemed to have been made by human hands. She went to that pile of stones and, to rest for a while, sat down. Nanak untied his waistband, brushed off a flat stone, and spread it out. Rambholi sat down upon it and gestured for Nanak to sit beside her.

These two had barely begun to rest when, from the front, a rider dressed in scarlet appeared, coming toward them. As the figure drew near, it became clear that this was a young woman, who, with great style and armed like a man, sat astride her horse, displaying a show of bravery. She came and halted beside Rambholi, cast a knowing glance at her, and laughed. Rambholi replied to her laughter with a smile of her own and, with a sidelong glance, indicated Nanak. The woman beckoned Rambholi to come closer; and when Rambholi stood by the horse, the woman dismounted. From her waist, she opened a small pouch, took out a letter and a ring set with a crimson gem, and placed them in Rambholi's hand.

Rambholi's face made it clear that receiving this ring had filled her with boundless joy. With a gesture of respect, she touched the ring to her forehead, then slipped it onto her finger. She tucked the letter into her waistband, swiftly mounted the horse, and in the blink of an eye disappeared into the forest.

Nanakprasad, witnessing this spectacle, stood dumbfounded, unable to do or say anything. No words escaped his lips, nor could he even gesture to ask a question—but whom could he have asked? Rambholi had not even glanced back at him. Nanak had no idea who this woman in scarlet was, who had suddenly appeared here and, with a few gestures, spirited Rambholi away on her horse. The woman came up to Nanak and said with a laugh—
Woman: "The woman who was with you has ridden away on my horse. No harm in that, but why have you become so downcast? Was there some relation between you and her?"
Nanakprasad: "There was no relation, but there was to be one. You have ruined everything."
Woman (smiling): "So, you were set on marrying her?"
Nanakprasad: "Indeed, that was so. She was already mine; you do not know what hardships I have endured for her. I ruined my ancestral estate and was ready to become her slave."
Woman (sitting down): "Whose slave?"
Nanakprasad: "The same Rambholi who rode off on your horse."
Woman (startled): "What name did you say? Say it again!"
Nanakprasad: "Rambholi."
Woman (laughing): "Very well, then. Since when do you know my friend, that is, that woman?"
Nanakprasad (a bit annoyed, making a face): "I have known her since childhood, but as for you, I have never seen you before today. How could she possibly be your friend?"
Woman: "You liar, fool, and owl—no, the very essence of an owl! What could you possibly know of my friend? If you do not know me, how could you recognize her?"
The woman's words drove Nanak quite out of his senses. He became thoroughly irritated, and in his anger drew his sword from its sheath and said—
Nanakprasad: "Wretched woman, you make a fool of me! You speak cutting words and try to throw dust in my eyes! I'll cut off your head right now!"
Woman (laughing): "Well done! Why not, after all, you are a brave man! (snapping her fingers in front of Nanak's face) Come now, Eighth Singh, take a dose of sense!"

Now Nanakprasad could bear it no longer, and exclaiming, "Here, suffer the consequences of your deeds!" he struck at the woman with his sword. The woman nimbly dodged, and reaching out, seized Nanak's wrist and gave such a powerful twist that the sword flew from his hand and landed far away. Nanak, astonished, stared at her face. The woman laughed and said to Nanak, "So, this is the bravery with which you intended to marry my friend! Go now, join the eunuchs and dance with them!"

With these words, the woman moved away and set off towards the west. Nanak's anger had not yet subsided. He picked up his sword, which lay some distance away, sheathed it, and, grinding his teeth and deep in thought, followed after the woman. The woman, too, was clever enough to keep an eye out, lest Nanak attack her from behind with his sword; she kept glancing back at him from the corner of her eye.

After a short distance, the woman reached a well whose stone platform was no less than a man's height. Steps were built on all four sides for climbing up. The well was very large and beautiful. The woman climbed up to the well, sat down, and began to sing softly.

It was midday, the sun was shining brightly, but around the well, the dense shade of trees and the cool breeze made Nanak's spirits soar. All thoughts of anger, grief, and revenge vanished completely, and the woman's melodious voice added even more charm. He went and sat before her, gazing at her face. After singing just two or three lines, the woman fell silent.
And Nanak said—

Woman: "Why are you still following me? Go wherever you wish and mind your own business. Why waste your time in vain? You will never be able to find your Rambholi now, no matter what you do. Cast her from your heart."
Nanakprasad: "Rambholi will have no choice but to come to me; she is within my grasp. I possess something of hers, something she could never abandon while she still lives."
Woman (laughing): "There is no doubt that you are mad. Your words make me laugh. Well, you do as you please, what do I care!"
Saying this, the woman peered into the well and called out, "Koopdev, I am thirsty, give me some water!"

Hearing the woman's words, Nanak grew uneasy and thought to himself, "What a strange woman this is, commanding the well as if it were her servant, telling it to give her water. She calls me mad, but I think she is the mad one. How could a well possibly give her water? Whatever the case, this woman is very beautiful, and her singing is truly exquisite."

Nanak was still lost in these thoughts when something startled him; in fact, he sprang to his feet in fright, trembling and staring at the well in terror. A hand had emerged from inside the well, holding a silver bowl filled with clear, cold water. It was this sight that had so unnerved Nanak.

The hand reached the edge; the woman took the bowl, drank the water, and then placed the bowl back on the hand, which withdrew into the well. The woman began singing again as before. Nanak said to himself, "No, no, this woman is not mad—rather, I am the mad one, for I have not yet recognized her. Surely she must be a Gandharvi or an Apsara—no, a goddess herself, come in disguise. How else could she possess such strength, that she could seize my wrist and with a single jerk make me drop my sword? But how does she know Rambholi?"
As she sang, the woman suddenly sprang to her feet and, with a loud cry, leapt into the well.
chapters.summary: Chandrakanta, disguised as a man, throws a mysterious box into the Ganga and then startles Nanakprasad with a magical request at a forest well.

chapters.title: Nanak’s Flight and Fear
paragraphs: The strange words and actions of the woman in the red dress had left Nanak bewildered. He looked around anxiously, and fear took such a hold of him that he was in a most peculiar state. He could not remain by the well, and, moving quickly, he hurried away, hoping that—

He set off towards the Ganga, hoping that by walking along the bank, he might reach the barge. But even this was not possible, for the jungle was crisscrossed with many narrow paths, and following them, he lost his way and began heading in a completely different direction.

Nanak had gone barely half a kos when he became restless with thirst. He began searching for water, but in that forest, he could not find a single spring or stream to quench his thirst. At last, while wandering about, he caught sight of a hut made of leaves. Taking it for a fakir's hermitage, he made his way towards it. But upon reaching, he realized he had been mistaken. There were several trees there whose branches had bent down and intertwined, forming a shelter that, from a distance, looked like a hut.

Nevertheless, that place proved most fortunate for Nanak. For among those very trees, he saw a clear spring of water flowing, with lovely, shady trees on both sides, their branches casting a cool shadow over the stream. Overjoyed, Nanak hurried to the edge of the spring, washed his hands and face, drank deeply, and then sat down to rest.

After sitting by the spring for a while, Nanak saw something floating in the water, drifting towards him from afar. As it drew near, he saw it was a piece of cloth. He waded into the water, pulled the cloth out, and examined it closely, for it was the very cloth RamBholi had wrapped around her waist when disembarking from the barge.

Astonished, Nanak gazed at the cloth for a long time, pondering many things. He had seen RamBholi ride away on horseback before his eyes—how, then, could he believe this cloth was hers? Yet he rubbed his eyes several times and looked again at the cloth. At last, he had to accept that it was indeed RamBholi's shawl. Hoping to meet RamBholi, he set off along the bank of the spring, thinking that after riding away, she must have come to this very spot, and for some reason, the cloth had fallen into the water.

Nanak walked for about a kos along the spring, shaded trees lining both banks, until in the distance he saw the white gleam of a small house. He was delighted, thinking perhaps he might meet RamBholi there. Quickening his pace, he soon reached the house.

The house was built like a bridge across the middle of the spring. The stream was not very wide—no more than twenty or twenty-five hands across. The land on both banks came right up to the house, and in the center, to allow the water to flow, there was an archway like a canal under the bridge. Nanak, seeing this house—

He became very pleased and began to think that this must surely have been built by some whimsical lover of beauty. From here, the splendor of this spring and the surrounding forest could be seen in all its glory. He thought to himself, "I should go inside this house and see whether it is empty or if someone lives here." Nanak walked to the front of the house. Its porch was very high; after climbing fifteen steps, he reached the door. The door was open, and he entered boldly.

At each of the four corners of the house was a small chamber, and on all four sides were verandahs, with railings waist-high in front of them. In other words, each verandah was flanked on both sides by chambers, and in the center was a large room. There was no sort of decoration in this house, but it was clean.

As soon as Nanak stepped inside the door, his gaze fell upon a sadhu sitting in the central room. The sadhu was seated on a deer skin. He must have been over eighty years old. His hair was as white as cotton, long locks spread out wildly, dry and unkempt, and his beard hung down to his navel. Around his waist, a loincloth was tied with a rope of munj grass, and he wore no other garment. A sacred thread hung around his neck, and his radiant face bore the marks of age and spiritual power. When Nanak saw him, the sadhu was seated in the lotus posture, deep in meditation, his eyes closed and his hands resting on his thighs. Nanak stood before him for a long time, but the sadhu took no notice. Nanak looked up and examined the surroundings carefully, but apart from two large paintings, covered with cloth and placed against the wall behind the sadhu, he saw nothing else.

Nanak was astonished and began to wonder: "There is no sign of any belongings in this house, so how does this holy man sustain himself? And what are those two paintings, whose presence in this house seems so necessary?" Absorbed in such thoughts, he began to wander about and look around. He explored every verandah and chamber, but not even a straw was to be seen anywhere. However, there was one chamber he could not enter, for its door was closed, though there was no visible lock or chain upon it. It was not clear how it was shut. Wandering thus, Nanak came to the side verandah and, leaning over the railing, gazed at the beauty below, spending nearly an hour in this way.

After wandering about, he returned to the babaji, but found him still sitting with eyes closed. Helpless, he sat down in a corner, hoping that eventually the sadhu would open his eyes. As evening approached, from within the chamber whose door was closed and into which Nanak had not been able to enter, came the sound of a conch being blown. Nanak was greatly astonished.
The sound broke the sadhu's concentration. As soon as his eyes opened, they fell upon Nanak.
Sadhu: "Who are you, and why have you come here?"
Nanak: "I am a traveler, lost and tormented by misfortune, who happened to wander this way. Seeing you here, I felt a surge of hope in my heart."
Sadhu: "One should never place hope in another human being. Well, tell me, where is your home, and how did you come to this jungle, where even returning is difficult?"

Nanak: "I am from Kashi. Due to certain circumstances, I came here with a woman who lived next door to me. In this forest, I was separated from her, and I witnessed such strange things that my heart still trembles with fear."

Sadhu: "Very well, your story seems long indeed, and I do not have the leisure to hear it right now. Wait a while; let me finish some work, and then I shall speak with you. Do not be anxious, I will return in exactly one hour."

Saying this, the sadhu left. From the sound and manner of the door, Nanak realized that the sadhu had gone into the very room whose door had been closed, and into which Nanak had not been able to enter. Helpless, Nanak sat down, but the thought that the sadhu would take a whole hour to return made him anxious, and he began to wonder what he should do in the meantime. Suddenly, his attention was drawn to the two pictures hanging on the wall. He thought, "It is so quiet here, the sadhu is not present—why not lift the curtain and see whose portraits these are?" No, no, what if the sadhu returns? He would be displeased; one should never look upon a veiled picture without permission. But then again, what harm if he does see? The sadhu himself said he would be gone for an hour—what is there to fear?

Nanak approached one of the pictures and, trembling, lifted the curtain. The moment his eyes fell upon the portrait, he cried out in terror, the curtain slipped from his hand, he staggered back, gasping, and returned to his seat. He could not summon the courage to look at the second picture.

The portrait depicted two women and a man. Nanak recognized all three. One woman was Rambholi, the other was the one who had ridden away on horseback with Rambholi and, before Nanak's eyes, had leapt into the well. The third figure was Nanak's father. The scene showed Nanak's father lying on the ground, the second woman clutching his hair, while Rambholi sat astride his chest, drawing a knife across his throat.
Seeing this picture, Nanak was overcome with a strange sensation. He was seized by sudden panic.

And the events of the past began to appear before his eyes as if they had happened just today. Remembering the condition of his father, his eyes welled up with tears, and for some time, with his head bowed, he remained lost in thought. At last, he heaved a deep sigh, raised his head, and said, "Oh! Was my father killed at the hands of these women? No, never, such a thing cannot be. But then, why does this painting depict such a scene? Surely, the picture on the other side must be of a similar nature, and it too must be connected to me in some way. My heart feels restless; it is difficult to stay here any longer!" Saying this, Nanak stood up and began to pace in the veranda outside.

The sun had completely set, the first darkness of evening had spread all around, and gradually, the night began to reveal its true form. Darkness filled the house as well, and Nanak wondered why there seemed to be no arrangement for light here. Do the Babaji live in darkness? Such a beautiful, clean house, yet not even a lamp to light it, and apart from the deerskin upon which Babaji sat, there was not even a mat to be seen. Perhaps the reason for this was that the floor here was very clean, smooth, and well-washed.

Lost in such thoughts, two hours passed for Nanak. Suddenly, he remembered that Babaji had promised to return in an hour; by now, he must have come back to his place, and what must he be thinking, not finding me there? Without meeting him and conversing, nothing about this place could be known. Let me go and see whether he has returned or not.

Nanak went to the room where he had met Babaji, but there, apart from darkness, nothing could be seen. For a while, he strained his eyes, looking carefully in every direction, but could discern nothing. Helpless, he called out—"Babaji!"—but received no reply. He called twice more, but to no avail. At last, feeling his way, he reached Babaji's deerskin, but finding it empty, he turned back and came to sit in the veranda outside, beneath which the spring flowed.

After sitting quietly, lost in thought for an hour, he rose again, hoping to meet Babaji, and walked towards that room. This time, he found the door of the room locked from within. Trembling with surprise and fear, he returned once more and sat at his place in the veranda. In this manner, more than a quarter of the night passed, and from all sides, the sounds of wild beasts calling in the jungle began to reach his ears. Fear made it impossible for him to descend below the house; indeed, he even disliked remaining in the veranda, and so he slipped into the adjacent storeroom, shut the door, and lay down to sleep.

Nanak had gone hungry all day, and even now he had nothing to eat; how then could sleep come to him? Besides, throughout the day he had witnessed and heard many astonishing things, which still revolved before his eyes, disturbing his rest. After midnight, he witnessed even more wondrous things.

It was well past midnight when Nanak heard the voices of two people conversing. He began to listen intently, for he could clearly hear and understand what was being said. The following conversation reached his ears; the voices were delicate, so Nanak realized that both were women—
First: Nanak has mistaken love for mere flirtation.
Second: What possessed this wretch to abandon his home and set out after a woman in this way?
First: That is something we ought to ask him.
Second: Babaji did not deem it proper to meet him. Who knows what connection there is.
First: Whatever it may be, this Nanak is a very clever and cunning man. It would not be surprising if he manages to accomplish whatever he has set his mind to!

Second: That is rather unlikely. I do not believe the queen will spare him, for she is thirsting for his blood. Yes, if he manages to reach the bajra and seize that box, then no one will be able to harm him.
First: (laughing, and Nanak heard this laughter clearly) That is impossible.
Second: Well, what concern is it of ours? What wisdom do we, mere maidservants, possess to debate such matters?
First: Does being a maidservant diminish one's intelligence?
Second: No, but when do maidservants ever learn of the true affairs?
First: I know.
Second: So what?
First: Only that, in a moment, Nanak will be arrested. There is no use talking further; Harihar must be arriving any minute.

After this, Nanak heard nothing more, but these words left him deeply unsettled. Trembling with fear, he sat up and resolved to slip away quietly from there. He opened the door softly and stepped out of the room. All around was silence. Though there was certainly the danger of encountering bears, leopards, or lions in the jungle outside this house, he saw no way to save himself by staying within, for the words of those two women had left him utterly hopeless. The thought of reaching the bajra and seizing that box, however, made him desperate, and he decided that getting to the bajra as quickly as possible was his best course.

Passing through the veranda, Nanak reached the main door and was about to descend the steps when, rushing out from another hall, several men pounced upon him and arrested him. They forcibly blindfolded Nanak with a sheet.
and said, "Go quietly wherever we take you, otherwise it will not be good for you." Helpless, Nanak had no choice but to obey.

Though Nanak's eyes were closed and he was powerless in every way, he paid close attention to the path being taken. For half an hour he walked steadily on; from the rustling of leaves and the dampness of the ground, he realized he was passing through dense jungle. After this, he had to cross a threshold, and he sensed that he was now inside some gate, walking upon stone or some paved ground. From there, he had to turn left and right several times. After a long while, he again had to cross a gate, and then found himself walking on unpaved earth once more. After traveling about a kos, he crossed yet another threshold and began walking on paved ground again. At this point, Nanak became convinced that he was being led in circles to confuse him about the route. It would not be surprising if this was the very place he had already passed before.
After going a short distance, Nanak was made to ascend a staircase. After climbing twenty or twenty-five steps, he was then led down again, and when the steps ended, his eyes were uncovered.

Nanak found himself in a strange place. Behind him was a high wall and a staircase; in front of him was a beautiful garden, surrounded on all sides by lofty walls, and brightly illuminated. Small glass lanterns hung from the fruit-laden, grafted trees, each with a burning candle, and many people could be seen strolling about. In the center of the garden stood a magnificent bungalow. Nanak had arrived there, and glancing up at the sky, he realized that very little of the night remained.

Though Nanak was clever, cunning, brave, and bold, at this moment he was deeply anxious. The main reason for his alarm was that his weapons had been taken away, and he was no longer in a position to defend himself against an enemy's attack or to save himself by any means. Yet, since his hands and feet were free, Nanak was not without hope; if an opportunity to escape arose, he would seize it.

It was apparent from outside that the house was brightly lit. Several wall lamps burned in the outer courtyard, and chobdars stood at attention, holding golden staffs. Nanak was made to stand near them, while the men who had captured him—eight in number—went inside the house, but not before instructing the chobdars, "Be vigilant with this man; we are going to inform the authorities." Nanak had to stand there for half an hour.
When those who had arrested him and gone inside to give the news—
When they returned, one of them looked at Nanak and said, "The message has been delivered. Now you may go inside."
Nanak replied, "How am I to know where I must go, or which way to take?"
The man answered, "This house itself will show you the way. There is no need to ask!"

Helpless, Nanak stepped over the threshold and found himself in a three-doored hall. He turned to look back, but the door through which he had entered was now closed. He thought he had been imprisoned in this very place, and that there was no escape; that all this arrangement had been made solely for him. But no, his suspicion was unfounded, for immediately the door before him opened and light began to shine from that direction. Fearful, Nanak moved forward, and as soon as he set foot across the threshold, his eyes fell upon two young women dressed in clean, elegant attire. Both took hold of his hands and led him along.

Nanak was afraid, but he kept his heart under control, though his chest was pounding and all manner of thoughts were swirling in his mind. At times, he despaired for his life; at others, he took comfort in the thought that he had committed no crime; and sometimes he reasoned, "Whatever is to happen will happen, but at least I must discover the truth behind these matters that have left my soul restless. Until the real secret of these astonishing events I have witnessed since yesterday is revealed, my senses will not be at peace."

The two women led him through several halls and chambers, finally bringing him to a mirrored pavilion, where Nanak beheld a most wondrous scene. The pavilion was splendidly decorated and brightly lit. All the trappings of a royal court were present. In the center, upon a bejeweled throne, sat a young woman clad in an exquisite southern-style gown, adorned from head to toe in dazzling jewels. Never in his life had Nanak seen such a beautiful woman. He could scarcely believe that this woman belonged to the mortal world.

To her right, upon a golden dais covered with a deerskin, sat the same sadhu whom Nanak had seen in the canal chamber that evening. Beyond the sadhu, arranged in a circle, were twenty more bejeweled chairs, upon which sat women, each more beautiful than the last, dressed in southern attire, each girded with shield and sword. To the left of the throne, upon a smaller bejeweled seat, sat Rambholi, attired in the same fashion as the others, also armed with shield and sword. Nanak's astonishment knew no bounds, but at the same time, he felt certain that his life was no longer in danger. Beside Rambholi, upon a jeweled chair, sat the woman who had spirited Rambholi away on horseback before Nanak's very eyes. After her, on twenty more bejeweled chairs, sat twenty young women, arrayed in the same splendor as those on the right of the throne.

In front, twenty women stood in respectful silence, adorned with shields and swords, each holding a jeweled staff in hand, their heads bowed, ready to obey any command at a mere gesture. In their midst, Nanak was brought and made to stand.

At the sight of this court, Nanak's eyes were dazzled. He was suddenly overcome with anxiety and began to look all around. Whatever object his gaze fell upon in this pavilion, he found it unparalleled. Nanak was the son of a wealthy noble and had seen many grand royal courts, but never in his wildest dreams had his eyes beheld such things as he saw here. The vases arranged in the alcoves were entirely artificial, and instead of flowers and leaves, they were filled with priceless jewels. Just looking at these vases, Nanak wondered where these people had acquired such wealth! Besides these, every other object of decoration there was such that obtaining it would be considered nearly impossible for ordinary mortals. To estimate the value of the women's attire and jewelry was beyond comprehension.
After glancing all around, Nanak's eyes finally came to rest upon Rambholi, and he gazed at her fixedly.

The woman who sat upon the jeweled throne with great authority cast a glance at Nanak from head to toe, then turned her eyes toward Rambholi. Rambholi immediately rose from her place, stepped forward, stood beside the throne with folded hands, and said, "If I have your permission, shall I proceed as per your command?"
In response, the woman—whom it is proper to call the Maharani—shook her head with great pride, indicating refusal, and then looked toward the other woman who sat beside Rambholi.

This was a matter of great astonishment for Nanak. Today, his ears heard a voice he had never heard before, nor ever expected to hear. First, it was astonishing enough that Rambholi, who lived in his neighborhood, whom Nanak had known since childhood, and who, except for that day when she set out on a journey by boat, had never been seen leaving her home nor had her parents ever let her out of their sight, now appeared here in such a state and of such high rank. Second, Rambholi, who had been mute since birth, whom even her parents had never heard speak, today, from her lips, came forth such a sweet voice! What effect that voice had on Nanak's heart, only he could know. How could Nanak possibly comprehend how Rambholi, who had never set foot outside her home, was now found among these people, and who all these women were!
Nanak had no opportunity to ponder these matters at length. The other woman, who was sitting beside Rambholi on a chair and whom Nanak had seen before as well...
She saw, and at the signal, she stood up and, stepping forward a little, began to converse with Nanak.
Woman: "Nanakprasad, it goes without saying that you have been brought here as a criminal, and you will be punished accordingly."
Nanak: "Yes, indeed, I have been brought here as a criminal, but in truth, I am not guilty, nor have I committed any crime."

Woman: "Your crime is simply this: you looked at that large painting in Babaji's room, the one that was covered with a curtain, without permission. Do you not know that one should never look at a painting covered by a curtain without being granted leave?"
Nanak (after thinking for a moment): "Indeed, that is a fault."
Woman: "Our law here is that whoever commits such a crime shall have his head cut off."
Nanak: "If that is the law, then it can only be called tyranny!"
Woman: "Be that as it may, but now there is no way for you to escape."
Nanak: "Very well, I do not fear death, and I accept it gladly—if you will answer a few questions of mine!"
Woman: "You cannot refuse death in any way, but out of mercy, you may be granted the answer to one question. You may not ask more than that. Ask—what do you wish to know?"

Nanak (after pondering for a while): "Well then, if I may ask only one question, I wish to know this: (pointing towards Rambholi) How did she come here, and how did she receive such great honor in this place?"
Woman: "That is two questions! Very well, I shall answer one of them: the one you ask about is the younger sister of our Maharani, and that is why she is seated beside her on the throne."
Nanak: "How am I to believe that you speak the truth?"
Woman: "I swear by my faith that this is not a lie. Whether you believe it or not is your own choice!"
Nanak: "Very well, if that is so, then I do not wish to die in any way."
Woman (laughing): "Do you think your life will be spared simply because you do not wish to die?"
Nanak: "Indeed, it is so. Until I consent to die, you people cannot kill me."

Woman: "We know well that you possess great powers, and because of them you can accomplish mighty deeds, but here, your powers will avail you nothing. However, if you agree to one thing, not only will your life be spared, but—"
As a reward, whatever you ask for shall be given to you.
Nanak: "What is that?"
Woman: "The lives of Kunwar Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh, who are in your custody, hand them over to the Maharani."

Nanak (His eyes blazing red with anger): "Wretch, beware! Do not ever utter such words again! I never imagined that such a beautiful assembly would turn out to be enemies of Kunwar Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh. I would sacrifice thousands like you for them! Now it is clear to me that you are all mere puppets. Who has the power to kill me or to force me in any way?"

The woman's face, upon hearing these words from Nanak, turned red with rage, just like his. In fact, the other women present there also began to tremble with fury at Nanak's boldness, but there was no sign of anger on the Maharani's face.

Woman (Drawing her sword): "Surely, now you shall die. Each one of us here (pointing towards the chairs) possesses the strength of twenty men, as do I. Do not think that just because your hands and feet are free, you can do anything. Have you forgotten that I made you drop your sword?"
Nanak: "If you all possess such strength, then why do you ask me for the lives of the two princes? Why don't you go and cut off their heads yourselves?"

Woman: "There is a special reason why we do not do this with our own hands. We could, but it would take time, which is why we ask you. Even now, accept our terms, or else I shall not rest until I have taken your life."
Nanak (Pointing towards Rambholi): "The life of that woman, whom you claim to be the Maharani's sister, is in my hands. You would do well to remember that."

No sooner had Nanak said this than Rambholi stood up from her place and spoke, "Never think that the box you brought, I left behind in the boat and that it is in your or your soldiers' possession. I threw it into the Ganga, and now, if you wish, (pointing with her hand) look, it is hanging from the ceiling in that corner."

Nanak turned and looked, and saw the box hanging from the ceiling. At this sight, he was suddenly overcome with fear; his senses deserted him, a cry escaped his lips, and he fell unconscious to the ground.

For half an hour, Nanak lay there senseless. When he finally regained consciousness, he did not have the strength to stand. Sitting there, he began to think as if he had lost all hope in life. The woman, sword still drawn, stood by his side. Suddenly, some thought struck Nanak, changing his condition entirely; the strength he had lost returned to his body, and saying to himself, "Why am I worrying in vain?" he stood up and, turning to the woman, again…
They began to converse.
Nanak: "No, no, I can never die."
Woman: "Now, who is there to save you?"
Nanak (Looking towards Rambholi): "The key to that chamber where the book written in someone's blood is kept."

At these words, Rambholi started. Her face fell, her head began to spin, and she leaned against the side of the throne, exclaiming, "Ah, what a calamity! What a mistake! The key was left right there! Curse you, wretch, for forcing me with your own hand!"

It was not just Rambholi who was struck in this manner; all the women present there turned pale, the flush of blood vanished from their faces, and every single one of them stared fixedly at Nanak. Now Nanak too was convinced that his life was saved, that what he had guessed had proved true. After waiting a moment, Nanak spoke again—
Nanak: "I have already read that book, and in fact, I have made a friend my companion in this matter. If I do not meet him within three days, he will certainly begin some action."

Nanak's words increased everyone's anxiety even more. The queen, her eyes brimming with tears, looked at the Babaji sitting beside her in such a way as if she had lost all hope in life. Babaji reassured her with a gesture, then looked at Nanak and said—
Baba: "Bravo, my son, you have done well! I am very pleased with you. I too was searching for such a clever man to make my disciple!"

Saying this, Babaji rose and, grasping Nanak's hand, led him away. Babaji's grip was so firm that Nanak's wrist began to ache; it felt as if a hand of iron had seized his wrist, one that could not be softened or loosened in any way. By now, morning had fully broken, and the crimson of the sun had claimed the upper branches of the garden's delightful trees, when Babaji, with Nanak in tow, reached the door of a chamber that was locked. With his other hand, Babaji produced a key from his waistband, unlocked the chamber, pushed Nanak inside, and then shut and locked the door behind him.

Though day had dawned, inside that chamber it seemed to Nanak as if it were still night. It was utterly dark, not even a single crack through which the faintest light could enter. Nanak could not even tell how large the chamber was; but the stone floor was so cold that within an hour Nanak's hands and feet had grown numb. After an hour, Nanak began to see the walls around him. It seemed as if some kind of glow was emanating from the walls themselves.
And that glow was gradually increasing. Soon, the place was well-lit, and every object in that chamber became clearly visible.

The room was not very large. In each of its four corners lay piles of bones. In the walls on all four sides were four openings, each about the height of a man's waist—not very big, but large enough for a person's head to pass through. Nanak saw that in the opening directly in front of him, something was gleaming. After observing closely for a while, he realized that they were two large eyes, staring straight at him.

Nanak had already been frightened by the gradual appearance of light in that dark chamber, but now those eyes terrified him even more. His fear kept growing, for he discovered several other things there that chilled his heart.

As we have mentioned above, the floor of that chamber was made of stone. Gradually, the floor began to heat up, and Nanak felt the warmth spreading through his body. The cold that had rendered him helpless now vanished. Eventually, the floor became so hot that Nanak had to rise from his place—but where could he go? The entire floor of the chamber was heating up evenly; wherever he stepped, his feet burned. Nanak's attention returned to the opening in which he had seen those gleaming eyes, for now, from that very opening, a hand was reaching out toward him. Nanak shrank back into a corner, hoping the hand would not reach him, but the hand kept advancing until it seized his wrist.

Who knows what kind of hand it was that gripped Nanak's wrist so firmly? The moment it touched his skin, a strange tingling sensation shot through him, growing so intense in an instant that Nanak could neither steady himself nor free himself from that grip. At last, he lost consciousness and completely forgot himself.

When Nanak regained his senses, he found himself on the banks of the Ganga, at the very spot where he had disembarked from the boat with Rambholi. Beside him lay a ripe bunch of plantains. There was little daylight left, and the sun was descending toward the western horizon.
chapters.summary: Lost in the jungle, Nanak seeks RamBholi, finds a strange house with a mysterious sadhu, and glimpses a terrifying portrait, leading to a shocking encounter.

chapters.title: Babaji’s Secret Council
paragraphs: Now, let us return to the court of that Maharani, from where Nanak had been taken and transported to the banks of the Ganga.

After pushing Nanak into the chamber, Babaji did not return to the Maharani, but instead went off in another direction and arrived at a barahdari (a pavilion with twelve doors). There, several men were seated.

Some people were busy with their work. As soon as they saw Babaji, they stood up. Babaji looked at them and said, "I have sent Nanak to his place. He turned out to be a most formidable ayyār; we could do nothing to him. Anyway, take him to the same spot on the banks of the Ganga where he had disembarked from the barge, and leave some food for him there as well." Saying this, Babaji returned and went to the Maharani.

At this time, the Maharani's court was not in its usual state, nor was there any crowd. There was no sign of the throne or chairs; only a carpet was spread on which the Maharani, Rambholi, and the woman who had ridden away on horseback with Rambholi to escape from Nanak, were sitting and conversing among themselves.

As soon as Babaji arrived, he said, "I did not expect Nanak to be such a cunning and shrewd man. Dhanpati had said he was very simple, that the task would be accomplished easily, but all this trouble was for nothing!"

Readers should remember, Dhanpati is the name of the same woman who, mounted on her horse, had escaped with Rambholi from Nanak. It is not surprising if some keen-minded readers are startled by the name Dhanpati and wonder why such a woman is called Dhanpati! It is indeed something to ponder, and as the story progresses, this name will play a significant role.
Dhanpati: "Well, what had to happen has happened. At least we have learned that we have fallen into Nanak's clutches. Now we must devise some way to save ourselves and escape from Nanak's grasp."

Babaji: "I would still advise you not to get entangled in this affair. Kunwar Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh are men of great power; to bring them under your control and snatch away what belongs to them is very difficult, not at all easy. See, you were deceived at the very first step. God forbid, if Nanak dies or someone kills him and the book remains in his possession and cannot be found, is there any way you could be saved?"
Rambholi: "Certainly not, we would surely meet a terrible end."
Babaji: "I would insist, and never allow such a thing to happen, but apart from giving advice, I can do nothing more."
Maharani (looking at Babaji): "I will make one more attempt; if it does not succeed, then whatever you say shall be done."
Babaji: "As you wish, I cannot say anything more."
Maharani (looking at Dhanpati and Rambholi): "Besides you two, there is no one else fit for this task."
Dhanpati: "When have I ever shrunk from risking my life?"
Rambholi: "Whatever the command, I shall obey."
Maharani: "Both of you go, and do whatever you can!"
Rambholi: "Divide the work between us."
Maharani (looking towards Dhanpati): "It is your task to retrieve the book from Nanak's possession, and (turning to Rambholi) it is your task to capture Kishori and bring her here."
Babaji: "But remember two things, or you will not escape with your life!"
Both: "What are they?"

Babaji: "First, do not lay a hand on Kunwar Indrajit Singh or Anand Singh. Second, act in such a way that Nanak does not discover your involvement; otherwise, he will never let you go without knowing the truth, and all your efforts will be in vain. (Looking at Rambholi) Do not think that he will show you any leniency; now that he knows the real situation, he will do everything in his power to uproot and destroy us."

Maharani: "That is certain, there is no doubt about it. But these two are clever; they will protect themselves. (Looking at both) Well, go now, let us see what fate has in store. Be very careful and look after yourselves."
Both: "As you command!"
chapters.summary: Babaji cautions the Maharani and her accomplices, Dhanpati and Rambholi, about the dangers of underestimating Nanak and failing in their assigned tasks against him and.

chapters.title: Captives in the Underground Vault
paragraphs: Now let us turn our attention to Rohtasgarh, and see what has become of poor Kishori, helpless in the underground chamber, as well as Kunwar Anand Singh and the others.

When Kunwar Anand Singh, Bhairon Singh, and Tara Singh were captured in the underground vault and brought before Raja Digvijay Singh, the king's men introduced the three of them, and upon hearing this, the king was astonished and began to wonder how they had managed to arrive there. Kishori was also standing in that place. When she heard who they were, she became anxious. She was convinced that now their lives could not be saved. At that moment, she silently prayed to God, wishing that somehow their lives might be spared—even if it meant her own life in exchange, she would not mind. But she could not bear to see them die before her eyes. There was no doubt in her mind that they had come solely to rescue her; otherwise, why would they have endured such hardship?

All those present in the underground chamber knew that at this moment, Kunwar Anand Singh had no one to help him. But our esteemed readers know that Pandit Jagannath Jyotishi, who was now present there in the guise of a daroga, would surely aid Kunwar Virendra Singh. Yet, what can one man accomplish in such a situation? Nevertheless, Jyotishi did not lose courage and began conversing with the king. Jyotishi knew that he alone could do little at such a critical time, and the situation there...

By reading the book, he had also come to know that, according to the rules of this underground chamber, they were certain to be killed. Yet, Jyotishiji still held some faint hope for their survival, for Pandit Badrinath had said, "Today, Kunwar Anand Singh will come into this chamber, and shortly after, we too shall arrive with some men." Now, Jyotishiji could do nothing except delay the king with conversation, hoping that Pandit Badrinath and the others would arrive in time. And so he did exactly that.
Jyotishiji, that is, the Daroga Sahib, went before the king and said—
Daroga: I am very pleased that Kunwar Anand Singh has come into our hands of his own accord.
King: (Looking Jyotishiji up and down, from head to toe) It is astonishing that you say such a thing! It seems your wits have wandered off to graze on grass today! Shame! Shame!
Daroga: (Startled, folding his hands) Why so, Your Majesty?
King: (With displeasure) And yet you ask, "Why so?" Tell me yourself, Anand Singh has fallen into our trap of his own accord—why should that make you happy?
Daroga: I am pleased because, when Raja Virendra Singh hears of Anand Singh's capture, he will surely send word, "Release Anand Singh, and in exchange, we will release Kunwar Kalyan Singh."
King: Now I see that your wits truly have gone grazing, or else you are not the real Daroga, but someone else in disguise.
Daroga: (Trembling) Perhaps you say so because what I have just submitted is against the rules of this chamber.

King: Yes, now you are on the right path! Indeed, that is so. I am grieved that he has fallen into this trap. Now I have lost hope for my own life and that of my son.
