Surely, Rohtasgarh is now ruined. I cannot, under any circumstance, act against the rules, no matter what happens—Anand Singh must be killed. And Anand Singh is not the first to come here; several of his ayyars must have come before him and seen everything. The strange happenings in this place for the past several days are all a result of that. The truth is, hearing your words now, I even suspect you. The real Daroga of this chamber would never say he was pleased at Anand Singh's capture. He would know that, according to the rules, Anand Singh must be killed, and in exchange, Kalyan Singh would also die. Moreover, Virendra Singh's ayyars, abandoning the code of ayyari, would resort to poison instead of mere sleeping draughts, and within a week, Rohtasgarh would be destroyed. The real Daroga of this chamber would surely be distressed by all this.
Hearing the king's words, Jyotishiji's eyes were opened. In his heart, he...

They bowed their heads in acceptance of their mistake and began to ponder with downcast eyes. At that very moment, the king called out to his men and said, "Arrest this fake Daroga as well, and thoroughly investigate whether he is truly the Daroga here or one of Virendra Singh's spies in disguise!"

In the blink of an eye, the Daroga Sahib was bound, and the king ordered two men to bring hot water. The servants, thinking that it would take time to heat water here and that hot water was always available in the audience hall above, sought the king's permission to fetch it from there. The king approved this and ordered them to bring water from the audience hall above.
Two servants rushed to fetch the hot water, but soon returned and said, "The way upstairs is blocked."
King: "Why is that? How can the way be blocked?"
Servant: "We do not know, sir, why this has happened."
King: "That is impossible! (Showing the key) Look, I have the key right here—without this key, how could anyone lock those doors?"
Servant: "Whatever the case, I cannot say, Your Majesty. You may see for yourself."

The king went himself and found that the way upstairs, that is, the door, was indeed locked. He was astonished and began to wonder who could have locked the door, for he had the key with him! At last, he tried to open the door with the key, but the lock would not yield. Until now, this very key had always opened the way in and out of this underground chamber, but at this moment, the key would not work at all. This strange occurrence, which had never before entered King Digvijay Singh's mind, had suddenly arisen today. The king's astonishment knew no bounds. There were many other doors in that underground chamber that were also opened with this key.
Digvijay Singh tried the key on several other doors, knocking and tapping, but none would open.
Tears welled up in the king's eyes, and suddenly these words escaped his lips, "Now, the time of this underground chamber—and of our lives—has come to an end."

King Digvijay Singh, distraught, wandered about, trying the key in the doors again and again. Just then, from the mouth of that terrifying black statue—before which a woman had once been sacrificed—a strange sound began to emerge. This, too, was something new. Digvijay Singh and all those present were seized with fear and turned their gaze toward it. The trembling king went and stood before the statue, listening intently to discern what the sound might be.
For a while, the sound was unintelligible, but then these words became clear:
"Your key will only open the door to chamber number twelve. As quickly as possible, lock Kishori inside it, or else all your lives will be lost in vain!"
This new, wondrous, and uncanny event made the king's heart quiver, but he could not comprehend how the statue had spoken! Never before had such a thing happened...

This had never happened before. Hundreds of men had been sacrificed before this idol, yet such a situation had never arisen. Now the king was convinced that there was indeed something miraculous about this statue; otherwise, why would such great men have arranged for sacrifices? Although the king did not usually believe in such things, today he was overcome by fear. He did not waste much time in deliberation and, using the same key, opened the twelfth cell and locked Kishori inside.

King Digvijay Singh had barely finished this task when Pandit Badrinath arrived in the underground chamber with many men. Finding Kunwar Anand Singh and Tara Singh helpless, he rushed forward and quickly untied their hands and feet. The king's men tried to resist, but those who had come with Pandit Badrinath also joined the fray. Once Anand Singh, Bhairon Singh, and Tara Singh were freed, the battle intensified. Who could stand before them? The four ayyars alone were enough for so many foes. Several were killed, many fell wounded. King Digvijay Singh was captured, and not a single man from Virendra Singh's side was lost. After all these matters were settled, they began searching for Kishori.

Everyone had witnessed the astonishing events that had taken place in that underground chamber. Lali and Jyotishiji recounted everything to Anand Singh and the ayyars, including the fact that Kishori had been locked in the twelfth cell.

Pandit Badrinath took the key from Digvijay Singh's waist and opened the twelfth cell, but Kishori was not inside. They searched thoroughly with a lamp, but Kishori was nowhere to be found—as if she had vanished into the earth or been swallowed by the walls. Everyone was astonished: how could Kishori have disappeared from a locked cell? However, a slip of paper was found in the cell, which Bhairon Singh picked up and read aloud to everyone. It said—
"Dhanpati rang machayo, sadhyo kaam. Bholi bhali mud aihain yadi yahi thaam."

No one could understand the meaning of this 'barvai' (verse), but it was clear that finding Kishori here would now be difficult. Meanwhile, as soon as Lali heard the verse, she burst out laughing, but when asked the reason for her laughter, she gave no reply, only lowered her head and fell silent. When the ayyars pressed her further, she said, "There is no special reason for my laughter. I worked very hard to rescue Kishori from here. (After recounting all she had done to free Kishori) I had hoped that in return for my efforts, I would receive some reward from King Virendra Singh, but nothing happened. All my efforts were in vain; before my very eyes, Kishori was locked in this cell. When you opened the cell, I hoped to see her and hear her recount my labors in her own words, but nothing. Even God's...
What a strange fate it is! What he does, I cannot understand at all! That was the only thought that made me laugh—there was nothing else to it."
Perhaps everyone believed Lali's words, but our own ayyars' hearts were not convinced. We shall see now how they deal with Lali.

Pandit Badrinath was of the opinion that it was no longer wise to remain in this underground chamber. When even the king of this place is troubled by its wonders, what can we say for ourselves? There is little hope of finding any trace of Kishori at this time. Therefore, it is best to leave here as soon as possible.

Those who had died were buried in the same chamber, a pit dug for them. The remaining four or five men, along with King Digvijay Singh, were taken as prisoners, their faces covered with sheets. Jyotishiji gathered up the bunch of keys, took the daily logbook in hand, and, along with everyone else, exited the underground chamber. This time, as they passed through each door, Jyotishiji locked it behind them, so that no one could enter again.

Once outside, Lali said to Kunwar Anand Singh, "It is with regret that I must say all my efforts have gone to waste, and there is no longer any hope of meeting Kishori! If you permit, I would like to return to my home, for just like Kishori, I too was imprisoned in this fort."
Anand Singh: "Where is your home?"
Lali: "Mathuraji."
Bhairon Singh (to Anand Singh): "There is no doubt that Lali's story must also be grand and fascinating. She should certainly be taken to our Maharaj."
Badrinath: "Indeed, it must be so, or else the Maharaj will be displeased."

Kunwar Anand Singh understood the meaning behind the ayyars' words, and so he did not grant Lali permission to depart from there. Helpless, Lali had to go along with Kunwar Sahib, and without any trouble, they all reached the camp of King Virendra Singh, where Lali was respectfully placed in a tent.
chapters.summary: In the underground vault, Kunwar Anand Singh is captured, and Kishori vanishes from a locked cell, leaving the ayyars puzzled by Lali's reaction.

chapters.title: Council in the Royal Tent
paragraphs: The next evening, King Virendra Singh sat in his tent, discussing matters concerning Rohtasgarh. Pandit Badrinath, Bhairon Singh, Tara Singh, Jyotishiji, Kunwar...
Anandsingh and Tejsingh were seated nearby. Each, in their own manner, recounted the events of the underground chamber of Rohtasgarh, and at last, the conversation turned to Virendra Singh.
Virendra Singh: What should we do now regarding Rohtasgarh?

Tejsingh: There is no doubt that you have now become the master of Rohtasgarh! When both the king and the minister are in your custody, what else remains to be done? Yes, now we must consider what treatment should be given to King Digvijay Singh.
Virendra Singh: And what arrangements should be made for Kishori?
Tejsingh: Yes, these are the two matters at hand. As for Kishori, I cannot say anything just yet, but regarding King Digvijay Singh, I would first like to hear your opinion.
Virendra Singh: My opinion is that if he sincerely accepts subordination, then we should impose tribute (revenue) on Rohtasgarh and let him go.
Tejsingh: That is my opinion as well.
Bhaironsingh: But what if, after accepting now, he later resorts to treachery?

Tejsingh: I do not expect that to happen. From all I have heard, he is known to be honest, sincere, and brave. God forbid, even if his intentions change after some time, we need not concern ourselves with it.
Virendra Singh: How far can one consider such possibilities! (Looking towards Tarasingh) Go, bring Digvijay Singh here, but do not bring him before me in shackles or chains.
"At your command," said Tarasingh, and went to bring Digvijay Singh. In a short while, he returned, bringing him along. Meanwhile, they had been conversing about other matters.
Digvijay Singh respectfully saluted King Virendra Singh and stood before him with folded hands.
Virendra Singh: Tell me, what are your intentions now?
Digvijay Singh: My intention is to remain with you all my life and serve you faithfully.
Virendra Singh: There is no change in your intentions, is there?

Digvijay Singh: Only a complete fool would harbor ill will against such a mighty king as yourself. Only a true idiot would hope to defeat you in any way. There is no doubt that each of your ayyars has the power to destroy ten kingdoms. I had great faith in the strength of this Rohtasgarh fort, but now I am convinced that it was my mistake. You could conquer any kingdom you wish without a fight. My mind cannot comprehend what has happened, nor can I understand what...

What a spectacle the ayyars have created! For hundreds of years, the secret of that underground chamber had been kept hidden, and in truth, even I did not know its exact nature until now. Yet, in the blink of an eye, your ayyars have taken possession of that very chamber—if this is not a miracle, then what is! Surely, the grace of God is upon you, and all this is the result of your sincere devotion. To bear enmity with you is as good as cutting off one's own head.

Hearing Digvijay Singh's words, King Virendra Singh smiled and looked at him. There was a ring of truth in the manner in which Digvijay Singh spoke. Virendra Singh was greatly pleased, and seating Digvijay Singh beside him, he said—

Virendra Singh: Listen, Digvijay Singh, I set you free and, on my behalf, place you upon the throne of Rohtasgarh. But on one condition: that you always consider yourself my subordinate and pay a certain tribute as revenue.

Digvijay Singh: I already consider myself your loyal servant—what more is there to understand? As for the throne of Rohtasgarh, I do not accept it. Please appoint another deputy for that post and command me to remain with you.
Virendra Singh: I see no one more suitable than you to be the deputy of Rohtasgarh.
Digvijay Singh (folding his hands): Please, show me your mercy. I can no longer bear the burdens of rule.

For half an hour, this debate continued. Virendra Singh wished, with his own hand, to seat Digvijay Singh upon the throne of Rohtasgarh, while Digvijay Singh kept refusing. But at last, having no other choice, Digvijay Singh had to accept Virendra Singh's command. However, at the same time, he made Virendra Singh promise that for a month, he would remain his guest and stay in Rohtasgarh for that duration.

Virendra Singh gladly accepted this, for he was eager to learn more about the secrets of the underground chamber of Rohtasgarh. Both Virendra Singh and Tej Singh were convinced that the chamber was indeed some sort of tilism.

King Digvijay Singh folded his hands, looked towards Tej Singh, and said, "Please, have mercy and explain to me what you and your subordinate ayyars have done in Rohtasgarh. My mind is still bewildered."

Tej Singh recounted everything in detail. Hearing the account of Diwan Ramanand, Digvijay Singh laughed heartily, even laughing at his own foolishness, and said, "Nothing is hidden from you people." After this, Diwan Ramanand was summoned to that very place and handed over to Digvijay Singh, and Digvijay Singh's son, Kunwar...
Several men were also dispatched to Chunar Fort to bring Kalyan Singh.
After these matters were settled, the conversation turned to Lali. Tejsingh asked Digvijay Singh, "Who is Lali, and since when has she been here with you?"

In response, Digvijay Singh said, "I do not know Lali very well. It has not been more than a month—perhaps four or five days more or less—since Lali and Kundan, two young women, arrived at my place. From their manner and attire, I gathered that they belonged to a respectable family. When I inquired, both of them declared themselves to be daughters of a noble house and said that they wished to spend two or three months here to escape their troubles. Out of compassion, I allowed them to stay here with all due respect. Beyond this, I know nothing more."
Tejsingh said, "Undoubtedly, there is some mystery here. Those two are not ordinary women."
Jyotishiji spoke up, "Let me tell you something astonishing."
Tejsingh asked, "What is it?"

Jyotishiji replied, "You may recall that when I was describing the state of the underground chamber, I mentioned that when I saw Kishori and Lali there, I called out to them by name, which surprised them both."
Tejsingh said, "Yes, yes, I remember. I was about to ask you how you recognized Lali."
Jyotishiji continued, "That is precisely the astonishing thing I am about to tell you."
Tejsingh urged, "Please, tell us quickly."

Jyotishiji began, "Once, while sitting in the underground chambers of Rohtasgarh, I began to feel restless and started opening the rooms one by one to look around. Among the bunch of keys I had found, there was one particularly large key that fit all the rooms in the underground chamber, though I still do not know what many of the other keys are for."
Tejsingh interjected, "Well, what happened then?"

Jyotishiji continued, "All the rooms were dark. How far could I see by carrying a lamp? But in one room, I saw something shining on the wall. Although the room was dark, it was clear that it was a portrait. Some special substance had been applied to it so that the image was visible even in the darkness. The eyes, ears, nose, even the hair, were all distinctly visible. Beneath the portrait, the name 'Lali' was written. I stood there for a long time, marveling at the picture, and finally closed the room and returned to my quarters. Later, when I saw Lali with Kishori, I immediately recognized her as the one in the portrait. I had thought that Lali must be a resident of that place, which is why her portrait was there. But now, hearing Maharaj Digvijay Singh's account, I am astonished. If Lali is not from there, then how did her portrait come to be in that chamber?"
Digvijay Singh: " I have not yet seen that portrait; it is surprising."
Virendra Singh: " Not just that; when I take you with me to thoroughly investigate that underground chamber, you will witness many things that will astonish you."
Digvijay Singh: " God willing, may such an opportunity come soon. Now, you should go to Rohtasgarh as soon as possible."
Virendra Singh: " (looking towards Tej Singh) What arrangements are being made regarding Indrajit Singh?"

Tej Singh: " I am not unconcerned. Spies have been sent in all directions. Until now, I was entangled in the affairs of Rohtasgarh, but now I will personally go in search of him. Some clues have also been found."
Virendra Singh: " Oh! What clues have you found?"
Tej Singh: " I will tell you about it tomorrow; for today, please be patient for just one more day."

King Virendra Singh loved his two sons dearly. He was greatly distressed by the disappearance of Indrajit Singh, but he was also adept at concealing his feelings and always kept the importance of timing in mind. He had great trust in Tej Singh and held him in high regard. If Tej Singh advised against any matter, he would not mention it again until Tej Singh himself brought it up. This was the reason that, at this time, he said nothing about Indrajit Singh in front of Tej Singh.

The next day, Maharaj Digvijay Singh, along with his army, took Tej Singh to the fortress of Rohtasgarh. The name of Kunwar Anand Singh was proclaimed with great fanfare. It was an occasion fit for grand celebrations, but due to thoughts of Kunwar Indrajit Singh, no festivities were held.

King Virendra Singh and his companions were very pleased with the hospitality and conduct of King Digvijay Singh. The following day, a small committee of select men was convened in the audience hall to decide what should be done next. Only the brave and skilled individuals listed below were present in this committee—King Virendra Singh, Kunwar Anand Singh, Tej Singh, Devi Singh, Pandit Badrinath, Jyotipiji, King Digvijay Singh, and Ramanand. In addition to these, there was another man present, his face covered with a veil, whom Tej Singh had brought with him and included in the committee on his own guarantee.
Virendra Singh: " (looking towards Tej Singh) In the presence of this veiled man whom you have brought with you, can we discuss confidential matters?"
Tej Singh: " Yes, yes, there is no harm in it."

Virendra Singh: " Very well, then. First, we must arrange to find out about Kishori; second, to investigate the many matters in the underground chambers here that are worthy of knowledge and consideration; and third, to search for Indrajit Singh. These should be our top priorities."
(Looking towards Tejsingh) You had said that some news about Indrajitsingh has been discovered?

Tejsingh: "Yes, indeed, I did say so, and the full details will soon be revealed to you. But before that, I wish to ask Raja Sahib (gesturing towards Digvijaysingh) a few questions which are very important. After that, I will speak about my own matter."
Virendrasingh: "No objection."
Digvijaysingh: "Yes, yes, ask away."
Tejsingh: "Did you once have an ayyār named Shersingh¹ here?"

Digvijay: "Yes, I did. The poor fellow was a very noble, honest, and hardworking man, and a true master in the art of ayyāri. Ramanand and Govindsingh are both his disciples. I am deeply grieved by his departure. A few days ago, my grief was of a different kind, but today it is of another sort altogether."
Tejsingh: "Two kinds of grief and regret! I do not understand what you mean. Kindly explain clearly."

Digvijaysingh: "At first, my sorrow at his leaving was mingled with anger, but today I regret that the reasons for which he left were entirely justified. My resentment towards him was misplaced. If he were here now, he would gladly help you in your cause."
Tejsingh: "Why were you upset with him, and why did he leave?"

Digvijaysingh: "The reason is this: when I took Kishori into my custody, he tried hard to persuade me, saying, "Do not do this; rather, send Kishori to Raja Virendrasingh." I did not agree to this, and, displeased with him, I even resolved to imprison him. The truth is, I was friends with Randhirsingh, and Shersingh lived with me. His younger brother, Gadādharsingh, whose daughter is Kamla—you must know her..."
Tejsingh: "Yes, yes, we all know her well."

Digvijaysingh: "Well, Gadādharsingh lived with Randhirsingh. Gadādharsingh has been dead for many years now, and in the meantime, my friendship with Randhirsingh also soured. When I arranged for Randhirsingh's granddaughter Kishori to marry my son, Shersingh was greatly displeased. My own feelings towards Shersingh also changed. I thought that Shersingh's niece, Kamla, would certainly try to rescue Kishori from here, and that in this endeavor, she would enlist the help of her uncle, Shersingh."
1. Shersingh (Kamla's uncle), whose story is told in the thirteenth chapter of the third part of this series.
She will take help. This thought settled in my heart, and I resolved to capture Sher Singh. He learned of my intention and quietly disappeared—no one knows where he went.
Tej Singh: Now, what do you think? Was he at fault or not?
Digvijay Singh: No, no, he was completely innocent. In fact, it was my own mistake, for which I regret even today. God willing, if I find him, I will beg his forgiveness.
Tej Singh: If you grant me a reward, I can find Sher Singh for you!
Digvijay Singh: Whatever you ask, I shall give, and besides, I will be deeply indebted to you.
Tej Singh: Then, I ask only this reward: if I find Sher Singh and bring him here, you must hand him over to our king, Virendra Singh! We wish to make him our companion.
Digvijay Singh: I gladly accept this. What need is there for a promise, when I myself am a loyal subject of King Virendra Singh?

After this, Tej Singh looked at the masked man who sat beside them, whom he had brought with him to this committee. The masked man threw off his veil and, falling at King Digvijay Singh's feet, cried, "Forgive me my fault!" King Digvijay Singh recognized Sher Singh, lifted him up with great joy, embraced him, and said, "No, no, you have no fault—rather, it was my fault, and I ask your forgiveness."
Sher Singh went and sat beside the assembly. Tej Singh said, "Listen, Sher Singh, now you are one of us!"
Sher Singh: Certainly, I am yours now. Since you have taken a promise from His Majesty, what objection could there be?
King Virendra Singh had been listening to all this with astonishment. At last, looking toward Tej Singh, he asked, "How did you meet Sher Singh?"
Tej Singh: Sher Singh himself came to me and told me everything. In truth, Sher Singh has done us a great favor as well.
Virendra Singh: What is that?

Tej Singh: He has found the whereabouts of Kunwar Indrajit Singh and has already stationed several of his men to protect him. He has also assured me that Kunwar Indrajit Singh will not suffer any harm.
Virendra Singh: (happily, looking at Sher Singh) Well done! Where did you find him, and in what condition is he?
Sher Singh: Whatever I know, I have already told Diwan Sahib (Tej Singh). He will tell you; do not be impatient to know it all at once. At this moment...

The task for which I came here is now accomplished. I do not think it proper to stay here any longer. You all may continue your discussions as you wish, for I must reach Kunwar Indrajit Singh as soon as possible to render my assistance. However, if you would be so kind as to send one of your ayyars with me, it would be excellent, and the task would be completed more swiftly.
Virendra Singh (happily): "Very well, you may go, and take with you whichever of my ayyars you desire."
Sher Singh: "If you leave the choice to me, then I would ask for Devi Singh to accompany me."
Tej Singh: "Yes, you may gladly take him. (Looking towards Devi Singh) Prepare yourself."
Devi Singh: "I am always prepared. (To Sher Singh) Come, let us leave these people to their own affairs."

Taking Devi Singh with him, Sher Singh departed, and meanwhile, the others began to deliberate on what should be done next. Within an hour, it was decided that there was no need to question Lali further, for she would never tell the truth about herself. However, she should be kept under guard, and the underground chamber should be thoroughly examined and its secrets uncovered.
chapters.summary: King Virendra Singh discusses Rohtasgarh's future with his council, where Digvijay Singh's fate is debated, and the mysterious Lali's portrait is revealed, piquing Tejsingh's curiosity.

chapters.title: Kundan’s Vigil in the Garden
paragraphs: Now it is necessary to write of Kundan's situation. Esteemed readers must be eager to know her fate. We last left Kundan in the very garden of the Rohtasgarh palace where Kishori used to reside. Kundan was constantly anxious that Kishori should not, by any means, fall into Lali's clutches.

When Lali, taking Kishori with her, descended into that house through the tunnel—the house from which the underground passage began—and this news reached Kundan, she became greatly alarmed. She raised a commotion throughout the palace. She was at a loss as to what should be done. As we have previously written, after Kishori and Lali had departed, several men, shouting "Stop! Catch them!" also entered the same house through the tunnel by which Lali and Kishori had gone.

Blending in with those people, Kundan too, fastening a small bundle to her waist, entered the house, and in the confusion and tumult, no one noticed her. Inside the house, it was utterly dark. Lali had gone into another room and shut the door, so those who had been pursuing her were forced to turn back in frustration.
...was placed, and they informed the Maharaj of this, but Kundan did not return from that house; rather, she hid herself in some corner.

We have written before, and now write again, that there were three doors inside that house. One was the main entrance, outside which guards were always posted; the second stood open; and through the third door, Kishori had been taken away by Lali. The door that was open led into a small hall. It was up to this hall that those searching for Lali and Kishori had come, but finding no way forward, they had turned back. When those people had left the house, Kundan untied the bundle from her waist, took out her things, and after lighting a candle, began to look around.

It was a small hall, but closed off on all sides. On the walls of this hall were painted all manner of terrifying pictures, but Kundan paid them no heed. In the center of the hall stood eleven iron boxes, each about a hand's span in size, and on each box rested a human skull. Kundan began to examine these boxes closely. The boxes were arranged in a circle upon a low platform. On one box was only half a skull, while on the others, the skulls were whole. Kundan was amazed to see that one skull was lying on the ground—why did it not have a box beneath it like the others? Kundan began counting from the box with the half-skull. She realized that the seventh skull had no box beneath it. Suddenly, Kundan exclaimed, "Oh! Oh! Of course, Lali must have taken the box from beneath this one, for that was the real box with the key—but how did she come to know this?"

Kundan began counting again and stopped at the fifth box from the broken skull. She lifted the skull, set it aside, and picked up the box. Examining it carefully, she then struck it hard against the ground. The box broke into four pieces, as if it had been joined together at four points. From inside emerged a key. Seeing it, Kundan laughed and, delighted, said to herself, "Now let's see how I outwit Lali!"

Kundan began to use the key. In the same hall, there was a cupboard set into the wall, which Kundan unlocked with the key. Stairs leading downward were revealed, and she descended without fear. She arrived in a small chamber where, atop a small throne, lay a copper plate about a hand's length long and somewhat less wide. Kundan picked it up and examined it carefully. She saw that something was inscribed upon it—letters engraved, and smeared with some kind of oil or grease, which had protected the plate from rust all this time. Kundan read the inscription with great attention, then laughed and looked around. In the wall of that chamber were two doors on two sides, and one panel in the floor. She opened one door, which led upward...

She found a staircase leading upwards. Fearlessly, she climbed up and reached a cramped chamber, barely large enough to seat four or five people. Yet, in the walls of this chamber, there were several small holes. Extinguishing her lamp, Kundan pressed her eye to one of these holes and looked through.

Kundan found herself in a spot from where she could clearly see the terrifying idol before which a woman had already been sacrificed, as we have described above. After a short while, Kundan saw Maharaj Digvijay Singh, the warden of the underground vault, Lali, Kishori, and many other people there. Before her very eyes, another woman was sacrificed before that idol, and Kunwar Anand Singh, along with the ayyars, was captured. We have already recounted above the events concerning Kishori and Kunwar Anand Singh in this underground vault—all of which Kundan witnessed.

At last, Kundan descended and, using the same key, opened the trapdoor in the floor, entered the vault, and, lighting her lamp, began to look around. Glancing up at the ceiling, she realized that the terrifying idol seated on the throne—completely hollow from within, throne and all—was positioned directly above her head.

Kundan then ascended again and, opening another door set in the wall, entered a tunnel. After walking a few steps, she came upon a small window, which she also unlocked with her key. Now she had reached the passage that connected the audience hall to the underground vault—the very route used by the king. Kundan locked every door along the way from the vault to the audience hall with her key. Besides the locks, each door had an additional latch, which Kundan also secured. Having completed this task, she returned to the spot from where she could see the terrifying idol and all the people gathered there. With her own eyes, Kundan witnessed the anxiety that overcame Raja Digvijay Singh when he found the door locked.

Seizing the opportunity, Kundan descended and entered the vault beneath the terrifying idol. After muttering to herself for a while, it was Kundan herself who spoke the words that seemed to issue from the mouth of the idol—words that Raja Digvijay Singh and the others heard, and by which Kishori was ordered to be locked in cell number twelve. In truth, those words were spoken by Kundan, though everyone believed they came from the idol.

Kundan then left that place and, wishing to see whether the king would indeed imprison Kishori in that cell, returned to the chamber above from where she could observe everyone. When Kundan saw that Kishori had indeed been locked in that cell, she descended once more into the underground vault. From there, a passage led directly beneath the cell in which Kishori was imprisoned. The ceiling was so low that Kundan had to crawl. In the ceiling, there was a screw; turning it caused a stone slab to move aside, and with her face covered by her veil, Kundan stood before Kishori.

Poor Kishori, already distraught from so many calamities, was thrown into even greater panic when, in the darkness, she suddenly saw Kundan emerge, carrying a lamp. In her fright, she did not recognize Kundan at all; instead, she mistook her for a ghost, a spirit, or some other supernatural being, and, letting out a scream, fainted on the spot.

Kundan took out a vial of medicine from her waistband and held it to Kishori's nose, ensuring she remained deeply unconscious. Then, taking some items from her small bundle, she wrote "Dhanpati has created a spectacle, the task is accomplished…" and so forth, setting the note aside in the room. Next, she took a sheet she had brought from the palace, wrapped Kishori's bundle in it, and dragged her down below. Just as she had earlier turned the mechanism to move the stone slab, she now closed off the passage again.

The tunnel did not end beneath the small room; rather, it stretched on for quite a distance, growing wider and taller as it went. Carrying Kishori, Kundan proceeded along the passage. After walking about a hundred steps, she came upon a door, which she unlocked with the same key, and continued forward through the tunnel. After about half an hour, the tunnel ended, and Kundan found herself at the mouth of a cave.
Upon reaching this spot, Kundan blew a whistle. In a short while, five men appeared from different directions, and one stepped forward to ask, "Who is it? Dhanpati-ji?"
Kundan replied, "Yes, Rama, you all have had to endure much hardship here and have been stuck for many days."
Rama said, "When our master herself was caught up in such danger for so long, where escaping with one's life was nearly impossible, then what can be said of us? At least we were out in the open."
Kundan said, "Well, Kishori is now in our hands. Take her and get away as quickly as you can."
The men took Kishori and departed from there.

By now, the reader must have realized that Kishori had fallen into Dhanpati's grasp. Who is Dhanpati? This is the very same Dhanpati you have already encountered in the accounts of Nanak and Rambholi. My writing this will surely surprise the esteemed reader, and their astonishment will not diminish but only increase. Along with this, the reader will also recall Nanak's words: "That book, too, which was written in someone's blood…"—the secret of which had saved Nanak's life. The reader will surely also consider that if Kundan was in fact Dhanpati, then Lali must have been Rambholi, for Dhanpati knew the secret of the "book written in someone's blood," and Rambholi knew it as well. When Dhanpati mentioned that book before Lali in the Rohtasgarh palace, Lali trembled, which suggests that she was indeed Rambholi. If Lali was frightened at the mention of the book written in someone's blood, then Dhanpati must also have understood that—

Rambholi says, then why did Dhanpati (Kundan) not unite with Lali, since both of them were as good as one and the same? In such a situation, there arises a suspicion that Lali was not Rambholi. Then why did Lali laugh upon hearing the 'barwa' written by Dhanpati in the underground chamber? Thinking about such matters will surely increase the readers' anxiety, but what can be done, it is unavoidable!
chapters.summary: Kundan bravely navigates secret passages beneath the palace, determined to rescue Kishori from Lali's clutches, facing terrifying idols and hidden chambers along her perilous journey.

chapters.title: Kishori Awakens in the Wild
paragraphs: The next day, after midday, Kishori's unconsciousness faded. She found herself lying on the ground amidst the thickets of a dense forest, and saw Kundan and several other people nearby. Poor Kishori, in just these few days, had already fallen into all manner of troubles; in fact, from the very moment she had left her home, she had not known a single moment of happiness, as though happiness was simply not her fate. If she escaped one calamity, she fell into another; freed from the second, she was ensnared by a third. Even now, she found herself in a wretched state. Though Kundan sat before her, she had not the slightest hope of any kindness from her. Moreover, seeing several other men there, and finding herself regaining consciousness after a spell of faintness, she became convinced that Kundan had betrayed her. The events of the night came back to her like a dream, and even now she could not be certain what sort of treatment awaited her.

For a while, she brooded over her misfortunes and prayed to God for death. At last, she was roused from her despair when Dhanpati (Kundan) called out to her, "Kishori, do not be afraid, no harm shall come to you."
Kishori: "I do not understand what you are saying. What you have already done—what greater harm could there be than that?"
Dhanpati: "Your life will not be taken; rather, wherever you are kept, you will be given every comfort."
Kishori: "Will Indrajit Singh be there as well?"
Dhanpati: "Yes, if you wish it."
Kishori (startled): "What did you say? If I wish it?"
Dhanpati: "Yes, that is the matter."
Kishori: "How?"
Dhanpati: "Write a letter addressed to Indrajit Singh and give it to me, and write in it whatever I tell you."
Kishori: "What must I write in it?"
Dhanpati: "Only this much—'If you care for me, then...'"
Without further thought, come with this man to me and give whatever is asked—otherwise, abandon all hope of meeting me again!"
Kishori (after thinking for a while): "I understand now what your intention is. No, that can never happen. I cannot write such a letter and put my beloved Indrajit Singh in danger."
Dhanpati: "Then you cannot escape by any means."
Kishori: "So be it."
Dhanpati: "In fact, you will lose your life as well."
Kishori: "So be it! For the sake of Indrajit Singh, I am ready to give my life."

Hearing this, Dhanpati (Kundan)'s face turned red with rage. Looking at her companions, she said, "Now I cannot let her go. I am helpless. Bind her hands and feet and give me a sword!" At her command, her companions cruelly tied up poor Kishori's hands and feet, and Dhanpati, taking a sword, advanced to behead Kishori. At that very moment, one of Dhanpati's companions said, "No, it would not be proper to kill her like this. We can quickly gather dry wood, pile it up, lay her on it, and burn her. She will be reduced to ashes, and even the wind will not carry any trace of her remains."

Dhanpati approved of this suggestion and ordered them to do so. The heartless scoundrels soon gathered a heap of dry wood from the forest. Kishori, helpless and bound hand and foot, was laid upon it. One of Dhanpati's companions took out a small torch from his pouch and lit it, handing it to Dhanpati. Kishori, her mouth gagged, saw, heard, and endured all this in silence. When Dhanpati, torch in hand, approached the pyre, Kishori cried out in a loud voice—

"O Agnidev, bear witness! For the love of Kunwar Indrajit Singh, I gladly give my life. I know well that your flames are not fiercer than the pain of separation from my beloved. I shall feel no suffering as my life leaves me. Dearest Indrajit! Do not grieve for me, but rather, forget me completely!"

Alas! Even these heart-rending words, spoken by poor Kishori, overflowing with love, could not soften the hearts of those cruel wretches. And the vile Kundan—no, Dhanpati—placed the torch upon the pyre.
chapters.summary: Bound and threatened with immolation, Kishori defiantly proclaims her love for Indrajit Singh, steeling herself for death as the pyre is lit by Dhanpati.
